FIP.forcing_function: The approval order in docket EC26-92 is the trigger. Once the energy regulator signs off, the sale closes within days, and closing is self-executing: about $1.16 billion of debt at the asset level disappears with the business, roughly $291 to $300 million of parent debt is repaid, total debt falls from $3.814 billion to about $2.377 billion, and about $30 million a year of interest expense goes away. That is a mechanical change to the capital structure that no analyst has to be persuaded of. Two secondary forcing events follow inside twelve months. The first is the second-quarter report on 5 August 2026, which is where any change in the closing window will be disclosed and which is the nearest dated risk in either direction. The second is the sale of the Jefferson and Repauno terminals, which management has said are candidates over the next twelve to eighteen months with roughly $700 million of excess cash earmarked to cut parent debt further; the fourteen times multiple the power plant just fetched is the reference price for those. The deeper forcing function is arithmetic: once the conglomerate is reduced to railroads earning $220 million or more, the business becomes straightforwardly comparable to publicly traded regional railroads, and the discount that exists because nobody can model five unrelated assets at once stops being defensible.
FIP.consensus_delta: The market is treating this as a distressed balance sheet with a story attached, and is pricing the balance sheet while ignoring the mark. Three specific street assumptions look wrong. First, the shares have fallen since 30 April, when the sale was announced, from the mid-fives to $4.23, which means the market has assigned essentially no value to a signed, advised, financing-unconditional agreement with a single substantive approval outstanding. That is not scepticism about the deal; it is inattention to it, in a $500 million company that three analysts follow. Second, the market is anchoring on the reported loss rather than the transaction price. First-quarter loss per share of $1.32 against an expected $0.35 dominated the headlines, and the $82.5 million of quarterly interest and $45.9 million loss on extinguishing debt that caused it are the direct, one-time cost of the refinancing that makes the deleveraging possible. Third, and most concretely: the buyer is paying about fourteen times annualised earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for a merchant gas plant that had a planned outage in the quarter. If a power plant clears fourteen times in a private sale, the terminals and railroads are not worth the mid-single-digit implied multiple the public stub carries. Where we would part company with the bulls, however, is on how far this goes. The published street range of $10.00 to $13.00 appears to give little or no deduction for the $1.0 billion preferred sitting inside the rail holding company and the warrants over up to 20% of that entity, both of which rank ahead of the shareholder on the very asset the bull case is built on. Our disagreement with the market is therefore two-sided: the market is too pessimistic on the event and the private marks, and the sell-side is too generous on what actually reaches the common.
FIP.valley_of_death: The next three to nine months contain more dated risk than the catalyst window suggests. The nearest is 5 August 2026, when second-quarter results land: another quarter of heavy interest expense is certain, another negative operating cash flow quarter is likely after the negative $69.4 million printed in the first quarter, and this is the venue where a slip in the closing window would be disclosed. The regulatory path is the second hazard. No order has issued in docket EC26-92, and the PJM market monitor's 29 May filing asks for conditions on the approval. Conditions are more likely than refusal, but conditions take time to negotiate and the middle of the third quarter can become the fourth quarter without anything actually going wrong. Note also that the buyer publishes a wider window than the seller. Third, the maturity ladder does not wait. The Repauno term loan of $108.3 million matures 30 November 2026. The Jefferson bridge taken on 1 July 2026 matures 30 June 2027 and carries the benchmark rate plus 5.50% with step-ups, minimum liquidity of $20 million, and mandatory prepayment from excess cash flow; it is a bridge to a permanent financing that has not been arranged. Fourth, the liquidity language in the first-quarter filing states that management's planned actions, including the sale of Long Ridge, are considered probable and sufficient to meet obligations over the next twelve months. That is a sentence with a load-bearing conditional in it. If the sale slips past the year-end, auditors and lenders will revisit it, and that is the mechanism by which a timing problem becomes a solvency conversation. Fifth, Repauno's phase two reaches mechanical completion this autumn and does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027, so it consumes cash for two more quarters before it contributes any. The window between now and closing is where this position can lose a third of its value without the thesis being wrong.
FIP.positioning_washout: The forced selling has largely already happened, which is the constructive part of the setup. This was spun out of an aviation leasing company in 2022 and initially attracted an income-oriented, infrastructure-yield shareholder base. That base has been given every reason to leave: the dividend was eliminated, the balance sheet levered up, book equity is now negative $303.1 million, and the shares have fallen from a fifty-two-week high of $7.94 to $4.23, a decline of nearly half, with the fifty-day average at $4.51 and the two-hundred-day at $5.10, so the trend has been persistently downward rather than a single shock. At about a $500 million market value the company has fallen out of the size band where most institutional infrastructure and income mandates can hold it, and index membership at the small-cap end brings mechanical selling on rebalancing rather than support. The first-quarter miss of $1.32 against $0.35 was the kind of print that flushes the last of the quality-screen holders, and the shares traded down about 7.4% after hours on it. What that leaves is a thin, event-oriented holder base near the fifty-two-week low with a signed transaction pending, which is the composition you want going into a catalyst: the sellers who had to sell have sold, and the marginal buyer is now someone underwriting the event rather than the yield. The offsetting risk is liquidity itself: roughly 785,000 shares traded in the most recent session on a $500 million market value, so the same thinness that produced the overshoot down will produce a violent move on any adverse headline, and there is no natural long-term holder to absorb it.
FIP.moderator_conclusion: Buy it now, and size it as a levered stub with a live event rather than as an arbitrage with a floor. The event is genuine. A definitive agreement was signed on 29 April 2026 to sell the Long Ridge power plant to MARA for about $1.52 billion, the regulatory application was filed on 8 May in docket EC26-92, the buyer cleared its bondholder consents in June, no financing contingency exists, and management has guided to approval by the middle of the third quarter. Nothing about it has fired, and the shares have actually fallen since the announcement, so none of the re-rating has been spent. At $4.23, close to the fifty-two-week low of $3.90 and against a high of $7.94, you are being paid to wait for a transaction that reduces total debt from $3.8 billion to $2.4 billion and saves about $30 million of interest a year, on a company whose surviving railroads grew earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation 31% year over year. There is no wash-out worth waiting for; this is the wash-out. Two things keep this from being the maximum-conviction version of this setup. The first is the floor. The entry carried into this review assumes $3.90 of downside protection, and that number is a chart level, not a recovery value. Book equity is negative $303.1 million, there is no net cash, operating cash flow was negative $69.4 million last quarter, and the filing's own liquidity assurance is expressly conditioned on this sale closing. A deal-break realistically prices the shares at $2.50 to $3.00, which turns a claimed reward-to-risk of roughly 18 to 1 into about 3 to 1. That is still an attractive trade; it is not a defined-risk one, and the difference matters for sizing. The second is the capital structure that survives the sale. A $1.0 billion preferred, carried at $970.5 million with a $1.4 billion redemption value and paying 10% rising to 14%, sits inside the rail holding company, ahead of the parent's claim on the very asset the bull case rests on, and the same holder has warrants over up to 20% of that entity's common units. Value the railroads at fourteen times and forget those two items and you get the street's $10.00 to $13.00; remember them and you get closer to $6.50. Our base case is $6.50 with a range of $5.00 to $9.00, and the $9.00 end requires not just the sale closing but the rail run-rate arriving and the terminals being monetised near the multiple the power plant just fetched. Watch 5 August, when second-quarter results are reported, for any change in the closing window, and watch docket EC26-92 for the approval order and for whether the market monitor's requested conditions are attached. Enter now, keep the position modest, and treat a slip of the window past the third quarter as a reason to reassess rather than to add.
FIP.interrogator_dossier:
# FTAI Infrastructure Inc. (FIP) — Event Dossier

*Prepared 27 July 2026. This is an event-driven special situation, not a quality or compounding case. The question is whether a signed, regulator-gated asset sale closes inside the window, what the shares are worth once it does, and what actually catches the stock if it does not.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

FTAI Infrastructure was spun out of FTAI Aviation in August 2022 as a collection of five hard-asset businesses: two freight railroads, two river terminals, and a gas-fired power plant. The story it told at the spin was a build-out story — spend capital now, harvest later.

The story today is the opposite, and the turn happened fast. Over the past twelve months management has pivoted from assembling assets to selling them and paying down debt:

- **August 2025** — agreed to buy The Wheeling Corporation, owner of the Wheeling & Lake Erie Railway (a Class II regional railroad with more than 1,000 miles of track across Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia and Maryland), for $1.05 billion in cash. To fund it the company raised $2.25 billion: roughly $1.25 billion of new debt at the parent and $1.0 billion of preferred equity sold to funds managed by Ares Management, issued not at the parent but inside the rail holding company. The deal closed 25 August 2025.
- **30 April 2026** — agreed to sell Long Ridge Energy & Power (a 485–505 megawatt combined-cycle gas plant at Hannibal, Ohio, working interests in gas wells, and roughly 1,600 acres on the Ohio River) to a subsidiary of MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion, before closing adjustments.
- **1 July 2026** — refinanced $217.9 million of Jefferson terminal bonds with a $230 million secured bridge loan from Jefferies Finance, maturing 30 June 2027.
- **Stated next step** — Jefferson and Repauno are described as sale candidates over the next twelve to eighteen months, with roughly $700 million of expected excess cash earmarked to cut parent-level debt further.

So the arc is: conglomerate assembled, conglomerate now being taken apart, with freight rail as the intended survivor. That is a genuine change of direction, and it is the reason the shares are worth analysing at all.

---

## 2. THE EVENT: IS IT REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

**Real.** Yes. This is a signed definitive agreement, not a process or an exploration. MARA USA Corporation entered an equity purchase agreement on 29 April 2026 to acquire 100% of Long Ridge Energy & Power from FTAI Infrastructure subsidiaries for a base price of approximately $1.5 billion plus assumption of Long Ridge's existing debt. Both sides announced it the following morning. Jefferies and Lazard advised the seller; Skadden, Arps was seller's counsel.

**Binding, with a short conditions list.** The announced conditions are clearance under the Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust waiting period, approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for the change of control of the power plant, and customary closing conditions. On the first-quarter call management was unusually plain about how narrow the gate is: chief executive Ken Nicholson said the energy regulator "needs to approve the change of control" and that there are "no reasons why it should be a prolonged process." No financing contingency has been disclosed — MARA is not conditioning the purchase on raising money.

**Dated — but by guidance, not by contract.** This is the single most important qualification in the file, and the two sides do not say the same thing:

| Source | Stated timing |
|---|---|
| FTAI Infrastructure, 30 April 2026 release and first-quarter call | Close in the **third quarter of 2026**; regulatory approval expected **"mid-third quarter"** |
| MARA Holdings, same transaction | Close in the **second half of 2026** |

A seller guiding to one quarter and a buyer guiding to a half-year is not a contradiction, but it is a gap, and the looser of the two is the one that governs how patient the buyer has to be. The 30 September date this candidate carries is the seller's guided quarter-end, not a contractual drop-dead date that anyone has published.

**Where the approval actually stands.** The application under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act was filed with the energy regulator on 8 May 2026 in docket EC26-92, with a comment deadline of 29 May 2026. As of today no final order granting authorisation has surfaced in that docket. Two dated developments since:

- **29 May 2026** — the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments urging the regulator to approve the sale only on condition that the buyer commit to keeping the plant's output in PJM's markets. The concern is obvious: a bitcoin and data-centre operator buying a power plant has every incentive to take that power behind the meter and out of the grid. This is a live conditioning risk. It is more likely to attach conditions or add weeks than to kill the deal, but it is exactly the kind of intervention that turns "mid-third quarter" into "fourth quarter."
- **Early June 2026** — MARA completed a consent solicitation and obtained the necessary bondholder approvals to amend Long Ridge Energy's 8.75% notes due 2032. That removes a financing obstacle on the buyer's side and is a meaningful, dated piece of progress.

**Verdict on the event: a hard, dated catalyst (a firm, scheduled event) that has not yet fired.** The agreement is signed, the regulatory clock is running, the buyer has cleared its own financing hurdle, and the seller has guided to a close inside the window. What it is not is contractually date-certain, and the guided window is the tighter of two published views.

**Next scheduled checkpoint:** second-quarter results after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, with the call the following morning. That is nine days away and is where any slippage will be disclosed.

---

## 3. CREDIBILITY OF THE SPONSOR

Management is Fortress-affiliated, led by Ken Nicholson. The record cuts both ways and the split is important.

**On transactions they deliver.** They said they would buy the Wheeling railroad and they closed it. They said they would raise $2.25 billion to fund it and they raised it. They said they would sell Long Ridge and they signed it — at roughly fourteen times the plant's annualised first-quarter earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, which is a strong price for a merchant gas plant and a genuine validation that private buyers pay far more for these assets than the public market does. They said they would refinance the Jefferson bonds and they did, on 1 July.

**On the profit and loss statement they do not.** First-quarter 2026 loss per share was $1.32 against a consensus expectation of about $0.35 — a miss of nearly four times. Revenue nearly doubled to $188.4 million, but the company still lost $127.2 million, driven by $82.5 million of quarterly interest expense and a $45.9 million loss on extinguishing debt during the refinancing. Cash from operations was negative $69.4 million in the quarter. Consolidated adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation were $70.6 million, which management notes would have topped $80 million but for a planned outage at Long Ridge — a fair adjustment, but it also means the reported number and the number management wants you to use have diverged for several quarters running.

**The pattern to name.** Every financing has been done at a price that protects the lender or the preferred holder and leaves the common shareholder with the residual risk: a 9.75% parent term loan, a bridge at the benchmark rate plus 5.50% with a step-up, and a $1.0 billion preferred that pays 10% for three years, 12% in years four through six, and 14% thereafter. Management has been reliable about *getting deals done* and unreliable about *what those deals cost the equity*. Score the deal execution high and the capital-structure stewardship low.

---

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — WHAT ACTUALLY BACKSTOPS THE PRICE

This is where this candidate's own file needs correcting.

The floor carried in the watch entry is $3.90. That is the fifty-two-week low, a chart level. It is not an asset-backed recovery value, and nothing in the filings supports it as one. Here is what the balance sheet actually says as of 31 March 2026:

| Claim | Amount | Where it sits |
|---|---|---|
| Total debt | $3.84 billion | Parent term loan $1.315bn at 9.75% due Feb 2028; Long Ridge facilities and notes; Jefferson bonds; Repauno term loan $108m due Nov 2026 |
| Preferred sold to Ares | Carrying $970.5 million, redemption value $1.4 billion | Inside the **rail** holding company, ahead of the parent's claim on the crown jewel |
| Series B preferred | Carrying $152.6 million, redemption value $192.0 million | Parent |
| Total equity | **Negative $303.1 million** | — |
| Common shares outstanding | 118.2 million (6 May 2026) | Market value about $500 million at $4.23 |

Three things follow.

**First, the common stock is a thin slice at the bottom of a very tall stack.** Roughly $3.8 billion of debt and about $1.1 billion of preferred sit ahead of a $500 million equity market value. Book equity is already negative. There is no cash pile, no net-cash floor, and no contractual payout to the common in any scenario.

**Second, the Ares preferred is structurally senior to the parent on the best asset.** It was issued by the rail holding company, not by FTAI Infrastructure. So on the railroads — the business management says is the future — the parent's claim ranks behind a $1.0 billion instrument that compounds at 10% and steps to 12% and then 14%. Holders can demand redemption after the seventh anniversary (25 August 2032) and, if not redeemed within 120 days, can force a sale of the company. That is a long fuse, but it is a fuse.

**Third, and least discussed: Ares also holds warrants over up to 20% of the rail holding company's common units** (172,500 units at an exercise price of $857.748, exercisable on the earlier of the fifth anniversary or full repayment of the permanent debt financing, expiring 25 August 2035). So the parent's economic share of the railroads can fall toward 80%. Any sum-of-the-parts that values the rail business and forgets this is overstating what reaches the common by roughly a fifth of the rail stub.

**What the real floor looks like.** If the sale to MARA breaks or slips indefinitely, the following are simultaneously true: parent debt stays at $1.31 billion costing 9.75%; the $30 million a year of interest saving does not arrive; the Jefferson bridge still matures 30 June 2027 and has to be termed out again; the Repauno term loan matures 30 November 2026; operating cash flow is negative; and the language in the filings that liquidity is sufficient rests explicitly on the sale happening — management states that its planned actions, "including the sale of Long Ridge," are considered probable and sufficient to meet obligations over the next twelve months. Strip the sale out of that sentence and the sentence stops working.

A deal-break therefore is not a $3.90 event. A reasonable break price is **$2.50 to $3.00**, and that is a judgement about where a levered stub trades under refinancing stress, not a value anyone can point to on a balance sheet. The honest statement is that this position has a *defined catalyst* but **not** a *defined-risk floor*. Anyone sizing it as though $3.90 catches the fall is mis-measuring the trade by a wide margin.

---

## 5. CONCERNS AND POSITIVES

**Concerns**

- The stated floor is a chart level, not an asset value. Recovery risk-reward computed off it is inflated several-fold.
- Book equity is negative $303.1 million and operating cash flow was negative $69.4 million in the first quarter of 2026.
- The going-concern-adjacent language in the first-quarter filing is expressly conditioned on the Long Ridge sale closing.
- The energy regulator has not issued its order, and the PJM market monitor has formally asked for conditions on it (29 May 2026).
- Buyer and seller publish different closing windows — a half-year versus a quarter.
- The Ares preferred and its 20% rail warrant sit between the common and the best asset, and the preferred accretes at 10% rising to 14%.
- The Jefferson refinancing on 1 July was a bridge to June 2027, not a permanent solution — the same problem returns in eleven months.
- Management has said part of the proceeds may fund acquisitions rather than debt reduction. For a company at this leverage, that is the wrong instinct and the market has treated it as such.
- The shares are down from a fifty-two-week high of $7.94 to $4.23 and have kept falling *since* the sale was announced on 30 April. The announcement did not re-rate anything.

**Positives**

- The sale is signed, priced, and advised, with a narrow conditions list and no disclosed financing contingency.
- The price paid — about $1.52 billion for a business generating $26.4 million of adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the first quarter — implies roughly fourteen times annualised. That is a hard, third-party mark showing private buyers value these assets far above where the public stub trades.
- The buyer has already cleared its bondholder consents (June 2026), removing a financing obstacle.
- The transaction removes about $1.16 billion of asset-level debt and funds roughly $291–300 million of parent debt repayment, cutting total debt from $3.814 billion to about $2.377 billion and saving roughly $30 million a year in interest.
- The surviving business is genuinely good. Rail adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation grew 31% year over year to $40.2 million in the first quarter, with $23 million of identified annual cost savings ($10 million already taken) and more than $50 million of further integration upside identified.
- Selling the power plant removes the most volatile and most capital-hungry piece of the portfolio and sharpens the company into a rail-and-terminals story that is far easier to value.
- Sell-side coverage was initiated by Citizens on 15 July 2026 with a favourable rating and a $10 target, using a fourteen times rail multiple — deliberately below the fifteen times and above at which comparable regional railroads have historically traded.

---

## 6. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Financing at the subsidiary, not the parent.** Both the big 2025 raise (rail holding company preferred) and the 2026 Jefferson bridge were done one level down. That preserves parent optionality but it also means each asset is progressively encumbered before the parent's claim attaches. Watch whether the next terminal financing follows the same pattern.
- **The vocabulary changed.** A year ago the language was growth, build-out, and phases. On the first-quarter 2026 call it is deleveraging, cost savings, run-rate, and monetisation. That shift is real and it usually precedes either a successful simplification or a forced one.
- **Management would not put a leverage target on the record.** Asked about it, they spoke about metrics continuing to improve rather than naming a number. For a company whose entire equity story is a deleveraging story, declining to name the destination is notable.
- **Nobody asked about the Ares preferred on the call and management did not raise it.** The single largest claim standing between the common shareholder and the railroads went undiscussed. That silence is itself information about how the market is modelling this name.

---

## 7. WHAT THE DIRECTOR MUST WEIGH

The trade is honest about itself if you state it plainly: **a signed, regulator-gated asset sale expected to close inside the next ten weeks, on a stock sitting near its fifty-two-week low, where the catalyst is credible but the floor is not.**

The upside case does not depend on the sale alone. Closing removes about $1.4 billion of debt and $30 million of annual interest, but it does not by itself take a $4.23 stock to $9. What takes it there is closing *plus* the rail business hitting its $220 million-plus run-rate and the terminals being monetised at anything near the multiple the power plant just fetched. The sale matters most as proof that the private mark is real.

The single thing to weigh before sizing: **this is not defined-risk.** The catalyst is dated and live, which is the reason to own it. But the loss is not bounded by anything you can verify. Size it as a levered stub with an event, not as an arbitrage with a floor.

On the conventional questions this candidate is deliberately not built to answer: the surviving franchise — regional freight rail with captive industrial shippers, irreplaceable track, and regulatory barriers to entry — is a narrow but real competitive advantage, and it is stable rather than eroding. There is no structural force threatening its terminal value; if anything, selling the merchant power plant removes the portfolio's most exposed piece. But none of that is the thesis. The thesis is the event.

The 2024 credit agreement carries a maximum net first-lien leverage covenant tested at the end of every quarter, so a bad season does not merely dent earnings - it compresses the headroom in a maintenance test. That eviction of the yield-focused base is complete, not pending - it is the single biggest reason the shares de-rated from the low thirties. Similarly, the merger-arbitrage and merger-synergy holders who bought the 2024 Cedar Fair and Six Flags combination have had two years and a $1.19B goodwill write-off in the third quarter of 2025 to leave. With a market value under $1.8B, that flow moves the price. There is also index risk - a company this size with negative book momentum can face mechanical selling on a downgrade out of mid-cap benchmarks. On the constructive side, a register that has already lost its income holders and taken its impairment is a cleaner starting point than one still shedding them. But 'the washout has happened' is a reason to look, not a reason to own - and it does not create a floor.

Verification does not support either half of that. On the event: JANA Partners' demand that the board sell the company is real and still live, but it is undated, non-binding, and dependent on a buyer who has not appeared to finance an enterprise value above seven billion dollars. More importantly, the board has answered it without conceding it. The proxy window that could have forced the question in 2026 has closed, and the next one is unannounced and roughly six to nine months away. On the floor, which matters more: there isn't one. The shares traded at $12.51 within the past twelve months, 29% below the level the write-up treats as protected. Behind that price sits $116.5M of cash against $5.53B of total debt, book equity of $279M, retained earnings of negative $2.03B after the $1.19B write-off in the third quarter of 2025, and trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against interest expense near $380M a year. The only recent arm's-length transaction in these assets - EPR Properties paying $342M gross for seven parks - clears at roughly eight and a half times, below the ten and a half times the $31 target requires. Run the probabilities honestly and fair value lands at about $18 - a fifth of the outcomes around $30 on a sale, two fifths around $22 if the turnaround works, two fifths around $9 if attendance keeps sliding. That mean is within a dollar of the $17.59 market price. There is no edge in the valuation, and the near-term skew is negative: second-quarter results land 6 August 2026, July's wildfire-smoke attendance damage lands in the November print, Citi cut to $19 on 19 July and Guggenheim cut as well, and the quarterly net first-lien leverage covenant is tested through all of it. None of this says the business is worthless. The first quarter of 2026 was genuinely better - attendance up 4%, spending per visitor up 6% to $69.26, the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M - and the land under Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm and Magic Mountain cannot be replicated. If the new team closes the margin gap it has publicly acknowledged, this is a much better stock in two years. But that is a leveraged turnaround underwritten on execution, and it belongs in a different book with different sizing, not in an event sleeve where the whole justification is a bounded loss. What would change the answer: a formally announced strategic review or sale process; an identified bidder with committed financing; a JANA slate filed for the 2027 annual meeting; or the shares in the low teens after a capitulation print, where the reward-to-risk that was claimed at $17.59 would actually exist.
FUN.interrogator_dossier:
# FUN - Six Flags Entertainment Corporation

## Event-driven special situation: activist campaign for a sale of the company

**Interrogator dossier - forensic read of the EVENT, not the franchise.**
Prepared 28 July 2026. All prices and filings verified against live sources on that date.

---

## 0. WHAT THIS TRADE ACTUALLY IS

Six Flags Entertainment trades under the ticker FUN because the surviving legal entity of the
July 2024 merger is the old Cedar Fair vehicle. The company runs regional amusement parks
across North America - Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm, Magic Mountain, Great Adventure and
roughly forty others after recent disposals.

The reason this name reached our board is not the parks. It is JANA Partners, an activist
investment firm, which on 21 October 2025 disclosed an economic interest of about 9% alongside
the retired NFL player Travis Kelce, former Gap and Lululemon chief executive Glenn Murphy, and
technology executive Dave Habiger. On 17 March 2026 JANA sent the board a public letter
demanding it explore an outright sale of the company and remove the board chair. Our board
entry values a successful outcome at $31 a share against a supposed downside floor of $16.50,
implying reward-to-risk of about 2.6 to 1.

The core question for this dossier is narrow: is that event real, dated and binding, and is
that floor real? The answer to both is no.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC - HOW THE EVENT HAS ACTUALLY DEVELOPED

The campaign has moved through four visible stages, and the direction of travel is away from a
sale, not toward one.

**Stage one - the stake (21 October 2025).** JANA discloses roughly 9% economic interest with a
celebrity-plus-operator group. The framing is collaborative: work with the board and management
to improve the guest experience and enhance value.

**Stage two - the group dissolves into the company (24 November 2025).** In its own release
applauding the hire of John Reilly as president and chief executive, JANA discloses that Glenn
Murphy "has de-grouped from the JANA-led investor group to advance discussions with Six Flags on
a potential senior leadership role with the Board," and that Dave Habiger "remains de-grouped
from the JANA-led investor group to enable him to pursue a complementary, but separate,
opportunity involving the Company." This is the language of a settlement, not a proxy fight. Two
of the three named operating partners left the activist group to take company roles within five
weeks of the stake being announced.

**Stage three - the escalation (17 March 2026).** With the shares still falling, JANA publicly
demands an immediate sale process and the ouster of the board chair, naming Murphy and Habiger
as prospective directors. This is the high-water mark of the campaign and the moment our board
entry was almost certainly seeded.

**Stage four - the board absorbs the pressure without selling (March to July 2026).** The
company's answer has been governance and asset sales, not a sale process:

| Date | Action | What it substitutes for |
|---|---|---|
| Nov 2025 / Dec 2025 | John Reilly appointed president and chief executive | New management instead of new owners |
| 4 March 2026 | Agreements to sell seven parks to EPR Properties, $331.4M cash ($342M gross) | Piecemeal asset sales instead of a whole-company sale |
| 25 March 2026 | Richard "Dick" Haddrill named executive chairman, effective immediately | Chair replacement conceded, sale not conceded |
| April 2026 | US portion of the EPR sale closes | Cash in, but only about 6% of net debt |
| 19 May 2026 | Cooperation agreement with H Partners; Rehan Jaffer joins the board after the annual meeting, replacing Arik Ruchim | A different activist is settled with a board seat |
| 26 May 2026 | 2026 annual meeting of stockholders held | The 2026 proxy window closes |
| 17 June 2026 | Ash Walia appointed chief financial officer | |
| 15 July 2026 | Mark Pauls appointed chief operating officer | |

Read the table as a whole and the pattern is unmistakable. Every demand JANA made has been
answered with something other than the thing it asked for. The chair was replaced - with a
turnaround executive chairman, not with a banker running a process. Board refreshment happened -
through a cooperation agreement with a *different* activist, H Partners. Assets were sold - seven
peripheral parks, not the company. And no sale process, strategic review, or data room has been
announced in any filing or release through 28 July 2026.

---

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED AND BINDING?

**Real: yes, partially.** JANA is a serious, well-resourced activist with a genuine 9% economic
interest and a public demand on the record. The campaign has not been withdrawn. That is more
than nothing.

**Dated: no.** There is no date attached to anything. Our own board entry carries the catalyst as
undated, and the verification confirms it. Worse, the one date that mattered has passed: the 2026
annual meeting was held on 26 May 2026. Director nominations for that meeting closed months
earlier, and no JANA slate went to a vote. The next natural forcing point - the nomination window
for the 2027 annual meeting - sits roughly six to nine months out and has no announced date.

**Binding: no.** Nothing here is contractual. A sale requires a third party to appear, agree a
price, and finance a transaction with an enterprise value above seven billion dollars against an
equity market value of under two billion. No bidder has been publicly identified. Reports of
"private equity interest" trace to commentary about the turnaround-heavy composition of the new
board, not to a disclosed approach.

The honest classification is a soft, non-binding, serially open-ended catalyst: real pressure,
no date, no contract, and a counterparty that does not yet exist.

---

## 3. THE FLOOR - THIS IS WHERE THE THESIS BREAKS

The board entry claims a downside floor of $16.50 against a live price of $17.59. That would mean
risking about 6% to make about 76%. It is not credible, and the tape has already falsified it.

**Falsification one - the stock has already traded 29% below the claimed floor.** The 52-week
range is $12.51 to $31.99. The claimed floor of $16.50 was breached within the last twelve months.
A level the security has recently traded straight through is not a floor.

**Falsification two - there is no asset backstop, because the debt eats it.** From the balance
sheet at 29 March 2026:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Cash and equivalents | $116.5M |
| Total debt (incl. finance leases) | $5.53B |
| Net debt | $5.42B |
| Minority interest | $235M |
| Total shareholders' equity | $279M |
| Enterprise value at $17.59 | ~$7.21B |
| Market capitalisation | ~$1.80B |

The equity is a thin slice - roughly a quarter of enterprise value - sitting on top of $5.4B of
net debt. That is the definition of a levered stub. Small changes in the multiple the market
applies to earnings swing the equity violently. Working the arithmetic on a full-year 2026
adjusted profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (adjusted EBITDA) of about
$820M, and using year-end net claims of roughly $5.4B including the minority interest:

| Multiple applied | Implied enterprise value | Implied value per share |
|---|---|---|
| 7.5x | $6.15B | ~$7 |
| 8.5x | $6.97B | ~$15 |
| 9.25x | $7.59B | ~$21 |
| 10.5x | $8.61B | ~$31 |

Two things fall out. First, the $31 target is not a mystery - it is simply a takeover multiple of
about 10.5 times. Second, and far more important, a single turn of multiple compression from
today takes the shares to roughly $7. There is no cash, no net asset value, and no unencumbered
collateral underneath this equity to stop that. The relevant market data point cuts the wrong
way: EPR Properties paid $342M gross for seven parks, a price consistent with roughly eight and a
half times their earnings - below, not above, where the whole company trades today.

**Falsification three - the earnings themselves are unstable.** Free cash flow is close to zero
once capital spending is taken out: capital expenditure absorbed about 93% of operating cash flow
over the trailing twelve months, leaving trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M against a $1.8B
market value. Interest expense runs about $95M a quarter, or close to $380M a year. The company
wrote off a very large amount of merger goodwill in the third quarter of 2025, posting a $1.19B
net loss (a loss of $11.80 a share) in that quarter alone. Shareholders' equity is down to $279M
and retained earnings stand at negative $2.03B.

The verified floor is not $16.50. On the evidence it is somewhere between $10 and $12 - the recent
low of $12.51 with no support beneath it - and in a genuine attendance recession it is
meaningfully lower. The trade as written on the board risks roughly 35% to make roughly 75%, not
6% to make 76%.

---

## 4. CREDIBILITY OF THE SPONSOR AND THE COUNTERPARTY

**JANA: credible as an investor, compromised as a forcing agent.** The firm has a long record and
a real position. But it let two of its three named operating partners de-group into company roles
within weeks, and it did not run a slate at the 2026 annual meeting. A separate activist, H
Partners, took the board seat that was available. An activist whose personnel end up inside the
company, and whose board seat goes to someone else, has been managed rather than obeyed.

**The board: credibly resistant.** Executive chairman Haddrill, a new chief executive, a new chief
financial officer and a new chief operating officer, all appointed within nine months, form a
management team assembled to fix the business, not to sell it. Boards that intend to sell hire
bankers and announce reviews. This one hired operators.

**Management on the numbers: early and mixed, but not evasive.** The first quarter of 2026 was
genuinely better - revenue up 12% to $225.6M, attendance up 4% to 2.9 million visits, spending
per visitor up 6% to $69.26, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M to a $123M adjusted EBITDA
loss. The first quarter is the smallest quarter of the year and carries little information. Mr
Reilly has been candid that the 27% margin the company earned in 2025 is not acceptable against
regional peers in the low thirties, which is honest, but he has not put a number or a date on the
improvement.

**The tape since has gone the other way.** On 19 July 2026 Citi cut its price target from $24 to
$19 with a neutral rating, and Guggenheim also cut on softer attendance, citing hazardous air
quality from Ontario wildfires affecting fourteen parks across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes
during the peak season. Jefferies carries a below-consensus full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA
estimate of about $865M and warns that street attendance and revenue assumptions are too high.

---

## 5. RED FLAGS

- **The claimed floor is not a floor.** The shares traded at $12.51 within the last year, 29%
  below the $16.50 the board entry treats as protected.
- **The proxy window for 2026 has closed.** The annual meeting was held 26 May 2026 without a
  contested vote. The nearest hard forcing point is the 2027 nomination window, unannounced.
- **The activist group has been partially absorbed.** Two of three named operating partners
  de-grouped in November 2025 to pursue roles with the company.
- **Leverage is the dominant variable.** Net debt of $5.42B against about $820M of expected
  annual earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation is roughly six and a half
  times. The credit agreement carries a maximum net first-lien leverage covenant tested every
  quarter, which limits how much room a bad season leaves.
- **No free cash flow to deleverage with.** Trailing free cash flow of roughly $29M cannot move a
  $5.4B debt load. Deleveraging depends entirely on further asset sales.
- **The dividend is gone.** The payout is zero, which for a business that spent decades as an
  income vehicle means the natural holder base has already been evicted.
- **Peak-season demand is deteriorating right now.** Two brokers cut targets in July on soft
  attendance, in the quarter that makes the year.
- **The asset-sale comparable prices the company below the target multiple.** EPR paid roughly
  eight and a half times for the seven-park package; the $31 target needs about ten and a half.

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

- The activist campaign is live and has not been withdrawn; the 9% economic interest remains
  disclosed.
- The board has visibly conceded on governance - a new executive chairman in March 2026 and a
  cooperation agreement seating H Partners' Rehan Jaffer in May 2026 - which is the pattern that
  sometimes precedes a sale by a year or more.
- The asset base has genuine local scarcity. Cedar Point, Knott's Berry Farm and Magic Mountain
  sit on land that cannot be replicated, which is why a financial buyer can underwrite a bid at
  all.
- Operating momentum in the first quarter of 2026 was real - attendance, pricing and spending per
  visitor all moved the right way, and the seasonal loss narrowed by $48M.
- The seven-park disposal closed and brought in $331.4M of cash, proving the board will sell
  assets under pressure.
- A management team built for a turnaround is now fully in place: chief executive from December
  2025, chief financial officer from 17 June 2026, chief operating officer from 15 July 2026.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling detail is the substitution pattern. Every time JANA asked for the company to be
sold, the company gave it something adjacent and cheaper: a chair, a director seat to a rival
activist, seven parks. That is a board that has read the leverage on its own balance sheet and
concluded that a forced sale at a depressed multiple hands the entire premium to the debt. With
net debt at roughly six and a half times earnings, a buyer at eight and a half times leaves
shareholders with a stub; a buyer at ten and a half times leaves them with $31. The board is
holding out for the second, and it can afford to wait far longer than a shareholder can.

The second signal is the H Partners agreement. When a company settles with the second activist
on the register while the first is publicly demanding a sale, it has found a way to look
responsive without doing the thing that was demanded. That is skilful defence, and it is bearish
for anyone underwriting a near-term sale.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: deteriorating.** Not because the business is collapsing - the first quarter
genuinely improved - but because the *event* has weakened at every step since March 2026. The
demand was made, the proxy window passed without a vote, the board answered with governance and
asset sales, and the shares have fallen from the low twenties toward the bottom of their range
while two brokers cut targets on soft peak-season attendance.

**The single thing the director must weigh:** this position is not the defined-risk special
situation the board entry describes. The catalyst is undated, non-binding and dependent on a
buyer who has not appeared, and the downside floor of $16.50 has already been broken by the
market within the past twelve months. Sizing it as a 6%-risk trade would be a serious error. It
is a levered equity stub in which one turn of multiple compression is worth roughly $10 a share.

**On the franchise, for completeness:** the moat is narrow and real - irreplaceable regional
land and local scarcity - but the evidence says it is eroding, with a 27% margin against peers
above 30%, a return on invested capital of about 4.4%, and attendance that needs weather and
consumer health to cooperate. The structural threat from competing experience spending is
manageable rather than terminal; this is a leverage and execution problem, not a melting
industry.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 2 | TRAJECTORY: DETERIORATING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: ERODING | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

GDOT.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a signed, shareholder-approved break-up closes on schedule and pays out more than the market currently marks it at. Green Dot is being dismantled into two halves under an Agreement and Plan of Merger dated 23 November 2025: Smith Ventures buys the non-bank financial-technology business for $690 million in cash, and CommerceOne Financial Corporation, a small Birmingham, Alabama bank holding company, takes Green Dot Bank into a newly listed parent (to trade on the New York Stock Exchange as CONE). Each Green Dot share converts into $8.11 in cash plus 0.2215 shares of that new company.

Four things make completion the strong base case. First, the vote is banked: at special meetings on 23 June 2026, Green Dot holders approved by 40,869,891 for against 139,918 opposed - over 99% of votes cast, roughly 72% of shares outstanding - and CommerceOne holders approved unanimously. Second, there is no financing hole. The $8.11 is funded directly out of the $690 million purchase price, which is split $155 million into the combined bank as regulatory capital, $65 million to repay debt, and $470 million to Green Dot shareholders. No lender can withdraw a commitment because there is no commitment to withdraw. Third, two independent buyers each underwrote a different half, so the price was tested twice, and the terms have not moved in the eight months since signing. Fourth, a contractual outside date of 23 November 2026 - automatically extending 90 days to 23 February 2027 if regulatory approvals remain outstanding - bounds how long capital can sit trapped.

If the deal closes and the new bank is valued anywhere near the bankers' own work, the payout is well above today's price. Citi's dividend-discount analysis, disclosed in June 2026 supplemental filings, valued the combined bank's equity at $590 million to $755 million, which implies total consideration of $15.45 to $17.51 per Green Dot share. Management's own illustrative range, given on the 24 November 2025 call, was $14.23 to $19.18. The $155 million capital injection lands inside the bank you end up owning, and the seven-year exclusive sponsor-bank agreement with the privatised fintech gives the new company a contracted revenue stream from day one rather than a standing start.

The conditions that must hold are narrow and specific: the Federal Reserve, the Alabama State Banking Department and the Utah Department of Financial Institutions all approve; the new shares list without incident; and the newly public bank finds enough natural buyers in its first weeks of trading that the forced supply from Green Dot's existing holders does not overwhelm it.
GDOT.bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require the deal to break. It only requires the stock leg to be worth what the market already says it is worth - which is what makes this position unattractive at $13.16 rather than merely risky.

Only $8.11 of today's price, about 62%, is contractual cash. The other 38% is 0.2215 shares of a company that does not trade yet, cannot be hedged (there is no listed CommerceOne security to sell short), cannot be elected out of, and carries no collar, no cash election and no contingent value right. Back out the cash and the market is paying $5.05 for that stub, implying about $22.80 per new share and roughly $399 million for the entire new bank - some 32% below the low end of Citi's own valuation. That persistent discount is not inattention. Roughly 12.6 million shares, about 72% of the new company's register, are about to be handed to people who bought a Provo, Utah fintech: small-cap growth funds, payments funds, and index funds that will be mechanically deleted from Green Dot and have no mandate to hold a two-state community bank. The supply is forced and the natural buyer base has to be built from zero.

The approval risk is also real rather than procedural. Green Dot Bank operates under a Federal Reserve consent order dated 19 July 2024 carrying a $44 million civil money penalty, covering compliance risk management, unfair and deceptive practices in prepaid card marketing and servicing, and anti-money-laundering failures including inadequate disclosure of refund-processing fees between 2017 and 2022. The order required a third-party root-cause review, an outside transaction-monitoring firm and written board-oversight plans. The acquirer inheriting that problem is a bank founded in 2018 with under $1 billion of assets, buying a bank with roughly $6.65 billion of assets and $4.6 billion of deposit-type liabilities as of 31 March 2026. A much smaller acquirer absorbing a larger bank under live enforcement is exactly the profile that slows an application. The guided close has already drifted about one quarter, from an expected second quarter of 2026 at announcement to the third quarter now, and as of 28 July 2026 no Federal Reserve order has been published and no approval has been announced.

If it does break, there is no contractual backstop. Tangible book value is about $10.03 a share ($940.5 million equity less $369.0 million intangibles over roughly 57 million shares). The undisturbed price of $11.80 on 21 November 2025 is not a safe anchor either - the shares had already run from $10.56 on 18 November that same week, and that price embedded eight months of public strategic-review optionality. A failed process on a business with negative trailing return on equity of about -7.7% plausibly resolves to $10.50-$11.00, with the 52-week low of $9.31 as the overshoot. Against that, the shares at $13.16 sit about 20% above the floor and above both the 50-day ($13.06) and 200-day ($12.34) averages, having been flagged repeatedly by momentum screens through June and July 2026. You would be buying strength, not capitulation, in a name whose upside is contractually capped at the offer.

That single event releases the $8.11 cash payment and triggers the New York Stock Exchange listing of New CommerceOne under the ticker CONE. Three separate Federal Reserve approvals are required: for the merger subsidiary to become a bank holding company by acquiring Green Dot Bank, for New CommerceOne to become a bank holding company by indirectly acquiring both banks, and for the merger of CommerceOne into New CommerceOne. Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust clearance and the exchange listing approval also sit in the queue. The hard boundary is the 23 November 2026 termination date, extending to 23 February 2027 if approvals are still pending. The complication is that this forcing function resolves the deal but not the valuation: the moment approval lands, the price question shifts entirely to what an orphaned community bank stub prints at in its first week of trading.
GDOT.consensus_delta:
The interesting disagreement here is not between us and Wall Street - it is between the market and the company's own bankers, and the market is winning the argument.

The published sell-side and management framing says Green Dot holders are receiving $14.23 to $19.18 a share (chief financial officer, 24 November 2025), with Citi's dividend-discount work implying $15.45 to $17.51. The shares have never traded at any of those levels. They closed at $11.81 on announcement day, one cent above the prior close - the deal was worth essentially nothing to the market on the day it was struck - and eight months later, with both votes banked, they sit at $13.16, still below the floor of management's range. That is not a slow-moving market. It is a considered, persistent discount on the one part of the package nobody can observe.

Where the street assumption is factually weak is the treatment of the stock leg as though it were currency. Only $8.11 is money. The rest is 0.2215 shares of an unlisted bank, and the valuations quoted in support of the higher numbers are forward constructs: Performance Trust applied 110%-130% of projected 31 December 2029 tangible book value, and Citi used a 2.5% perpetuity growth rate against a 12.63% discount rate. Those are answers to 'what might this bank be worth in three-plus years if it executes', not 'what will 12.6 million orphaned shares fetch in week one'. Quoting $19.18 as deal proceeds is a category error, and quoting $14.23 as a target embeds an assumption that the new bank trades at $27.63 when the market currently says $22.80.

Our disagreement with the board's own catalyst entry is sharper than our disagreement with the street. That entry carried a $14.23 target against an $11.80 floor for a risk-reward of 1.56, which back-solves to an entry near $12.75. At $13.16 the identical arithmetic gives 0.79, and against a properly derived $11.00 floor it gives 0.49. The thesis has not changed; the price has, and the compensation has gone with it. A second, quieter delta: the recent buyers are momentum and value screeners (top-tier Zacks rank, 'near 52-week high' and 'attractive price-to-sales' lists through June and July 2026), not merger arbitrageurs. They are buying a fintech chart and will be handed a community bank.
GDOT.valley_of_death:
There is no cash-burn hump or maturity wall here - the $65 million debt repayment out of the purchase price handles the balance sheet, and the business is improving into the close, with June-quarter earnings of $0.40 a share against a $0.30 estimate. The next three to nine months carry a different kind of risk: regulatory silence, followed by a listing.

The first hazard is the Federal Reserve application itself. Green Dot Bank has been operating under a consent order since 19 July 2024, carrying a $44 million civil money penalty for compliance risk management failures, unfair and deceptive practices in prepaid card marketing and servicing, and anti-money-laundering deficiencies including inadequate disclosure of refund-processing fees between 2017 and 2022. The remediation obligations - third-party root-cause review, outside transaction monitoring, written board-oversight plans - are still live. The Federal Reserve must now satisfy itself that CommerceOne, a bank founded in 2018 with under $1 billion of assets, has the management capacity and capital to run a $6.65 billion bank with roughly $4.6 billion of deposit-type liabilities sourced through prepaid and banking-as-a-service programmes. That is a genuine supervisory question. The guided window has already drifted one quarter, and every additional month of silence between now and the 23 November 2026 outside date will be read by the market as rising break risk, pressuring the shares toward the $11.00 floor well before any decision arrives.

The second and more probable hazard is the listing itself. Assume approval lands and the deal closes in the third or fourth quarter. Holders receive $8.11 in cash and a fractional share of a new company. There is no lock-up on a merger-consideration share, no supportive sponsor bid, no research coverage on day one, and no index membership. The stub could easily print below the $22.80 per new share the market currently implies before it finds the regional-bank buyers who would naturally own it. In that scenario the deal succeeds and the position still loses money - which is the specific way this trade goes wrong, and it does not require anything to break.
GDOT.positioning_washout:
This is the most under-priced dynamic in the situation, and it runs the wrong way for a buyer at today's price.

Green Dot is currently owned as a small-cap financial-technology and payments name: index and small-cap growth funds, payments-sector specialists, and - visible in the June and July 2026 tape - momentum screeners drawn in by a top-tier Zacks rank, a price above the 200-day average of $12.34, and appearances on 'near 52-week high' and 'undervalued price-to-sales' lists. At closing, roughly 12.6 million New CommerceOne shares, about 72% of that company's register, land in those accounts. Essentially none of them can or will hold it. Index funds are mechanically deleted from Green Dot and have no mandate for a newly listed two-state bank holding company. Payments and fintech funds have no mandate either. The natural owner - a regional-bank investor - has never heard of it and has no research to read.

So the forced selling in this situation happens after the catalyst, not before it, and it falls on the asset you are left holding rather than the one you are buying. That is the inverse of the setup this funnel is built to exploit. In a classic washout you buy from distressed sellers ahead of an event; here the event hands you a security into a wave of distressed sellers.

Note also what is absent: Green Dot itself is not washed out. At $13.16 it trades above both its 50-day ($13.06) and 200-day ($12.34) averages, roughly 20% above its broken-deal floor and only 15% off its 52-week high of $15.41. There is no capitulation to buy. The only genuine capitulation on the horizon belongs to the stub, and it is worth waiting for rather than paying ahead of.
GDOT.moderator_conclusion:
The event is real, binding and very likely to complete. That is not the question. The question is whether $13.16 pays you for taking it, and it does not.

What is verified: an Agreement and Plan of Merger signed 23 November 2025; shareholder approvals completed 23 June 2026 with over 99% of Green Dot votes cast in favour and CommerceOne unanimous; consideration fixed at $8.11 in cash plus 0.2215 shares of a new listed bank holding company; the cash funded from Smith Ventures' $690 million purchase price rather than from any financing commitment; no renegotiation in eight months; a contractual outside date of 23 November 2026 extending to 23 February 2027; and, as of 28 July 2026, no Federal Reserve order published and no bank approvals announced against a guided third-quarter close that has already drifted a quarter.

The reason this is a wait rather than a buy is arithmetic, not scepticism. Only 62% of the price is contractual cash. The remaining 38% is an unlisted, unhedgeable stub, and the market marks it at $5.05 - about 32% below the low end of the company's own banker's valuation. That discount is rational: at closing, roughly 12.6 million shares of a small orphaned bank get handed to fintech and index holders who cannot own it. Probability-weight the outcomes honestly - 85% chance of closing at about $14.10, 15% chance of breaking to $11.00 - and fair value is about $13.64, some 3.6% above the price. Mark the stub at the market's own number instead and fair value is $12.84, below the price. Either way the upside is capped at the offer while the downside to an $11.00 floor, which is an estimate rather than a contract, is 16%. That is roughly 0.5 to 1, and it is a material deterioration from the 1.56 recorded when this position was struck near $12.75. The spread has been collected.

The residual risk is not the one the file was opened for. It is not 'will the Federal Reserve say yes' - though Green Dot Bank's live July 2024 consent order and a sub-$1 billion acquirer taking on a $6.65 billion bank make that a real, non-procedural question. The residual risk is that the deal closes exactly as promised and the position still loses money, because an orphaned community bank stub prints below $22.80 in its first week of trading. A trade whose main failure mode is the successful outcome does not deserve fresh capital at this price.

Wait for the price, not the news. Below roughly $12.60 the reward against the $11.80 undisturbed-price reference returns to two-to-one; below roughly $12.15 it does so against the harder $11.00 floor. Either level would likely appear on the first headline of regulatory delay, which on the current drift is more likely than not. Hold what is held; do not add here.
