KDP.bull_thesis:
The bull case is a plumbing case, not a growth case: Keurig Dr Pepper owns two good businesses that the market refuses to value properly while they sit inside one holding company, and management has committed to separating them. On 1 April 2026 the company completed its roughly $18.4 billion purchase of the European coffee group JDE Peet's, and it intends to spin off a worldwide coffee company, provisionally Global Coffee Co., leaving behind a North American drinks company, provisionally Beverage Co. A spin-off means existing holders receive shares in the new company directly, and the transaction is structured to be tax-free.

The value gap is genuine. In 2025 the North American refreshment beverage segment earned $2.94 billion of operating income on roughly $10 billion of net sales, a margin near 29%, and it grew net sales 11.9% in the first quarter of 2026 with Dr Pepper taking share in carbonated soft drinks. That is a growth-rate and margin profile that trades at premium beverage multiples in its own right. It is currently bolted to a coffee business with shrinking pod and brewer volumes, and the blended company trades at roughly twelve times enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, well below where a standalone drinks peer set would clear. Separating them lets each shareholder base pay the multiple it actually wants to pay.

Three things support the case beyond the arithmetic. First, execution has been good: management closed the acquisition on the date it promised, funded it without selling a stake in the better business, and reaffirmed 2026 guidance of $25.9 to $26.4 billion of net sales twice this year, including on a day it disclosed bad leadership news. Chief executive Tim Cofer said early integration work confirmed the planning assumptions behind $400 million of expected savings. Second, sophisticated money underwrote the structure well above today's price: Apollo, KKR, Goldman Sachs Alternatives and T. Rowe Price committed $8.5 billion, with the convertible preferred struck at a $37.25 conversion price, about 24% above the current $30.12. Third, the commodity headwind has turned. Arabica coffee has fallen roughly 20% during 2026 to about $3.11 a pound against a twelve-month high of $4.32, on a record Brazilian crop, so the coffee margin compression that dented first-quarter earnings should unwind through 2027.

The conditions that must hold are specific: net leverage has to come down from roughly 4.5 times to the 3.5-to-4.25-times range the company has set for the two entities; a permanent chief executive has to be found for the coffee company; the Form 10 registration statement has to be filed and cleared; and the equity market has to stay open enough for the board to judge conditions supportive. If those land, the separation completes in 2027 and the parts are worth roughly $41 a share against $30.12 today.
KDP.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that you are paying a premium for an intention rather than a contract, on a business whose balance sheet no longer has any slack.

Start with what the catalyst is not. This is a spin-off, which is a discretionary corporate action. There is no counterparty, no signed agreement, no break fee, and no cash payment owed to anyone if the board changes its mind. As of late July 2026 no Form 10 registration statement has been filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, no record date has been declared, there is no pre-separation trading in the two future entities, and no shareholder vote is scheduled. The company's own language is that timing depends on 'appropriate leverage levels at each company, and supportive market conditions.' Those two conditions deteriorate together in a bad tape, so the option to postpone is most likely to be used exactly when a holder would most want the split to happen. The date has already moved once, from the end of 2026 to early 2027.

The gate itself is demanding. Net leverage is roughly 4.5 times, and the credit sits at the bottom rung of investment grade after Moody's set Baa3 and S&P set BBB- in March 2026. Getting to the 3.5-to-4.0-times target requires paying down debt with free cash flow while still funding a dividend of roughly $1.25 billion a year, in a year when coffee costs have already pushed first-quarter adjusted earnings per share down 7.1% to $0.39. A single bad coffee quarter, a tariff step-up, or a soft financing market pushes the separation into 2028 and the story goes quiet for a year.

The asset being spun is also the weaker one. United States coffee net sales fell 2.3% in the first quarter of 2026 with segment operating income down about 21%, brewer sales fell from $772 million in 2024 to $646 million in 2025, and pod volumes are negative. A pure-play coffee company arriving into the market with high leverage, a declining single-serve franchise, no permanent chief executive and a hundred-country integration underway is not obviously going to clear at a premium multiple. It may well trade at a discount, which is the usual fate of a newly spun company that index funds must sell because they are not mandated to hold it.

Finally, the disagreement with the market has closed. Between 21 and 23 July 2026, Bank of America added the shares to its top-ideas list and JPMorgan, UBS and Citi moved targets to $37 or $38, explicitly citing the separation savings and the parts-based valuation. Consensus now sits near $35 against a $30.12 price, and the stock is up about 20% this year. What confirms the bear case: the second-quarter report on 6 August 2026 pushing the timeline again, leverage failing to fall toward four times by year-end, or the coffee chief executive search running past the autumn.
KDP.sop_bull:
Event wins: the split completes in 2027 and each half is valued as a pure play. Using roughly 1,480 million fully diluted shares (about 1,360 million outstanding plus roughly 121 million from the $4.5 billion of convertible preferred at its $37.25 conversion price):
- Beverage Co: about $3.6 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, built from the 2025 North American refreshment beverage operating income of $2.94 billion plus Latin American and Canadian drinks, less allocated corporate cost, plus its share of the $400 million of separation savings. At 17 times, a premium to PepsiCo and a discount to Monster given roughly 29% margins and double-digit growth, that is $61.2 billion of enterprise value.
- Global Coffee Co: about $3.1 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, from United States coffee ($962 million of 2025 operating income), Canadian coffee, and JDE Peet's (2025 sales of EUR 9.9 billion and adjusted operating profit of about EUR 1.3 billion), with green coffee costs normalising. At 11 times, in line with where JDE Peet's traded standalone and below Nestle, that is $34.1 billion.
- Total enterprise value $95.3 billion, less about $27.5 billion of net debt after two years of free-cash-flow paydown, less the $4 billion minority interest the joint-venture partners hold in pod manufacturing, leaves $63.8 billion of equity.
That is about $43 a share, and the practical event-resolved target is roughly $41 once you allow for the usual slippage between a clean parts valuation and where two newly separated stocks actually settle in their first months.
KDP.sop_bear:
Event fails: the split is deferred past 2027 or shelved, coffee volumes keep falling, and the holding-company discount persists.
- Beverage Co: about $3.4 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation with no separation savings, at 13 times — the multiple a good but captive segment inside a levered parent earns — is $44.2 billion.
- Global Coffee Co: about $2.6 billion, at 7.5 times, reflecting a structurally declining single-serve base and an unfinished hundred-country integration, is $19.5 billion.
- Total enterprise value $63.7 billion, less about $30.5 billion of net debt (no deleveraging progress), less the $4 billion pod joint-venture minority, leaves $29.2 billion of equity, or roughly $19.50 a share.

That $19.50 is the modelled break-case, not the working floor. The working floor is about $25: the shares actually traded to $24.88 within the past twelve months, in the weeks around the April acquisition close, so that is a level at which real buyers demonstrably appeared on this same set of facts. At $25 the dividend yield is about 3.7% and the drinks franchise alone comfortably supports the capital structure. Critically, this is a valuation floor, not a contractual one — there is no deal-break price, no cash consideration, no contingent value right and no escrow, because the only binding transaction here (the JDE Peet's purchase) already completed on 1 April 2026. The $28.50 floor in the original board note is simply the two-hundred-day moving average and does not survive verification.
KDP.sop_breakdown:
Probability-weighted from the two cases, on roughly 1,480 million fully diluted shares:
- 60% weight on the split completing during 2027 and the parts clearing near $41.
- 30% weight on a further slip to 2028 or an indefinite deferral, with the stock drifting back toward the high-$20s where it traded before this year's run — about $28.
- 10% weight on the break-case near $19.50, where the split is shelved and coffee multiples compress.
That weights to about $34.50.

The underlying parts at base-case multiples: Beverage Co at roughly $3.5 billion of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation times 15.5 equals $54.3 billion; Global Coffee Co at roughly $3.0 billion times 9.5 equals $28.5 billion; total enterprise value $82.8 billion, less about $29 billion of net debt and the $4 billion pod joint-venture minority, leaves $49.8 billion of equity, or about $33.60 a share — the same answer from the other direction. For reference, the shares at $30.12 imply about 11.9 times blended, and eighteen analysts now average roughly $35.
KDP.risk_reward: About 2.1 to 1 against the event-win target, but below 1 to 1 against the honest base case. From $30.12: upside of 36% to the $41 event-resolved target and 15% to the $34.50 base case, against downside of 17% to the verified $25 floor and 35% to the $19.50 break-case. The original board note's 2.8-to-1 was an artifact of a $28.50 floor that is a two-hundred-day moving average rather than a backstop; correcting the floor to the level buyers actually defended this year takes the ratio to roughly 2.1 to 1 on the best case and under parity on the expected case.
KDP.catalyst_summary: Tax-free spin-off of a worldwide coffee company out of Keurig Dr Pepper, targeted for early 2027 but with no record date, no Form 10 filing and an explicit escape clause tied to leverage and market conditions; at $30.12 the parts are worth about $34.50 in the base case and about $41 if the split completes, against a soft, non-contractual floor near $25.
KDP.dated_milestone: There is no separation date. The only firm calendar item is second-quarter 2026 results before the market opens on 6 August 2026, which should refresh both the separation timeline and the coffee margin trajectory. The milestones that would actually create a date, none of which has occurred as of 28 July 2026, are: the filing of the Form 10 registration statement for Global Coffee Co. with the Securities and Exchange Commission and its declaration of effectiveness; the appointment of a permanent chief executive for the coffee company (the search opened 23 June 2026 after Rafael Oliveira resigned to run Heineken); confirmation that net leverage has fallen from roughly 4.5 times toward the 3.5-to-4.25-times separation targets; and the declaration of a record and distribution date. Management's stated markers are 'operational readiness to separate by year-end 2026' and a split 'likely in early 2027, subject to market conditions.'
KDP.forcing_function:
The filing of the Form 10 registration statement for the coffee company, followed by a declared record date, is the single event that converts this from an intention into a schedule. That filing makes the parts publicly visible — separate audited financials, separate capital structures, separate management — and it is what allows pre-separation trading in the two future entities, which is where the sum-of-the-parts argument stops being an estimate and becomes a quoted price. Nothing before that filing forces anyone to re-rate the shares.

Two supporting triggers sit ahead of it. The first is the appointment of a permanent chief executive for the coffee company; the board chair, Pamela Patsley, is personally running that search, and a spin-off cannot practically be launched without the seat filled, so the appointment is on the critical path. The second is leverage: the company has explicitly gated the separation on reaching appropriate leverage at each entity, so a quarterly print showing net leverage at four times or below removes the most cited reason for delay. The nearest checkpoint on both is the 6 August 2026 second-quarter report.

One correction to the original framing is worth carrying: the mechanical index buying and selling that a spin-off generates lands on the company being spun off, not on the parent that keeps the listing. Funds tracking an index receive coffee-company shares they are not mandated to hold and must sell them. That is a reason to want the coffee company after the split at a forced-selling discount — it is not, by itself, a reason to own the parent beforehand.
KDP.consensus_delta:
The honest finding is that the disagreement has largely closed, and that cuts against this position rather than for it. In the week of 21 July 2026, Bank of America added the shares to its top-ideas list, and JPMorgan, UBS and Citi all raised targets to $37 or $38, citing the separation savings and a parts-based valuation. Eighteen analysts now average roughly $35 against a $30.12 price, and the shares are up about 20% this year. The variant view that the parts are worth more than the whole is now the published house view at several large banks. When the argument you are underwriting appears in the consensus target, you are no longer being paid for insight; you are being paid for patience and for taking timeline risk.

Where a real difference remains, it runs in both directions. The street is capitalising the $400 million of separation savings and a full pure-play re-rating inside a twelve-month price target, while the company itself only commits to 'operational readiness' by the end of 2026 and a split 'subject to market conditions.' That is a probability of roughly one being applied to an event the issuer has explicitly refused to promise, and it is the assumption most likely to be wrong. Set against that, the street is arguably too gloomy on the coffee input cycle: arabica has fallen about 20% this year to roughly $3.11 a pound from a $4.32 high on a record Brazilian crop, and because roasters buy forward, the relief shows up in reported margins several quarters after it shows up in the commodity. Consensus is extrapolating the first-quarter margin damage rather than the cost curve that has already rolled over.

The net: no meaningful mispricing on the event, a modest one on the coffee margin path, and a crowded position on both.
KDP.valley_of_death:
The risky window runs from the August 2026 report through the first quarter of 2027, and it has four distinct hazards.

First, the coffee margin. Management guided the first quarter of 2026 as the peak of year-over-year cost pressure, with moderation to follow, but hedges and green-coffee contracts struck near the $4.32-a-pound highs are still working through the supply chain, and import tariffs sit on top. Adjusted earnings per share already fell 7.1% to $0.39 in the first quarter. Another quarter of coffee-driven misses would put the full-year guidance of low-double-digit constant-currency earnings growth at risk.

Second, the deleveraging race. Net leverage is roughly 4.5 times and has to reach 3.5 to 4.25 times before the separation, while the company pays roughly $1.25 billion a year in dividends and carries ratings at the bottom rung of investment grade (Baa3 from Moody's, BBB- from S&P, both set in March 2026). There is no headroom: a downgrade to sub-investment grade would raise financing costs precisely when two new capital structures need to be placed. Management has floated non-core asset sales to accelerate paydown, which is itself an admission that organic cash flow may not get there on schedule.

Third, the leadership gap. The designated chief executive of the coffee company resigned on 23 June 2026, eleven weeks after being named, to run Heineken. The parent's chief executive is now running both halves through the most complex phase of the project. If the search runs past the autumn, an early-2027 separation becomes impractical regardless of leverage.

Fourth, integration. A hundred-country coffee business was acquired on 1 April 2026 and must be carved into a standalone entity with its own systems, treasury and reporting while simultaneously delivering $400 million of savings. Separation work of that scale routinely produces one-time costs and dis-synergies that land before the benefits.

There is no debt maturity wall or cash-burn hump here — this is a cash-generative staples business — so the danger is not solvency. It is that any one of these four slips the date, and a soft, undated catalyst that slips again loses the audience that has just arrived.
KDP.positioning_washout:
The forced-selling story has already happened, and it happened to the upside. JAB Holding, the founding sponsor, sold its final 59.1 million shares — about 4.3% of the company — on 11 June 2026 in a single unregistered block through J.P. Morgan, completing a multi-year exit. That removed the last large, well-telegraphed mechanical seller. The shares absorbed it and are up roughly 20% this year, which tells you the supply-clearing part of the original thesis is spent rather than pending.

The shareholder base that remains is mostly index funds and income-oriented holders drawn by a roughly 3.1% dividend yield. Those holders face a real event at the separation, but it sits on the other side of it. When the coffee company is distributed, funds tracking large-capitalisation United States indices will receive shares they are not mandated to hold and will sell them mechanically, and income holders will find the combined dividend split across two policies — a levered coffee company at four times leverage is unlikely to pay much. That is a genuine, predictable wash-out, but it produces a discounted coffee stub after the split rather than pressure on the parent before it.

One overhang does still sit above the current price: $4.5 billion of convertible preferred stock held by Apollo, KKR and T. Rowe Price with a $37.25 conversion price. It ranks ahead of common shareholders and represents roughly 121 million shares of eventual dilution. It is not a seller today, but it caps how clean a move through the high $30s looks.
KDP.moderator_conclusion:
This is a real corporate action attached to a thin spread, and the honest answer is to wait rather than to pay up.

What is genuinely established: Keurig Dr Pepper closed its roughly $18.4 billion purchase of JDE Peet's on 1 April 2026, intends to spin off a worldwide coffee business tax-free, and has an outside investor group — Apollo, KKR, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, T. Rowe Price — committed for $8.5 billion at a conversion price of $37.25, about 24% above today's $30.12. Management has hit every hard milestone it set and reaffirmed guidance twice under pressure. The drinks business alone, at $2.94 billion of 2025 operating income on roughly 29% margins and growing net sales near 12%, is a genuinely good asset.

What is not established is the event itself. There is no record date, no Form 10 registration statement on file, no pre-separation trading and no shareholder vote. The company's own condition language names leverage and 'supportive market conditions', which is an escape clause most likely to be exercised in the tape where you would most want the split. The target has already moved from the end of 2026 to early 2027, and the executive designated to run the coffee company resigned eleven weeks after being appointed. This is a soft, non-binding catalyst — no contractual payout — dressed in the language of a scheduled one.

Two corrections to the original board note matter for sizing. The $28.50 floor is the two-hundred-day moving average, not a backstop; the shares traded to $24.88 this year on these same facts, and the modelled break-case is nearer $19.50. And the index-flow argument runs the wrong way: mechanical selling lands on the spun-off coffee company, not on the parent. Together those take the reward ratio from an advertised 2.8 to 1 down to about 2.1 to 1 on the best case and below parity on the expected case.

Add the crowding. Bank of America put the shares on its top-ideas list on 21 July and JPMorgan, UBS and Citi moved targets to $37 or $38 in the same week, on exactly this argument. Consensus near $35 against a base case of $34.50 means the market and this desk now agree, which is precisely when a special situation stops paying.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. Two things would change the answer. A price back under about $27 — a 17% discount to the base case with the floor only 8% below — restores the asymmetry without needing the event to improve. Or the Form 10 filing with a declared record date and a named chief executive for the coffee company, which converts an intention into a schedule and would justify paying today's price or a little more. The nearest look at both is second-quarter results on 6 August 2026. Until one of those arrives, this is a good business at a fair price with a popular story, not a defined-risk special situation, and it does not earn an aggressive entry.

On the value case standing alone, ignoring the event entirely: a 13% discount to a parts-based fair value of about $34.50, on a franchise with a narrow and eroding advantage, 4.5 times leverage, a credit rating one notch above junk and a return on invested capital near 4%, is moderate rather than compelling. The drinks half is excellent; the coffee half is contracting; the balance sheet leaves no room for error.
KDP.interrogator_dossier:
# Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) — Event Dossier

**Framing:** This is not a compounder note. The question is narrow: is there a real, dated, binding event that forces Keurig Dr Pepper's price toward a higher event-resolved value, and if the event fails, what actually stops the stock from falling?

**Verification date:** 28 July 2026. Last close used: $30.12 (27 July 2026). Fifty-two-week range $24.88 to $35.94.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — what the company has actually committed to

The story starts on 25 August 2025, when Keurig Dr Pepper announced it would buy the European coffee group JDE Peet's for roughly $18 billion and then split itself into two separately listed American companies: a North American drinks business provisionally called Beverage Co., and a worldwide coffee business provisionally called Global Coffee Co. The split is designed as a tax-free spin-off, meaning shareholders would receive shares in the coffee company without an immediate tax bill.

The arc since then has been one of steady execution on the *purchase* and steady slippage on the *split*.

| Date | What was said or done | Effect on the event |
|---|---|---|
| 25 Aug 2025 | Deal announced; separation to follow "as soon as practicable" after close | Event created |
| 27 Oct 2025 | Investor day; $4 billion pod-manufacturing joint venture with Apollo and KKR | Financing de-risked |
| 23 Feb 2026 | Financing updated: convertible preferred upsized to $4.5 billion (Apollo, KKR, T. Rowe Price); partial listing of the drinks business dropped; separation explicitly conditioned on leverage and market conditions | Financing solved, event *timing* made conditional |
| 10 Mar 2026 | Moody's rates the long-term debt Baa3, S&P rates it BBB-, both stable | Investment grade, but only just — one notch of cushion |
| 1 Apr 2026 | JDE Peet's acquisition completed at roughly $18.4 billion; Rafael Oliveira named future chief executive of Global Coffee Co. | The hard, binding half of the plan is done |
| 23 Apr 2026 | First-quarter results: net sales $4.0 billion, up 9.4%; adjusted earnings per share $0.39, down 7.1% on coffee costs; full-year guidance reaffirmed | Business on track, coffee margin under pressure |
| 11 Jun 2026 | JAB Holding sold its last 59.1 million shares, about 4.3% of the company, in a block trade through J.P. Morgan | Multi-year selling overhang cleared |
| 23 Jun 2026 | Oliveira announced he is leaving at the end of July to run Heineken; chief executive Tim Cofer takes direct charge of coffee; board chair Pamela Patsley leads the replacement search; 2026 guidance reaffirmed again | Credibility hit to the spin-off's leadership |
| 21–23 Jul 2026 | Bank of America adds the shares to its "US 1" list; JPMorgan raises its target to $38; UBS to $38; Citi to $37 | The sum-of-the-parts story is now the consensus view, not a variant one |
| Current | Separation targeted for **early 2027**, with "operational readiness" by end-2026 | Date has drifted from the original "by end of 2026" |

The important shift: what began as "buy the coffee asset and split by the end of 2026" is now "we are operationally ready by the end of 2026 and will split in early 2027, if leverage and markets allow."

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

**Real: yes.** This is not a rumour or an activist's wish list. The board has approved the plan, the $18 billion acquisition that enables it has closed, the two operating units are already run separately inside the company, outside investors have put $8.5 billion of fresh capital behind the structure ($4.5 billion of convertible preferred stock plus a $4 billion manufacturing joint venture with Apollo, KKR and Goldman Sachs Alternatives), and a chairman has been designated for the future coffee company's board.

**Dated: no.** This is the load-bearing weakness. For a spin-off, the markers that make a date binding are well defined, and *none of them exist yet*:

- No Form 10 registration statement — the filing that describes the company being spun off — has been submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission, let alone declared effective. The company's own disclosure lists filing it as a *future* condition.
- No record date has been declared. The record date is the day that determines who receives the spun-off shares.
- No when-issued market exists. That is the pre-separation trading in the two future entities that would let you price the parts directly.
- No shareholder vote on the separation is scheduled.
- Company language is "targeted," not committed: timing is subject to "appropriate leverage levels at each company, and supportive market conditions."

**Binding: no.** A spin-off is a discretionary corporate action, not a contract. There is no counterparty, no signed merger agreement, no break fee, no cash consideration. The board can defer it indefinitely and owes nobody a payment if it does. The two stated conditions — leverage and market conditions — are precisely the pair that deteriorate together in a bad tape, which means the option to postpone is most likely to be exercised exactly when a holder would most want the separation to happen.

The date has already slipped once, from "by end of 2026" to "early 2027."

## 3. SPONSOR AND MANAGEMENT CREDIBILITY ON HITTING THE EVENT

**The case for credibility is strong on everything except the date.** Management has delivered every hard, verifiable milestone so far. They said the acquisition would close in early April 2026; it closed 1 April 2026. They said they would fund it without selling a stake in the drinks business; they raised $4.5 billion of convertible preferred stock (initial conversion price $37.25 a share, which stays with the drinks company after the split) plus the $4 billion joint venture, and dropped the partial listing. They have reaffirmed 2026 guidance twice this year — net sales of $25.9 to $26.4 billion and adjusted earnings per share growing at a low-double-digit rate in constant currency — including on 23 June, the same day they disclosed bad leadership news. Chief financial officer Anthony DiSilvestro has been specific rather than vague, guiding to roughly 4.5 times net leverage at mid-year and naming free cash flow and non-core asset sales as the paydown levers. Chief executive Tim Cofer said early integration work "confirmed planning assumptions" on the $400 million of expected savings.

**The case against is material and specific.** Rafael Oliveira was named chief executive of the future coffee company on 1 April 2026 and announced his exit eleven weeks later, on 23 June, to run Heineken from October. Nobody walks away from the top job at a business about to be handed roughly $16 billion of revenue and a fresh listing unless the outside offer is far better or the inside job looks harder than advertised. Either reading is a mark against the spin-off. The parent's chief executive now runs both halves while a search proceeds, which is a stretched-attention risk during the most complex phase of the project. A spin-off cannot practically be launched without a permanent chief executive in the seat, so the search is now on the critical path to the date.

**Verdict on sponsor credibility: good on execution, weakened on the specific event.** They do what they say — but what they have said about the split's timing is deliberately non-committal, and the person who was supposed to lead it has left.

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — what actually backstops the price

The board note that surfaced this name carried a floor of $28.50. **That number does not survive verification.**

- $28.49 is the stock's two-hundred-day moving average — a chart line, not a claim on the business.
- The shares traded as low as **$24.88 within the past twelve months**, in the weeks around the April close. The market has already demonstrated it will pay less than $28.50 for this equity, this year, on this same set of facts.
- There is no deal-break price, because there is no deal to break. This is a spin-off, not a takeover: no cash consideration, no contingent value right, no escrow, no acquirer obliged to pay anything. The one genuinely binding transaction — the JDE Peet's purchase — has already completed.

What genuinely supports the price is softer, and worth naming honestly:

1. **A real cash-generating drinks franchise.** North American refreshment beverages produced $2.94 billion of segment operating income on roughly $10 billion of net sales in 2025 — a margin near 29% — and grew net sales 11.9% in the first quarter of 2026. Dr Pepper is a genuine share gainer in carbonated soft drinks. This asset is not going away.
2. **A dividend.** Roughly $0.92 a year, about a 3.1% yield at the current price, most recently declared on 20 May and paid 10 July 2026.
3. **The prior low as revealed demand.** Buyers showed up in size at $24.88 earlier this year.
4. **Falling green coffee costs.** Arabica has come down roughly 20% during 2026 to about $3.11 a pound in late July, against a twelve-month high of $4.32. That eventually relieves the coffee margin — with a lag, because hedges and contracts struck at the highs are still rolling through.

Against those: pro forma net leverage of roughly 4.5 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation is high for a consumer staples company, and leverage makes the equity move more than the business does. The credit sits at the bottom rung of investment grade (Baa3 and BBB-), so there is no room for a stumble. About $4.5 billion of preferred stock ranks ahead of common shareholders, and the joint-venture partners hold a $4 billion minority claim on the pod-manufacturing economics.

**Verified floor: approximately $25, not $28.50.** That is the observed 2026 low, roughly a 3.7% dividend yield, and consistent with the drinks business alone carrying the whole capital structure at a depressed multiple. It is a valuation floor, not a contractual one. It can be broken — a modelled break-case, with the split shelved and coffee multiples compressing to about seven and a half times, lands near $19.50.

## 5. RED FLAGS

- 🔴 **The asset being spun is shrinking.** United States coffee net sales fell 2.3% in the first quarter of 2026 and segment operating income fell about 21%, with brewer sales down from $772 million in 2024 to $646 million in 2025 and pod volumes negative. You are being asked to pay for a re-rating of a business whose core franchise is contracting.
- 🔴 **Leverage is a stated gate on the catalyst.** Roughly 4.5 times net leverage today against targets of about 3.5 to 4.0 times and 3.75 to 4.25 times at the two companies on separation. That converts a corporate-action catalyst into a deleveraging race, and it has to be won while paying roughly $1.25 billion a year in dividends.
- 🔴 **Tariffs and coffee input costs.** Management flagged peak year-over-year cost pressure in the first quarter, with relief expected to lag. This is the single most likely thing to push the leverage gate further out.
- 🔴 **Leadership vacuum at the spin-off.** No permanent chief executive for Global Coffee Co. as of late July 2026, with the search only opened on 23 June.
- 🔴 **No Form 10, no record date, no when-issued market.** Nothing yet forces the calendar.
- 🔴 **The variant view has gone mainstream.** Between 21 and 23 July, Bank of America added the shares to its top-ideas list and JPMorgan, UBS and Citi all moved targets to $37 or $38 on precisely the sum-of-the-parts and separation-savings argument that underpins this thesis. Consensus now sits near $35. Being right about the split is no longer a disagreement with the market.

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

- 🟢 **The hard part is done and cannot be undone.** The roughly $18.4 billion acquisition closed on 1 April 2026. The financing was raised and even upsized. The question of "will they get the deal done" is spent, in the shareholder's favour.
- 🟢 **The last structural seller is gone.** JAB Holding, the founding sponsor, sold its final 59.1 million shares on 11 June 2026 in a single block through J.P. Morgan, completing a multi-year exit. Whatever happens next, it will not be JAB selling into it.
- 🟢 **Sophisticated capital underwrote this structure well above the current price.** Apollo, KKR, Goldman Sachs Alternatives and T. Rowe Price put $8.5 billion behind it, with the convertible preferred struck at $37.25 — about 24% above where the shares trade now. Not proof of value, but a real, priced view from investors with full diligence access.
- 🟢 **Reaffirmed guidance under pressure**, including on the day of adverse leadership news.
- 🟢 **The commodity headwind has turned.** Arabica is down about 20% this year on a record Brazilian crop, with forecasters pointing to a surplus into 2027. The margin relief arrives late, but it arrives.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The language shifted from "separation" to "**operational readiness** to separate." That is a hedge. Being ready to do a thing is not doing it.
- Abandoning the partial listing of the drinks business in favour of more preferred equity is quietly good for common shareholders — it avoids selling a stake in the better asset at a conglomerate-discount price. It also adds $4.5 billion of stock that ranks ahead of you.
- Pamela Patsley was named chairman of the future coffee company's board and is personally running the chief executive search. Board-level ownership suggests urgency, and confirms the search is a gating item.
- **The index-flow argument in the original board note deserves a correction.** In a spin-off, the entity that gets mechanically sold is usually the *spun-off* company, because funds that track an index and own the parent receive shares they are not mandated to hold. Here that pressure lands on Global Coffee Co., not on the drinks company that keeps the listing. Forced selling is therefore a reason to want to buy the coffee company *after* the split at a discount — it is not, by itself, a reason to own the parent before it. The one piece of forced-seller supply that did apply to the parent, JAB's stake, has already cleared, and the shares have risen about 20% so far this year through it.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** The whole company is mid-transformation, and the identity of what you own changes materially within roughly nine months.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** the asymmetry is real but considerably thinner than the board note implied, because that note's $28.50 floor is a moving average rather than a backstop, and its 2.8-to-1 reward ratio is an artifact of that too-tight floor. Using the honest floor of about $25, you are risking roughly 17% to make roughly 15% to a base case near $34.50 and roughly 36% to a full event win near $41 — and the event has no date, no filing, no vote, and an explicit escape clause tied to leverage and markets.

This is a good business at a fair-to-slightly-cheap price with a genuine, sponsored, value-creating corporate action ahead of it. It is not a defined-risk special situation, and the crowd has now arrived at the same conclusion. The correct response is to want it at a better price or on a harder date — the Form 10 filing with a declared record date, or leverage confirmed at four times or below — not to pay up for an undated intention.

**On the moat, for completeness:** the drinks half has a narrow but genuine advantage from brand strength and distribution scale. The coffee half's advantage is eroding in plain sight, with pod volumes and brewer sales both falling. Blended, the durable earnings base is narrow and its trend is negative — return on invested capital is about 4% on the enlarged balance sheet. No structural force threatens the terminal value of the drinks franchise; the coffee franchise faces a persistent but manageable shift away from single-serve pods, plus tariff-driven input costs. The cheapness here is a conglomerate-and-transition discount, not a value trap on a melting base — but it is also not a franchise you can hold blind through a broken catalyst.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 3 | TRAJECTORY: PIVOTING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: ERODING | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

The milestones that would actually create a date, none of which has occurred as of 28 July 2026, are: the filing of the Form 10 registration statement for Global Coffee Co. with the Securities and Exchange Commission and its declaration of effectiveness; the appointment of a permanent chief executive for the coffee company (the search opened 23 June 2026 after Rafael Oliveira resigned to run Heineken); confirmation that net leverage has fallen from roughly 4.5 times toward the 3.5-to-4.25-times separation targets; and the declaration of a record and distribution date. Management's stated markers are 'operational readiness to separate by year-end 2026' and a split 'likely in early 2027, subject to market conditions.'
catalyst.binding_reason: No Form 10 for Global Coffee Co. exists anywhere on the SEC record: an EDGAR full-text sweep plus an independent universe-wide check of every 10-12B filed since April 2026 returns the other live spins (Honeywell Aerospace, Envirii, FedEx Freight, ADI Global, Marex, BioStem) and no coffee registrant of any kind, so the Spin_index_flow driver has no schedule behind it, and the 4.5x leverage presented as observed fact is a company projection.

LBTYK.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Liberty Global finishes taking itself apart and the market is forced to price the pieces instead of the conglomerate. At $9.59 (close, 27 July 2026) the whole company is worth about $3.27 billion on roughly 341 million shares. Against that, management's own raised year-end 2026 target for holding-company cash is about $2.0 billion, or roughly $5.86 a share, and the Liberty Growth portfolio of private investments carries an independently appraised value of $2.9 billion, or about $8.50 a share. Those two items alone come to roughly $14.36 a share. Buying the stock today therefore means paying about a third less than the cash and the investment portfolio are said to be worth, and receiving every operating telecom business for nothing. Chief executive Mike Fries made exactly that point on the 24 July 2026 call, noting the price then implied “essentially zero equity value attributed to our Liberty Telecom operations.”

The event meant to close that gap is the separation and Amsterdam listing of Ziggo Group, which combines VodafoneZiggo in the Netherlands with Telenet in Belgium into a single Benelux operator of roughly 13 million customers and about 6.6 billion euros (roughly $7.7 billion) of annual revenue. Liberty intends to distribute about 90% of it to its own shareholders, with Vodafone keeping 10%.

What makes this credible rather than promotional is that the sponsor has done it once already and the sub-milestones keep clearing. Liberty spun off Sunrise, its Swiss operator, in November 2024; management values that distributed stake at about $12 per Liberty Global share today, and it trades in Zurich at roughly 8 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Since then: the Belgian regulator approved the Wyre-Proximus fiber-sharing agreement (cleared the day before the July call); every approval needed to buy Vodafone's half of the Dutch joint venture has been obtained, with closing due by the end of July 2026; new leadership for Ziggo Group was named and starts 1 September 2026; and management has raised about $1.2 billion this year, roughly $900 million from portfolio disposals plus a $340 million loan against the Wyre stake, which let it lift the year-end corporate cash target from about $1.5 billion to about $2.0 billion. On the strength of that progress Fries pulled the timing forward rather than pushing it back, saying the company is “a bit more ambitious on the timing of the spin off. And we are currently saying mid-2027 versus H2 2027.”

The private marks are also getting validated in cash rather than in slides. The company fully exited EdgeConneX in the second quarter for $604 million of proceeds, described as about four times the original investment over roughly ten years and better than a 30% annual return.

Underneath the event, the asset actually being separated is improving. VodafoneZiggo added 7,200 broadband customers in the quarter, its best result in more than six years, plus 31,700 postpaid mobile customers, with fixed revenue per user up 0.6%. Telenet added 6,100 broadband and 2,200 postpaid customers. If management delivers the stated equity story for Ziggo Group - leverage down to 4.5 times and free cash flow of 500 million euros by 2028 - and the market applies the free-cash-flow yield it already applies to Sunrise, Fries argues the listed Benelux group is worth up to $14 per Liberty Global share on its own.

Conditions that must hold: the Dutch stake purchase closes on schedule; the Belgian and Dutch asset sales of 1.2 to 1.4 billion euros execute and bring subsidiary debt down; the Benelux customer recovery continues rather than reverses; the private portfolio marks hold up as further positions are sold; and the board actually files and completes the listing rather than exercising its right to abandon it.
LBTYK.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the discount is real, deserved, and self-perpetuating - and that nothing forces it to close for at least a year while the business underneath it shrinks.

Start with what actually broke. The board entry for this name carried a downside floor of $9.50. On 24 July 2026, the day second-quarter results landed, the stock traded as low as $9.30 intraday and closed at $9.60 on about 4.1 million shares, roughly five times its recent daily volume. The floor was breached within hours of the print and has not been recovered: the 27 July close was $9.59. It was never a floor; it was a recent price level, and the stated risk-to-reward of 4.7 to 1 was computed when the stock was near $11, which is where it traded when the results deck was written. The setup has moved materially against that entry.

The second-quarter numbers themselves were poor. Revenue of $1,172.0 million fell 7.7% as reported and 6.0% on a like-for-like basis. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of $324.9 million fell 3.1%. Adjusted free cash flow was negative $150.4 million, and the company posted a net loss of $357.8 million. Retained earnings have fallen from about $8.02 billion at September 2025 to about $5.08 billion at June 2026 - close to $3 billion of accumulated losses in three quarters. Consolidated net debt stands at about $6.66 billion.

The clearest problem is the asset that is not being separated. Virgin Media O2, the UK business Liberty owns half of alongside Telefonica, is deteriorating: revenue down 7.9% on a like-for-like basis, 28,200 broadband customers lost and 63,000 postpaid customers lost in the quarter, with full-year guidance for both revenue and earnings to decline 3% to 5% against capital spending of 2.0 to 2.2 billion pounds and adjusted free cash flow of only about 200 million pounds. Chief financial officer Charles Bracken conceded that “leverage is above our 4 to 5x target, and that credit spreads are currently elevated,” and on refinancing added “we acknowledge recent trading levels” - an admission the bonds have widened. A leveraged, shrinking half-stake can be worth zero, and in a bad enough outcome it can consume holding-company resources rather than contribute them.

Now attack the floor itself. The roughly $2.0 billion of corporate cash is not shareholder cash. It is the purchase price for Vodafone's half of the Dutch business. Fries said plainly the company will “end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view” - the asset sales funded the acquisition. That cash converts into an illiquid, leveraged telecom equity, and there is no dividend and no share repurchase creating a bid underneath the stock. The $2.9 billion investment portfolio is an appraisal, not a bid, with the top five positions accounting for more than half of it; concentrated private marks are exactly what gets cut when funding markets tighten. Haircut the portfolio by half and assign the operating telecoms nothing, and the honest floor is about $8.00 a share, roughly 17% below the current price rather than the 2% the board entry implied.

Finally, the event is soft and distant. There is no record date, no listing prospectus, no scheduled shareholder vote. The company's own words are “as early as mid-2027” - about eleven months away - the transaction still requires shareholder and exchange approvals, and the board explicitly retains discretion to abandon it. The headline value target also leans on 2028 assumptions: the $14-per-share figure for Ziggo Group requires free cash flow of 500 million euros, against combined guidance today of roughly 100 million euros at VodafoneZiggo and 20 million euros at Telenet. That is close to a fourfold increase in two years, and it is the weakest load-bearing number in the entire case.

What would confirm the bear: the mid-2027 language slipping back toward late 2027 or later; the Wyre stake sale missing its year-end 2026 to first-quarter 2027 window or clearing below the carrying mark; a writedown in the investment portfolio; further widening in Virgin Media O2 credit; or the Benelux customer recovery stalling before the listing.
LBTYK.sop_bull: Roughly $30 a share if the separation completes on the guided path and the market pays Sunrise-like multiples for the pieces. Built up on roughly 341 million shares: holding-company cash of about $2.0 billion, or $5.86 a share, taken at face value; the Liberty Growth private portfolio at its full independently appraised $2.9 billion, or $8.50 a share, which the EdgeConneX exit at about four times cost supports; Ziggo Group at management's stated ceiling of $14 a share, which requires the Benelux group to reach 500 million euros of free cash flow and 4.5 times leverage by 2028 and to be valued on the 10.5% to 13.5% free-cash-flow yield the market already applies to Sunrise; the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake recovering to about $1.50 a share as leverage comes down; and Virgin Media Ireland plus residual items at about $0.50. Note that the $12 a share of already-distributed Sunrise stock is deliberately excluded - shareholders hold it directly and it is not value inside these shares. Management's own “from an $18 stock we have a clear opportunity to create $37 to $40 of value” framing double-counts it; this figure does not.
LBTYK.sop_bear: About $8.00 a share, and this is the verified floor, not the board's $9.50. Built up on roughly 341 million shares: holding-company cash of about $2.0 billion, or $5.86 a share, using management's own raised year-end 2026 target and crediting it in full even though it is committed to the Vodafone purchase; the Liberty Growth portfolio haircut by half to about $1.45 billion, or $4.25 a share, on the grounds that appraisals are not bids and the top five positions are more than half the total; and the operating telecoms - the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake, Ziggo Group and Virgin Media Ireland - carried at zero, which is close to what the market pays for them today. That sums to about $10.11, from which roughly $2 a share is deducted for holding-company running costs, the risk that resources are drawn down to support a leveraged Virgin Media O2, and the discount the market persistently applies to a holding company that has not completed its break-up. For cross-reference, tangible book value - equity less goodwill and other intangibles - is about $13.32 a share and reported book value about $27.05, so the bear case is well inside accounting values. The severe case, in which the listing is abandoned and the portfolio is written down further, is closer to $6.50.
LBTYK.sop_breakdown:
Two numbers matter and they answer different questions. The sum of the parts, if the break-up completes and the value is recognised, is about $17.50 to $18.00 a share: holding-company cash $5.86, the Liberty Growth portfolio at a 25% haircut to its appraised mark $6.38, Ziggo Group at about half of management's $14 ceiling to reflect that the 500-million-euro free-cash-flow target is a 2028 number against roughly 120 million euros guided today $7.00, the 50% Virgin Media O2 stake $1.00, and Virgin Media Ireland plus residuals $0.50 - about $20.74 before applying a 15% discount for holding-company frictions and the eleven months of execution still required, giving roughly $17.60.

The base case actually used is lower, because the event is not certain. Weighting the event-resolved target of $18.00 at 60% and the verified downside floor of $8.00 at 40% gives about $14.00 a share. Against the 27 July close of $9.59 that is roughly 46% of expected upside. The 60% weighting reflects a sponsor that has completed this exact transaction before and has cleared every sub-milestone so far, offset by the absence of any binding date, filing or vote, and the board's retained right to walk away.
LBTYK.risk_reward: About 5.3 to 1 on corrected inputs, better than the 4.7 to 1 the board claimed but for a different reason than the board gave. From the 27 July 2026 close of $9.59, upside to the event-resolved target of $18.00 is about +88%; downside to the verified floor of $8.00 is about -17%. That is $8.41 of upside against $1.59 of downside. The board's stated ratio used a $9.50 floor and a price near $11 - and that floor was breached intraday at $9.30 on 24 July 2026 and has not been regained. So the ratio has improved only because the price fell through the advertised floor, not because the floor held. Measured against the probability-weighted base case of $14.00 rather than the target, the ratio is a more sober 2.8 to 1.
LBTYK.catalyst_summary: Ziggo Group, the combined Dutch and Belgian business, is set to be spun off and listed in Amsterdam “as early as mid-2027” - no record date, no filing, about eleven months out - offering roughly +88% to an $18 event-resolved value against about -17% to a verified $8.00 asset floor, with the stock at a 52-week low of $9.59 after the 24 July 2026 results.
LBTYK.dated_milestone:
Verified on 28 July 2026 against the second-quarter results released 24 July 2026, the investor call of the same date, and the 1 June 2026 leadership announcement; no new disclosure has landed since the 24 July current report and quarterly report, so the status below is current.

No binding date exists for the event itself. The firm dates that do exist are preparatory: closing of the purchase of Vodafone's 50% interest in VodafoneZiggo by 31 July 2026, with all approvals already obtained; the new Ziggo Group chief executive and chief financial officer taking office on 1 September 2026, with the balance of the leadership team to be announced in September 2026; the sale of a stake in Wyre targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027; and 1.2 to 1.4 billion euros of Belgian and Dutch asset sales under way to reduce subsidiary debt. The listing itself is guided only as “as early as mid-2027”, accelerated from a prior “second half of 2027”, and remains subject to shareholder and exchange approval with the board retaining the right to abandon it.
LBTYK.forcing_function:
There is no single hard date that forces a re-rating, and that is the central weakness of this setup. The genuine trigger is the filing of a listing prospectus for Ziggo Group together with a scheduled shareholder vote, because that is the moment the separation stops being a plan and becomes a transaction with a calendar. That filing has not happened and has not been scheduled.

Before it, four checkpoints will move the odds. First, closing the purchase of Vodafone's half of the Dutch business by 31 July 2026 - imminent, fully approved, and foundational, because Ziggo Group cannot be formed without it. Second, the September 2026 completion of the Ziggo Group management team, which converts an intention into an operating company with its own leadership and reporting line. Third, the sale of the Wyre stake, targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027, which both tests the private marks in cash and funds the Belgian deleveraging the equity story depends on. Fourth, third-quarter results in late October 2026, the next occasion on which the mid-2027 language will either be reaffirmed or quietly stretched.

There is also a mechanical flow event further out. Because the shares to be distributed will list on Euronext Amsterdam rather than in the United States, index funds and mandates that cannot hold a foreign listing will be forced to sell the distributed stock. That is the classic post-separation supply that tends to create a better entry in the spun business than in the parent - a reason to expect the value to be recognised after the listing rather than on the day it happens.
LBTYK.consensus_delta:
The market is treating Liberty Global as a leveraged European cable operator and valuing it off consolidated, declining earnings - revenue down 7.7% in the second quarter, adjusted free cash flow of negative $150.4 million, a net loss of $357.8 million. On that lens the stock looks like a melting ice cube and $9.59 looks generous.

What that lens misses is that the consolidated figures include businesses being actively dismantled while excluding where the value sits. Holding-company cash at the raised year-end 2026 target of about $2.0 billion is $5.86 a share. The independently appraised Liberty Growth portfolio at $2.9 billion is $8.50 a share. Together that is roughly $14.36 against a $9.59 stock - a 33% discount to cash and investments alone, with every operating telecom business thrown in free. That is not a soft claim: management raised the cash target from $1.5 billion after beating its own disposal plan by a wide margin, banking about $1.2 billion year to date, and it realised EdgeConneX in the quarter for $604 million at roughly four times cost and better than a 30% annual return. The street is marking a portfolio to scepticism that has just been marked to cash at a premium.

The second thing the street has wrong is direction of travel on the event. The consensus reflex on any European telecom break-up is that it slips. This one was pulled forward: mid-2027 from the second half of 2027, on the back of a Belgian regulatory approval, full approval to buy out Vodafone's Dutch stake, and named leadership.

But there is a bull-side consensus error too, and honesty requires naming it. Published bullish work has run base cases as high as $27 a share by treating the holding-company cash as shareholder value and the appraised portfolio at face. It is neither free nor liquid: the cash is the purchase price for the Vodafone stake and converts into an illiquid leveraged equity, and the portfolio is five big private positions carried at appraisal. The market's discount is not irrational - it is a reasonable haircut for concentration, illiquidity, and a half-stake in a UK operator whose bonds have widened and whose leverage management admits sits above target. The genuine disagreement is narrower than the bulls claim: roughly $18 of parts value, not $27.
LBTYK.valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months are the hard part, because every source of support is switched off while the trigger is still a year away.

Cash generation is negative right now. Adjusted free cash flow was negative $150.4 million in the second quarter and the company posted a $357.8 million net loss, on top of roughly $3 billion of accumulated losses since September 2025. Consolidated net debt is about $6.66 billion.

The holding-company cash cannot help the share price. It is earmarked for the Vodafone purchase closing by 31 July 2026 - Fries said the company will “end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view” - and there is no dividend and no share repurchase. Nothing bids for the stock on weakness, which is precisely why it cut through the $9.50 level on the print without pausing and has stayed below it since.

The sharpest near-term risk is Virgin Media O2. Revenue fell 7.9% on a like-for-like basis; the business lost 28,200 broadband and 63,000 postpaid customers in the quarter; guidance is for revenue and earnings both to decline 3% to 5% while capital spending runs at 2.0 to 2.2 billion pounds, leaving adjusted free cash flow of about 200 million pounds. Management acknowledged leverage above the 4 to 5 times target, elevated credit spreads, and unfavourable trading levels on its bonds. If UK credit widens further, the market will start pricing the possibility that the parent has to support it - which attacks the cash floor directly.

There is also execution risk in the Belgian restructuring itself. Wyre is drawing a large underwritten facility to repay a roughly $2.3 billion intercompany loan to Telenet and pay a $400 million dividend, with Telenet then retiring 2028 maturities. That plumbing has to work, in a market where the company itself says spreads are elevated.

Finally, the calendar. Third-quarter results in late October 2026 are the next opportunity for the mid-2027 language to be stretched. Any softening there, or a Wyre stake sale that misses its window or clears below the carrying mark, would take the stock toward the $8.00 floor well before any listing document exists.
LBTYK.positioning_washout:
The forced selling has partly already happened, and the more interesting wave is still ahead.

This shareholder base is not yield-driven - there is no dividend to cut - so the classic income-fund exodus does not apply. It is a value and event-driven register, and that register capitulated on the results. The stock traded to $9.30 intraday on 24 July 2026 on about 4.1 million shares, roughly five times its recent daily volume, closing at $9.60 and setting a 52-week low against a $13.12 high in February. It closed 27 July at $9.59 on continued heavy turnover of about 4.5 million shares across the share classes, so the break has been held rather than reversed. That is what exhaustion looks like: a heavy break of a widely watched level, then a market that will not bid it back. One secondary source reported an unusual spike in put buying on the A shares around the print - roughly 33,000 contracts against a typical 714 a day - which, if accurate, points to hedging or bearish positioning immediately after the results rather than accumulation. That is a single low-quality source and should be treated as colour, not evidence.

The absence of a company bid matters more than usual. With repurchases off while cash funds the Vodafone purchase, there is no price-insensitive buyer to absorb tax-loss selling into year-end 2026, and this stock is sitting on losses for anyone who bought above $11.

The larger mechanical event comes at the separation itself. Liberty holders will receive shares in a company listed on Euronext Amsterdam, not in the United States. Index funds tracking US benchmarks, and mandates barred from holding foreign-listed securities, will have to sell the distributed stock regardless of value. That indiscriminate supply is the well-worn reason spun-off companies are often cheapest in the weeks after listing. For this thesis it cuts two ways: it argues the value gets recognised after the listing rather than at it, and it argues the better entry may eventually be in Ziggo Group itself rather than in the parent today.
LBTYK.moderator_conclusion:
This is a good ratio attached to a slow, soft trigger, and it arrives after the advertised safety net has already given way. Both halves of that sentence need to be held at once.

What is genuinely strong: the sponsor. Liberty Global has completed this exact manoeuvre before - Sunrise, spun in November 2024, is worth roughly $12 per Liberty share to holders who received it - and every checkable sub-milestone for the second one has cleared. Belgian regulatory approval is in hand, all approvals to buy Vodafone's half of the Dutch business are obtained with closing due by 31 July 2026, leadership is named for 1 September 2026, about $1.2 billion has been raised against plan, and the year-end cash target was raised rather than cut. Management pulled the timing forward, to mid-2027 from the second half of 2027. Meanwhile the asset being separated is improving: VodafoneZiggo posted its best broadband quarter in more than six years. The valuation gap is real and arithmetic, not rhetorical - about $14.36 a share of cash and appraised investments against a $9.59 stock, with the operating telecoms free.

What disqualifies it from size today: the event is not dated. “As early as mid-2027” is roughly eleven months away, with no record date, no listing prospectus, no scheduled vote, and an explicit board right to abandon. That is a plan, not a scheduled event, and nothing forces the market's hand in the meantime. Worse for the entry premise, the $9.50 downside floor this name was admitted on did not survive its first test - the stock traded through it to $9.30 on 24 July 2026 and has closed below it every session since, at a 52-week low. Rebuilding the floor honestly from the balance sheet puts it near $8.00: holding-company cash of $5.86 a share, which is committed to an acquisition rather than distributable, plus the private portfolio at a 50% haircut, with the telecoms at zero. A real floor exists. It just sits about 17% lower than the one that was underwritten.

And the interim is genuinely unpleasant. Free cash flow is negative, there is no buyback and no dividend to support the shares, and the half-owned UK operator is losing broadband and mobile customers with leverage above target and credit spreads management concedes are elevated.

So: wait, with named conditions rather than a vague hope of a flush. Three things would change this from a watch to a purchase. First, a Ziggo Group listing prospectus filed or a shareholder vote scheduled - the moment the event acquires a calendar. Second, the Wyre stake sale completing at or above its carrying value in the year-end 2026 to first-quarter 2027 window, which would test the private marks in cash for a second time after EdgeConneX. Third, price: the balance-sheet floor is near $8.00, and a wash toward $8.50 would offer a genuine margin of safety rather than the notional one this name was entered on. Conversely, if the October 2026 results stretch the mid-2027 language, the thesis weakens rather than merely waits.

The value case underneath is sound - a verifiable discount to cash and investments, run by a team that has delivered a separation before - and the odds have improved slightly as the price fell while the parts did not. It simply does not need to be owned this month, and the discipline of this funnel is that an undated event eleven months out, entered below a floor that has already broken, does not earn real capital.
LBTYK.interrogator_dossier:
# Liberty Global (LBTYK) — Event Dossier

**Event under examination:** the planned separation and Euronext Amsterdam listing of "Ziggo Group", the newly formed Benelux telecom company combining VodafoneZiggo in the Netherlands with Telenet in Belgium.
**Prepared:** 28 July 2026. **Live price:** $9.59 (close, 27 July 2026; the A shares closed at $9.83). **Market value:** about $3.27 billion on roughly 341 million shares.
**Re-verification:** checked again on 28 July 2026. Nothing new has been disclosed since the second-quarter results — the company's most recent filings remain the current report and quarterly report both dated 24 July 2026. The event status below is unchanged, and the share price has slipped a further eleven cents to a fresh low.

---

## 0. THE HEADLINE FINDING

Two things are true at once here, and the board entry for this name captures neither cleanly.

First, the sponsor is credible and the plan is moving forward, not backward. On the 24 July 2026 second-quarter call, chief executive Mike Fries said the company is "a bit more ambitious on the timing of the spin off. And we are currently saying mid-2027 versus H2 2027." That is an acceleration. Most soft catalysts in this funnel slip; this one was pulled forward, and it was pulled forward because real, checkable building blocks were completed.

Second, the event is still not a dated, binding one. There is no record date, no listing prospectus, no shareholder vote scheduled. The company's own language is "as early as mid-2027" — roughly eleven months away — and the board retains the discretion to abandon the transaction. An eleven-month soft target is a plan, not a hard, scheduled event.

The more damaging finding concerns the downside floor. The board entry carries a floor of $9.50. On 24 July 2026, the day of the second-quarter results, the stock traded as low as $9.30 intraday and closed at $9.60. The floor has already been breached, and the stock has not recovered it — the 27 July close of $9.59 is below it again. It was not a floor; it was a recent price. The board's stated risk-to-reward of 4.7 to 1 was struck when the stock was near $11, which is where it was trading when the results deck was written. The setup has moved against the entry since.

That said, when I rebuild the floor from the balance sheet rather than from the chart, a real one does exist — it just sits lower, around $8.00. On corrected inputs the asymmetry is intact and slightly better than a week ago, because the price fell while the parts did not. The problem with this name today is not the ratio. It is that the event is undated and far away, the near-term cash generation is negative, and the advertised safety margin was overstated.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — what management is actually doing

Liberty Global is deliberately taking itself apart. This is not a compounding story and management does not pretend otherwise.

The template was set in November 2024, when the company spun off Sunrise, its Swiss operator, to shareholders. Fries now values that distributed stake at about $12 per Liberty Global share, noting Sunrise trades in Zurich at roughly 8 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, or a 10.5% to 13.5% free-cash-flow yield (free cash flow divided by market value). Importantly, that $12 sits in shareholders' hands already — it is not value still inside the shares being analysed here, and any thesis that counts it twice is wrong.

Ziggo Group is the second act. It combines the Dutch and Belgian operations into a single Benelux group of roughly 13 million customers and €6.6 billion (about $7.7 billion) of annual revenue. The structure is a hybrid: Liberty Global intends to distribute about 90% of the shares to its own shareholders, with Vodafone retaining 10% following Liberty's purchase of Vodafone's half of the Dutch joint venture.

Alongside that, the company has been converting its private investment portfolio — "Liberty Growth" — into cash. Fries described the strategy plainly: "despite the size and scale and growth prospects of our businesses, we believe our stock today reflects no value for these assets."

**Read:** the narrative has been consistent and it is being executed against, not merely narrated. That is unusual and it counts.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs EVIDENCE (forensic)

| Management claim | Hard evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| The separation is "on track" and now targeted for mid-2027 | Belgian regulator approved the Wyre–Proximus fiber-sharing agreement (announced on the 24 July call as having cleared "yesterday"); all approvals obtained to buy Vodafone's 50% of the Dutch business, closing by end-July 2026; chief executive and chief financial officer for Ziggo Group named, effective 1 September 2026 | **Supported.** Each block is verifiable and each has actually cleared |
| Cash generation from asset sales is ahead of plan | About $1.2 billion raised year to date: roughly $900 million of Liberty Growth disposals plus a ~$340 million loan secured against the Wyre stake. Year-end corporate cash target raised from about $1.5 billion to about $2.0 billion | **Supported, and over-delivered** |
| The private portfolio marks are real | Full exit of EdgeConneX completed in the quarter for $604 million of proceeds, described as about four times the original investment over roughly ten years and above a 30% annualised return | **Supported by one large realisation.** One data point is not the whole portfolio, but it is the right kind of evidence |
| The stock prices the telecom operations at nothing | At about $11, management called it a 20% discount to the appraised value of cash plus the growth portfolio alone. At the 27 July close of $9.59 that discount is roughly 33% | **Arithmetically correct.** Whether the appraisals are worth their marks is the open question |
| Ziggo Group can be worth "up to $14 per Liberty share" | This requires leverage down to 4.5 times and free cash flow of €500 million by 2028. Today the two halves guide to roughly €100 million (VodafoneZiggo) and €20 million (Telenet) | **Aspirational.** It needs free cash flow to rise roughly fourfold in two years. This is the single weakest load-bearing number in the bull case |

Where the story is poorer than the numbers: the second quarter itself was soft. Revenue of $1,172.0 million fell 7.7% as reported (6.0% on a like-for-like basis); adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of $324.9 million fell 3.1%; adjusted free cash flow was **negative $150.4 million**, and the company posted a net loss of $357.8 million. Retained earnings have fallen from about $8.02 billion at September 2025 to about $5.08 billion at June 2026 — close to $3 billion of accumulated losses in three quarters.

---

## 3. THE OPERATING BUSINESSES — where the risk actually sits

The Benelux assets going into the spin are stabilising. VodafoneZiggo added 7,200 broadband customers, its best quarter in more than six years, plus 31,700 postpaid mobile customers, with fixed revenue per user up 0.6%. Telenet added 6,100 broadband and 2,200 postpaid customers. That matters: the asset being separated is improving into the event.

The problem is the asset **not** being separated. Virgin Media O2, the UK business Liberty owns half of alongside Telefónica, is deteriorating. Revenue fell 7.9% on a like-for-like basis; it lost 28,200 broadband and 63,000 postpaid customers in the quarter; full-year guidance is for revenue and earnings both to decline 3% to 5%, with adjusted free cash flow of only about £200 million against capital spending of £2.0–2.2 billion. Chief financial officer Charles Bracken acknowledged directly that "leverage is above our 4 to 5x target, and that credit spreads are currently elevated," adding that on refinancing "we acknowledge recent trading levels" — an admission the bonds have widened.

This is the honest reason the shares are at a 52-week low. The market is not disputing the Benelux plan; it is marking the UK stake toward zero and questioning whether it stays there.

---

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — rebuilt from the balance sheet

The board entry's $9.50 floor does not survive contact with the tape. Here is what does, per share on roughly 341 million shares:

- **Corporate cash after the Vodafone purchase**, using management's own raised year-end 2026 target of about $2.0 billion: **$5.86**. Note carefully what this cash is for. Fries said the company will "end the year exactly where we started the year from a cash point of view" — the asset sales funded the acquisition of Vodafone's stake. This is a war chest that converts into an illiquid, leveraged telecom holding. It is not distributable to shareholders and there is no buyback supporting the stock.
- **Liberty Growth portfolio** at the appraised $2.9 billion: **$8.50**, with the top five holdings more than half the total. At a 50% haircut for the fact that appraisals are not bids: **$4.25**.
- **Operating telecoms at zero** in the adverse case.

That gives a defensible floor near **$8.00**, roughly 17% below the 27 July close — not the 2% the board entry implied when it was written. For cross-reference, tangible book value (equity less goodwill and other intangibles) is about $13.32 per share, and reported book value about $27.05, against a $9.59 stock.

**Red flags on the floor:** the cash is committed, not free; the portfolio marks are appraisals concentrated in five positions; consolidated net debt is $6.66 billion; free cash flow is currently negative; and there is no dividend or repurchase creating a bid. **Green flags:** the EdgeConneX realisation validated the marks at one large position, more than $4 billion has been refinanced across the credit silos this year, and a further €1.2–1.4 billion of Belgian and Dutch asset sales is under way to cut subsidiary debt, with a Wyre stake sale targeted for year-end 2026 or the first quarter of 2027.

---

## 5. SPONSOR CREDIBILITY

High, with one caveat. This management team has completed a separation of exactly this type before, and the result was good — Sunrise is worth roughly $12 per Liberty Global share to holders who received it. They have beaten their own cash-raising plan this year rather than missed it. They obtained every approval needed for the Dutch stake purchase. They named the incoming leadership. They pulled the timing forward rather than pushing it back. And they told shareholders that internal estimates of the synergies now exceed the $1 billion of net present value previously announced, while declining to publish the higher number — restraint rather than promotion.

The caveat: the equity story they are selling for Ziggo Group rests on 2028 targets, and the value they quote for it is prefaced with "up to". Fries framed the whole endeavour as "from an $18 stock when we announce the Sunrise spin off, we have a clear opportunity to create $37 to $40 of value" — a promotional figure that includes the already-distributed Sunrise shares. Read the parts, not the headline.

---

## 6. WHAT THE DIRECTOR MUST WEIGH

The asymmetry is genuinely attractive and the sponsor is genuinely credible. But the event is roughly eleven months away, carries no record date and no filing, and can be abandoned at the board's discretion — while the company burns cash, the UK stake deteriorates, and no repurchase supports the shares. Nothing forces the market's hand before a listing prospectus exists.

The single most important thing to weigh: **this is a good ratio attached to a slow, soft trigger, entered after the advertised floor already gave way.** The correct response to that is patience with named conditions, not size.

---

## 7. VERIFIED EVENT STATUS

A real, well-progressed, company-guided separation with credible sub-milestones already cleared — but no fixed date, no filing, no binding obligation, and a target window that begins about eleven months out. It is strengthening, not slipping. It is still soft. Re-checked 28 July 2026: no change, no new disclosure since 24 July 2026.

The entry credits $5.86 a share of holding-company cash, drawn from management's raised ~$2.0 billion year-end target, and calls the resulting $8.00 a 'verified floor'. It is not verified.
