LZM.bull_thesis:
Lifezone Metals owns 84% of the Kabanga project in north-west Tanzania -- one of the largest and highest-grade development-ready nickel sulfide deposits in the world -- with the Government of Tanzania holding the other 16%. The July 2025 Feasibility Study (the definitive engineering and economic study that precedes a build decision) put the after-tax net present value (NPV, the discounted value of future cash flows, at an 8% discount rate) at about $1.58 billion, the internal rate of return at 23.3%, payback at 4.5 years, and all-in sustaining costs at $3.36 per pound net of copper and cobalt credits. That cost sits in the cheapest quarter of world supply, so Kabanga earns money even in a poor nickel market. Against that, the whole company is worth about $298 million at $3.31 a share on 28 July 2026 -- roughly a quarter of Lifezone's own attributable share of its study value.

The event that closes the gap is a sale. Lifezone cannot build this itself: pre-production capital is about $942 million, or $950 million to $1.2 billion once financing and construction-period costs are capitalised, against a $298 million market value. So it is running a competitive process through Standard Chartered Bank, which reached term-sheet stage with multiple offers in hand from a pool spanning major miners, sovereign investors and private equity. On the 30 April 2026 call the chief executive said the company had entertained offers for 100% of the project, called the field very competitive with strong contenders, and described the process as very advanced. On 8 June 2026 the company issued a formal response to a Reuters article that had named a specific bidder, confirming that a process to find a new strategic partner exists while declining to discuss parties. That the leak was specific enough to require a response is itself evidence the negotiation is live and well progressed. A clearing bid at a defensible fraction of study value re-rates the equity toward $7.00, which is also the single published sell-side price target.

Three supports make this more than a hope. First, redundancy: three financing tracks run in parallel -- the $60 million Taurus senior secured bridge, Societe Generale-led project finance with development finance institutions and export credit agencies, and the Standard Chartered strategic process. The U.S. Development Finance Corporation completed its due diligence in the first quarter of 2026 and has given an anchor expression of interest, and a United States-Tanzania critical-minerals push adds geopolitical tailwind. Second, the named driver is turning the right way: at our last verification, Indonesian supply discipline was tightening, the first market deficit since 2021 was forecast for 2026, and consensus nickel prices sat well above Kabanga's cost base, so a buyer would be bidding into an improving cycle. (Those specific nickel figures were not re-verified today -- treat the direction as carried forward.) Third, the selling looks close to exhausted: only about 33 million of 90 million shares float freely, the stock has held a $3.02 to $3.33 band for eleven sessions after a roughly 40% fall, and the latest session closed up about 4%. A concluded transaction into that positioning would move the price a long way, quickly.
LZM.bear_thesis:
The catalyst has no date, and the one date the company did give has already passed. Lifezone guided in December 2025 to a final investment decision -- the board's formal commitment to build -- by the middle of 2026. That milestone lapsed with no announcement and no replacement date. On 30 April 2026 the chief executive said the sale process was concluding shortly; eighty-nine days later, as of 28 July 2026, nothing has been announced. The only calendar item that exists is first-half results and an investor webcast on 29 July 2026, and that is a place to hear news, not an event that resolves anything.

Nothing is binding. There is no merger agreement with an outside date, no regulator on a clock, no spin record date, and no contractual payout to shareholders if a partner does appear. Two hard prerequisites for financial close are themselves undated: the Framework Agreement, the binding bilateral instrument governing the fiscal relationship with the Tanzanian government, is under active renegotiation, and the 220kV power line and supply agreements with the national utility are unresolved. A sovereign fiscal negotiation cannot be scheduled.

Management's word has been tested and found wanting. A December 2025 assurance that shareholders would not need to fund the gap was falsified in April 2026 by a $25 million placing of 5.7 million shares at $4.40 -- those buyers are down about a quarter in three months. Third-party analysis published on 25 June 2026 reports that the company has required waivers under its Taurus bridge loan, with covenant fragility and liquidity constraints; the financing meant to carry Lifezone to a build decision has already needed accommodation from its lender. That lender's security sits directly on the shares in Kabanga Nickel Limited itself, ahead of shareholders, and the facility matures on 31 July 2027.

The balance sheet cannot wait indefinitely. At 31 December 2025 the company held $20.1 million of cash against $58.4 million of total debt -- net borrowings of $38.3 million -- while burning about $16.9 million a year in operations and a further $22.0 million in investing, roughly $3.2 million a month. Even after the April raise the company is still net borrowed. And the shape of a 'good' outcome is not unambiguously good for the stock: a strategic investment into the project dilutes the 84% stake at the asset level at the bottom of the cycle rather than paying a premium for the shares, and management has never bridged either structure to a per-share number. If the process drags toward the bridge maturity, this becomes a distressed option on a stranded asset.

1) The process concludes on acceptable terms within twelve months -- 40% weight, $7.00 a share. Discounted from a higher prior because the guided mid-2026 milestone has already lapsed once.

3) Distress: the process fails or is concluded on terms set by the secured lender as the 31 July 2027 bridge maturity approaches -- 30% weight, $2.00 a share, per the asset-backing floor above.

The immediate event is one day away. Interim results on 29 July 2026 will show a first half with no revenue of consequence, continued spending on engineering and exploration, and a cash position that has to be read against the $25 million raised in April. Two questions get answered there whether management likes it or not: why the mid-2026 build decision lapsed, and what the reported waivers under the Taurus bridge actually were.

Behind that sits arithmetic. Cash outflows ran about $16.9 million from operations and $22.0 million from investing in 2025, roughly $3.2 million a month combined, against $20.1 million of cash and $58.4 million of debt at the last filed balance sheet. The April placing bought months, not years. If the strategic process has not concluded by late 2026, the company faces another financing at a price that will by then be lower still -- and the April round, done at $4.40 into a $3.31 market, shows how that goes.

The structural risk is subtler and worse. The good outcome and the bad outcome share a mechanism. A partner injecting capital into Kabanga at anything near today's implied valuation dilutes the 84% stake at the asset level, at the bottom of the cycle, inside the very re-rating shareholders are waiting for. And the Tanzanian Framework Agreement renegotiation is a sovereign fiscal negotiation with its own timetable, immune to shareholder impatience.

The forced selling is already well advanced, and that is the strongest argument for waiting rather than passing outright.

The mechanics are unusually clean. Lifezone came public through a blank-cheque merger, which leaves a shareholder base of event-driven money that bought a build decision rather than a decade-long development story. That milestone was guided for mid-2026 and did not arrive. The shares fell roughly 40% while a competitive sale process was supposedly reaching its conclusion, which is the signature of holders leaving on the clock rather than on the facts. Only about 33 million of 90 million shares float freely, so a modest amount of determined selling moves this price a great deal -- in both directions.

Two markers suggest the seller is close to done. The stock has held a $3.02 to $3.33 range for eleven sessions after that fall, and the latest session closed up about 4% into the results announcement. But a quiet base on thin volume ahead of a scheduled disclosure is more plausibly an absence of sellers than the arrival of buyers, and the April placing at $4.40 planted a fresh cohort of underwater holders who become supply on any bounce. The washout is late-stage, not complete.
LZM.moderator_conclusion:
This is a real event on a broken clock, and the discipline that makes this funnel work is the discipline to say so.

Start with what is true. Kabanga is a genuine tier-one orebody -- among the largest and highest-grade development-ready nickel sulfide deposits anywhere, in the cheapest quarter of the cost curve, with an independently prepared study value of $1.58 billion against a $298 million company. The sale process is real, competitive and advanced, corroborated by a wire-service leak specific enough that the company had to respond on 8 June 2026. If it concludes at a defensible fraction of study value, $7.00 is a defensible number and this roughly doubles.

Now what is not true. This is not a defined-risk event position, and treating it as one is the error the catalyst discipline exists to prevent. There is no date: the guided mid-2026 build decision lapsed silently, and 'concluding shortly' was said eighty-nine days ago. There is nothing binding: no agreement, no outside date, no regulator on a clock, no contractual payout. Two hard prerequisites -- a sovereign fiscal amendment and a utility power agreement -- are themselves undated, and one of them cannot be scheduled by anybody. And the floor our board carried at $2.60 is folklore. There is no net cash beneath this price (the company is $38 million net borrowed), no deal-break level, no recovery claim -- only a secured lender whose collateral is the shares in the project company itself and whose facility has reportedly already required waivers. On asset backing the honest floor is about $2.00.

So the arithmetic looks like a special situation -- +111% to the event-win against -40% to the floor, about 2.8 to 1, with a probability-weighted fair value of $4.35 -- while the structure does not. Our rule says a hard, dated catalyst inside the window with a verified floor earns an aggressive entry and should not be reflexively capped. The converse of that rule is that a serially slipping, undated process with a floor that failed verification must be penalised, and it is penalised here. Add a management team whose December 2025 no-dilution assurance was falsified by an April 2026 placing at $4.40 -- 25% above today's price -- and the credibility discount is earned, not reflexive.

The recommendation is to wait for the wash-out rather than pass. The distinction is deliberate. This is not a broken thesis; it is an unpriced clock. The next genuine information point is one day away, on 29 July 2026, when management must produce the concluded process or explain a second missed milestone, and must be asked about the reported bridge-loan waivers. Committing capital the day before that is paying for optionality we can buy tomorrow with better information. If a partner is announced with terms that leave shareholders exposed to the upside rather than diluted into it, the case re-rates immediately and we can pay up for certainty. If the milestone slips again, the entry is materially lower and the floor question gets answered the hard way. Either way, tomorrow tells us more than any position sized today can earn.
LZM.interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Lifezone Metals Limited (LZM)
### Event-driven special situation | Driver: supply timing | Prepared 28 July 2026

**Bottom line up front.** Lifezone owns one of the best undeveloped nickel deposits on earth and cannot afford to build it. The entire investment case therefore rests on one private negotiation: the sale of a stake in — possibly all of — the Kabanga nickel-copper-cobalt project in north-west Tanzania, run for the company by Standard Chartered Bank. That process is real and competitive. It is also late, undated, and now eighty-nine days past the point at which the chief executive told the market it would conclude "shortly."

Today, 28 July 2026, the shares trade at $3.31, valuing the whole company at about $298 million. The 52-week range is $3.02 to $6.40; the 50-day average price is $4.20 and the 200-day is $4.49. The flagship project needs roughly $942 million of construction capital. The single published sell-side price target is $7.00.

One thing has changed since our examination yesterday, and it is procedural rather than substantive. On 27 July 2026 the company confirmed that first-half 2026 interim results will be published on **29 July 2026**, with an investor webcast at 10:00 a.m. New York time hosted by chief executive Chris Showalter and chief financial officer Ingo Hofmaier. That is a genuine dated venue at which management must address a milestone it has missed. It is not the catalyst. It is the room in which we find out about the catalyst.

**A note on verification.** General web search was unavailable when this dossier was prepared (the session's search allowance was spent). Everything dated below was confirmed today against the company's own press-release wire and live market data — not from memory. What could not be re-confirmed today is flagged as carried forward rather than presented as fresh.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has moved from *proving the orebody* to *proving that somebody will fund it*. The second question is proving far harder than the first.

- **July 2025 — the technical case lands.** The Feasibility Study (the definitive engineering and economic study that precedes a build decision) confirmed Kabanga as one of the largest, highest-grade, development-ready nickel sulfide deposits in the world: an after-tax net present value (NPV — the discounted value of future cash flows, here at an 8% discount rate) of about $1.58 billion, an internal rate of return of 23.3%, a 4.5-year payback, and all-in sustaining costs of $3.36 per pound net of copper and cobalt credits. That cost sits in the cheapest quarter of world supply, meaning Kabanga would still earn money in a poor nickel market.
- **December 2025 — a date is offered, and an assurance with it.** Management guided toward a final investment decision (the board's formal commitment to build, known in the industry as FID) by the middle of 2026, and indicated that shareholders would not need to fund the gap.
- **22–23 April 2026 — the assurance is falsified.** The company priced and closed a $25 million registered direct offering: 5.7 million shares at $4.40 each. Those buyers are down roughly a quarter in three months.
- **30 April 2026 — "shortly."** On the first-quarter call the chief executive said the company had entertained offers for 100% of the project, described the field as very competitive with strong contenders, and characterised the process as very advanced and concluding shortly.
- **8 June 2026 — the leak.** Reuters named a specific bidder. The company issued a formal response: it does not comment on speculation about specific parties "in connection with the process to find a new strategic partner," and material updates will come when appropriate. The response confirms the process exists and is advanced enough to leak. It supplies no date and no price.
- **19 June 2026 — a mechanical upgrade.** Zacks raised the shares to a Buy rank on estimate revisions. This is a screen output, not information about the deal.
- **25 June 2026 — the uncomfortable third-party read.** A published analysis rated the shares a hold at $4.50 and reported that the company has required **waivers under its Taurus bridge loan**, citing covenant fragility, liquidity constraints and persistent dilution risk, and concluding that binding financing terms have not arrived. If accurate, the financing meant to carry Lifezone to a build decision has already needed accommodation from its lender.
- **Mid-2026 — the milestone lapses.** The guided build decision passed without an announcement and without a replacement date.
- **9 July 2026 — a sustainability report.** Genuine work; no bearing on the funding question.
- **27 July 2026 — a venue is scheduled.** Interim results and webcast set for 29 July 2026.

The pattern is consistent: the *project* advances while the *equity* decays. What has decayed is the financing clock, the balance sheet, and the credibility of every date management has offered.

---

## 2. IS THE CATALYST REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

Take the three tests in turn.

**Real — yes.** This is not a rumour the company has declined to confirm. Lifezone has publicly acknowledged a process to find a new strategic partner, has said multiple offers reached term-sheet stage from a pool spanning major miners, sovereign investors and private equity, and has said it entertained offers for the whole project. A national wire service obtained a specific bidder name. Standard Chartered is a real bank running a real auction.

**Dated — no.** There is no regulatory decision on a calendar, no merger agreement with an outside date, no spin record date, no regulator on a clock. There is a private negotiation whose only guided date has already lapsed. The 29 July results call is a *disclosure* date, not a *resolution* date. The only genuine deadline in the structure is the Taurus bridge maturity on 31 July 2027, and that is a deadline for the lender's benefit, not the shareholder's.

**Binding — no.** Nothing contractually compels a counterparty to transact, and nothing contractually pays shareholders anything if one does. This is the crucial distinction between this name and a merger-arbitrage position: in an arbitrage, the payout is written down and the risk is that it fails. Here neither the payout nor the timing is written down anywhere.

Two further gates sit behind the deal, both undated. The Framework Agreement — the legally binding bilateral instrument governing the fiscal relationship with the Government of Tanzania, which holds the other 16% of Kabanga — is under active renegotiation covering the staging concept and the sharing of fiscal benefits, and its completion is a prerequisite for financial close. The 220kV power line and supply agreements with the national utility sit in the same bucket. One of these is a sovereign fiscal negotiation, which by its nature cannot be scheduled.

---

## 3. CREDIBILITY OF THE SPONSOR

Management is technically capable and promotionally overconfident, and the gap between those two facts is the risk.

- They delivered a Feasibility Study that stands up to independent scrutiny, consolidated control of the asset, produced first platinum, palladium and rhodium from the recycling pilot in April 2026, and opened a second orebody option in Burundi. Execution on things they control is good.
- They said shareholders would not be diluted, then diluted them four months later at a price now 25% above the market.
- They said the sale process would conclude shortly, on the record, on 30 April 2026. Eighty-nine days have passed.
- They allowed a guided build decision to lapse without volunteering a replacement date.
- A vocabulary substitution runs through the transcripts: "toward a 2026 final investment decision" became a description of transitioning into engineering execution readiness. One is a commitment; the other is an activity. The company stopped promising an event and started describing work.

The most revealing sentence management has said was said almost in passing: *they have entertained offers for 100% of the project.* A team confident it can fund and build does not run a whole-asset sale in parallel. The strategic process is not opportunism. It is the plan.

**Credibility on the specific claim that matters — that a transaction is close — is moderate.** The Reuters leak corroborates it independently, which is worth more than management's own assurances at this point. But a leak also tells you information is escaping a negotiation the company cannot control, which weakens its hand on price.

---

## 4. THE VERIFIED DOWNSIDE FLOOR

Our board carried a $2.60 floor. **It does not survive examination, and neither does any other simple floor.** Test each candidate backstop against the filed numbers.

*Net cash?* No. The last filed balance sheet, at 31 December 2025, shows $20.1 million of cash against $58.4 million of total debt — net borrowings of $38.3 million. The April 2026 raise added $25 million gross, against an operating cash burn of about $16.9 million and investing outflows of about $22.0 million in 2025, roughly $3.2 million a month combined. Pro forma, the company is still net borrowed. There is no cash floor.

*A deal-break price?* No. Lifezone is not a target under a signed agreement. There is nothing to break.

*A recovery or earnings claim?* No. The company is pre-revenue apart from small laboratory income. Reported book equity of about $73 million, or roughly $0.81 a share, is not a floor either — it is dominated by revaluation and reclassification lines rather than realisable value.

*Asset backing?* This is the only real one, and it is a range rather than a level. Lifezone's 84% of a $1.58 billion study value is about $1.33 billion attributable. Today's $298 million market value, plus $38 million of net debt, implies the market is paying roughly **25% of attributable study value**. A distressed sale into a lender-driven process would plausibly clear nearer 15% — about $200 million, less net debt, or roughly **$1.80 a share**. Adding room for further dilution at depressed prices during a drawn-out process, the honest floor is **approximately $2.00**, not $2.60.

And the security matters: the Taurus facility is senior secured **on the shares in Kabanga Nickel Limited itself**. In distress, the lender's claim sits directly on the only asset, ahead of shareholders. That is what sits beneath this price — not cash, not a contract, but a secured lender whose facility has reportedly already required waivers.

---

## 5. WHAT NOBODY HAS ASKED

- **Stake sale or whole-asset sale?** These are radically different outcomes for the equity. A strategic investment *into* the project dilutes the 84% stake; it does not pay a premium for the stock. A sale of 100% turns Lifezone into a cash shell plus its hydrometallurgical intellectual property. Management has never bridged either to a per-share number.
- **What are the waivers?** The Taurus covenant reports have not been put to management on the record. This should be Wednesday's first question.
- **When does the Framework Agreement amendment complete?** Nobody has forced a date, and management has not volunteered one.
- **Why did the shares fall roughly 40% while a competitive, near-complete sale process was running?** That question has never been asked on a call.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Red flags**
- The guided mid-2026 build decision lapsed with no announcement and no replacement date.
- "Concluding shortly" was said on 30 April 2026; nothing by 28 July 2026 — eighty-nine days.
- December 2025's no-dilution assurance was falsified by the April 2026 raise at $4.40, now 25% underwater.
- Reported waivers under the Taurus bridge (third-party analysis, 25 June 2026).
- The debt is senior secured on the Kabanga shares themselves — the lender's claim sits on the only asset, ahead of equity.
- Two undated sovereign and utility gates are hard prerequisites for financial close.
- BHP, the natural owner and funder, exited rather than committed.
- Single asset, single jurisdiction, pre-revenue, funding requirement roughly three times market value.
- Thin trading: only about 33 million of 90 million shares are free-floating, so an orderly exit on bad news is unreliable.

**Green flags**
- The orebody is genuinely tier-one and first-quartile on cost, corroborated by an independent study rather than merely asserted.
- Competitive tension is real: multiple term-sheet-stage offers, offers entertained for the whole project, and a wire-service leak specific enough to force a company response.
- Three financing tracks run in parallel — the Taurus bridge, Société Générale-led project finance with development finance institutions and export credit agencies, and the Standard Chartered strategic process. Redundancy is genuine risk reduction.
- The U.S. Development Finance Corporation completed diligence with an anchor expression of interest, and a United States-Tanzania critical-minerals push adds geopolitical tailwind.
- The nickel backdrop — the named driver — was improving at our last verification: tightening Indonesian supply discipline, a first forecast market deficit since 2021, prices comfortably above Kabanga's cost base. Carried forward, not re-confirmed today.
- The shares have stopped falling: eleven sessions in a $3.02 to $3.33 band, and the latest close was up about 4%.
- A confirmed, dated venue one day out.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The floor was folklore.** The $2.60 our board carried has no identifiable mechanism behind it and appears extrapolated from recent trading — which has already printed $3.02.
- **The asymmetry may point the wrong way at the asset level.** If a partner injects capital into Kabanga near the currently implied valuation, existing shareholders are diluted at the asset level, at the bottom of the cycle, inside the very re-rating they are waiting for.
- **A quiet base is not accumulation.** Eleven sessions of stability on thin volume ahead of a scheduled disclosure is more plausibly an absence of sellers than the arrival of buyers.
- **One analyst, one target.** The published consensus target of $7.00 has a high and a low of $7.00 — it is a single estimate, not a distribution. There is no crowd here to be wrong.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: deteriorating**, with the qualification that the project advances while the equity decays. The engineering, permitting groundwork, development-finance diligence and nickel market have all moved forward. What has decayed is the financing clock, the balance sheet, the credibility of management's dates and, if the waiver reports are right, the company's standing with its own lender. The director is buying the equity, not the orebody.

**Economic moat: none, and the concept largely does not apply.** A pre-revenue single-asset developer has no durable earnings base to defend. The irreplaceability of the orebody is real — a tier-one, first-quartile-cost nickel sulfide deposit cannot be competed into existence — but an undeveloped, unfunded resource is an option, not a franchise.

**Secular threat: manageable, arguably favourable.** The named worry, Indonesian oversupply, is cyclical rather than terminal, and the energy transition supports long-run demand for a low-cost sulfide deposit. The cheapness here is a financing and control problem, not a melting-terminal-value problem.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:**

Both halves of the special-situation discipline fail. The catalyst has no date and no contract, and is gated behind a sovereign fiscal amendment and a utility agreement that cannot be scheduled. Beneath the price sits not cash, not a deal-break level, not a recovery claim, but a secured lender whose collateral is the only asset. If the process concludes well, $7.00 is defensible and this roughly doubles. If it drags toward the July 2027 bridge maturity, the equity does not stop at $2.60 — it becomes a distressed option on a stranded asset, and $2.00 is the honest mark.

Size this as an undated option on a very good orebody, not as a defined-risk event trade. And note that the next genuine information point is one day away, on 29 July 2026, where management must either produce the concluded process or explain a second missed milestone. There is no good reason to commit capital in front of it.

skeptic.kill_fact: The floor has no mechanism, and four facts in the company's own filings -- none of which the dossier carries -- sit beneath it. (1) THE ISSUER DECLARES GOING-CONCERN DOUBT, AND THE BRIDGE CANNOT FUND THE COMPANY. The FY2025 Form 20-F, signed 19 March 2026, states: 'These conditions give rise to substantial doubt about our ability to continue as a going concern.' Critically, it also states that the $60 million bridge 'is ringfenced for the Kabanga Nickel Project', so corporate overheads, the Glencore PGM recycling investment and the IP segment 'will require near-term and alternative funding solutions', and that 'such solutions, which are required within the next 6 months, might include further equity offerings at the Lifezone Metals level.' Six months from that filing is about September 2026. This destroys the most favourable reading of the liquidity position: the $18.3 million still undrawn under the facility is NOT available to keep the parent alive, and the 20-F names further LZM-level equity as the expected route. The dossier never mentions the going-concern disclosure once, nor the ringfencing, across a document that purports to test what backstops the price. (2) SHAREHOLDERS HAVE NO ANTI-DILUTION PROTECTION. The same 20-F: 'the holders of Lifezone Ordinary Shares are not entitled to any preemptive rights or anti-dilution rights', and 'equity financing would dilute existing shareholders, who do not have pre-emptive or anti-dilution rights under our Articles of Association.' A declared going concern plus a named equity route plus no anti-dilution right is an unbounded downside, not a $2.00 floor. (3) THE COVENANT BREACH IS FILED, DATED, AND MISDATED BY THE DOSSIER. The 20-F sets a hard financial covenant: 'Lifezone is subject to financial covenants requiring it to maintain a current ratio of at least 1.1:1 on a consolidated basis while any amounts remain outstanding under the facility', plus a $5 million minimum cash balance at KNL. The Form 6-K furnished 29 June 2026 discloses that a waiver letter was executed on 7 MARCH 2026 by Lifezone, Kabanga Nickel Limited and Taurus, and that the company paid for it on 29 June 2026 with warrants over 500,000 ordinary shares at $6.25, five-year term. So the accommodation is not a 25 June third-party report that 'if accurate' would show fragility, and it is not an open question for the results call: it is a company-filed fact, dated nearly five months before the dossier places it, executed BEFORE the April placing and before management's 30 April 'concluding shortly' remark. The dossier also misses the 29 June 6-K entirely -- its timeline runs 25 June straight to 9 July. (4) THE FIRST BIG MONEY REPAYS THE LENDER, NOT THE EQUITY. The 20-F discloses a mandatory prepayment: KNL 'must apply any amounts received by it as repayment of the $60 million senior secured bridge loan facility on the date 10 business days after receipt' of proceeds from any transaction incurring financial indebtedness or any streaming, royalty, metals-prepay or forward transaction, 'provided that the total amount made available ... is at least $200 million' and funds Kabanga. The SocGen-led project financing that must accompany any build decision is precisely such a transaction. The security is on the shares in KNL itself, and a six-month maturity extension costs a further 1,500,000 warrants -- dilution priced into exactly the slip scenario being underwritten. Taken together: an issuer-declared going concern with a ~September 2026 parent-level funding need, no anti-dilution rights, a first-ranking lender that has already extracted equity once and holds a sweep over the refinancing, and a $2.00 'floor' derived by analogy to a peer trading multiple -- which is the identical criticism the dossier levels at the $2.60 it discards, and it fails the same test. A 2.8-to-1 ratio measured against an unbounded downside is not a defined-risk special situation, and this entry must not be carried as one.

MLYS.bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a dated, well-supported regulatory decision on 22 December 2026 converts Mineralys from a speculative clinical-stage company into the owner of a commercial cardiovascular drug, and that the market has already marked the shares down for the wrong reason.

Start with the event itself. The United States Food and Drug Administration accepted the filing for lorundrostat in March 2026 and set a decision date of 22 December 2026. That date has not moved. No advisory committee meeting has been called, which is normally a sign the agency does not think it needs outside help with the risk-benefit question. The filing rests on two registrational studies, the Phase 3 Launch-HTN trial and the Phase 2 Advance-HTN trial, both showing clinically meaningful reductions in systolic blood pressure on top of existing therapy, within a body of five completed successful Phase 2/3 trials.

The strongest single piece of evidence for approval is external. On 15 May 2026 the same agency approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, sold as Baxfendy, as the first aldosterone synthase inhibitor for adults with uncontrolled high blood pressure. Aldosterone synthase is the enzyme that makes aldosterone, the hormone that raises blood pressure and damages the heart and kidneys over time; lorundrostat blocks the same enzyme. The regulator has therefore already accepted the mechanism, the blood-pressure endpoint and the safety management that goes with it. A second entrant with two positive registrational trials into a class the agency has just blessed is about as de-risked as a first approval gets. A reasonable probability of approval is around 90%.

The second pillar is that management has voted with real money. On 3 June 2026 Mineralys paid Tanabe $200 million in cash to extinguish the royalty on lorundrostat and to secure assignment of the related patents, funding it with $150 million of stock sold at $26.50 a share and $100 million drawn from a new senior secured loan facility of up to $500 million from Pharmakon. Boards that doubt an approval do not spend $200 million buying out a royalty on an unapproved drug at a depressed share price. The consequence is that Mineralys will keep 100% of lorundrostat's future economics and own the underlying intellectual property outright, which both raises the value of a successful launch and makes the company a far cleaner acquisition target.

The third pillar is the size of the prize relative to what is priced. TD Cowen sizes the aldosterone synthase inhibitor market at more than $5 billion and expects an even split between the two drugs, with Mineralys plausibly securing a better label and better pricing and access. Post-selloff price targets from analysts who have refreshed their work sit at $42 at Goldman Sachs (4 June 2026), $48 at Guggenheim, $54 at LifeSci Capital and $56 at H.C. Wainwright, with a consensus near $49 against a live price of $26.71. Stripping out roughly $540 million of net cash, the market is valuing the drug itself at about $1.8 billion — less than one times a plausible peak-sales figure for a chronic cardiovascular medicine with patent protection.

The fourth pillar is positioning. The shares are down about 44% from a 52-week high of $47.65 and trade below both the 50-day average near $27.03 and the 200-day average near $31.87. Roughly 14.4% of the freely traded shares are sold short, a position that has grown about 22% over the past year. The June equity offering at $26.50 cleared a supply overhang and reset the marginal holder. An approval into that positioning has the fuel for a sharp move.

The conditions that must hold: the December date must not slip and no advisory committee may be called; the label must be broad enough to compete, ideally supported by the chronic kidney disease subgroup data presented on 30 May 2026 showing significant blood-pressure and urine-albumin reductions; and the company must not need punitive equity financing before it can show launch traction.
MLYS.bear_thesis:
The bear case is that investors are buying a high-probability event whose reward is already largely in the price, while the punishment for the low-probability outcome is severe and only loosely bounded.

Begin with the payoff, not the probability. Because AstraZeneca's baxdrostat was approved on 15 May 2026 and reached the market in early June, the December decision has stopped being a question of whether the drug works and become a question of whether anyone will buy it. That means the approval is largely expected, and an expected event does not pay much. A realistic reaction to a clean approval is a re-rate of perhaps 30% to 40%, not a move to the $49 consensus target — those targets are twelve-month launch valuations that require commercial proof Mineralys cannot deliver for a year or more. Meanwhile a rejection letter, at maybe a one-in-ten chance, would plausibly halve the shares. The shape of the payoff runs the wrong way for an event trade.

Second, the commercial case has been narrowing all year and the market noticed. The Phase 2 Explore-OSA study in obstructive sleep apnoea missed its primary goal on 10 March 2026 — evening-dosed lorundrostat produced no clinically meaningful improvement versus placebo on the apnoea-hypopnoea index. That closed off the second indication and reduced what was pitched as a multi-disease platform to a single-drug, single-indication launch. The chronic kidney disease data that survived is a post-hoc subgroup analysis, useful for the label and for prescribers but not an approval of its own. Bearish sell-side work argues lorundrostat is undifferentiated versus Baxfendy and is structurally disadvantaged in the kidney-disease and SGLT2-combination opportunity. Being seven months late to your own class against a company with a global cardiovascular sales force is a serious handicap that no amount of subgroup data fixes.

Third, the reimbursement wall. Both drugs are add-on therapies. Insurers will almost certainly require patients to fail cheap generic spironolactone — a decades-old drug that also blunts aldosterone — before paying for a branded aldosterone synthase inhibitor. That compresses both the price and the eligible volume for the entire class, and Mineralys, as the second entrant without a big-pharma contracting organisation, negotiates from the weaker position. Management has not addressed this in public materials.

Fourth, the floor is thinner than it looks. Gross cash of roughly $640 million pro forma sounds like protection until you note that the Pharmakon loan is senior secured — the lender's claim ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets, including the cash — and that the remaining three tranches of the $500 million facility carry drawdown conditions the company would likely fail in a rejection scenario. Net of the $100 million drawn, net cash is about $6.15 a share, only 23% of the current $26.71 price. There is also up to $265 million of commercial milestone money still owed to Tanabe, which is a tax on the good outcome. In a rejection, holders are relying not on cash but on the residual worth of a re-fileable asset, and history says that number is set by a demoralised market, not by a formula.

Fifth, the cost of winning. A branded cardiovascular launch against AstraZeneca is expensive. General and administrative spending already more than tripled to $21.0 million in the first quarter of 2026 from $6.6 million a year earlier, before a single prescription. Quarterly net loss was $39.3 million and will widen through the launch. The funding answers — the undrawn $400 million of secured debt and future equity — both cost shareholders, one in interest at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate plus 5.50% with a 3.25% floor, the other in dilution.

What would confirm the bear case: an advisory committee being called or the December date slipping; a narrow or restricted label; early prescription data showing Baxfendy taking the great majority of new starts; or a large equity raise in the first half of 2027 at a price below today's.
MLYS.sop_bull:
The favourable case values the company as the owner of an approved, wholly-owned cardiovascular drug in a class sized at more than $5 billion, with an even share split against the incumbent.

Parts:
- Lorundrostat in uncontrolled and treatment-resistant high blood pressure, United States: peak sales of roughly $1.8 billion to $2.0 billion, achieved in the early 2030s. Valued at about three times peak sales and discounted back at 12% a year, that is roughly $3.0 billion to $3.4 billion of business value. Applying a 90% probability of approval gives about $2.7 billion to $3.1 billion.
- Royalty ownership uplift: the June 2026 Tanabe repurchase removes all future royalties and assigns the underlying patents, so Mineralys keeps 100% of the economics. Net of the up to $265 million of remaining commercial milestones owed to Tanabe (a liability only in the success case), call this a net positive already embedded above, with roughly $0.2 billion deducted for the milestones on a present-value basis.
- Ex-United States and partnering optionality on an approved, wholly-owned asset: roughly $0.3 billion.
- Net cash: about $640 million of gross cash pro forma for the June transactions, less the $100 million senior secured tranche drawn, gives roughly $540 million, or about $6.15 a share.

Sum: approximately $2.9 billion of risk-adjusted drug value plus $0.3 billion of optionality plus $0.54 billion of net cash, less $0.2 billion of milestone present value, equals roughly $3.5 billion. Across about 88.2 million shares, and allowing a modest haircut for launch-period dilution, that supports roughly $38 a share as the value the shares should carry once approval is in hand, rising toward the $42 to $56 range published by Goldman Sachs, Guggenheim, LifeSci Capital and H.C. Wainwright if the launch demonstrably takes share through 2027.
MLYS.sop_bear:
The adverse case is a rejection letter on or around 22 December 2026 — a complete response letter — and values what is left.

Parts:
- Cash: roughly $640 million gross pro forma for the June 2026 offering, the $100 million drawn loan and the $200 million paid to Tanabe. Subtract the $100 million senior secured term loan, which ranks ahead of shareholders, and assume the remaining three tranches of the $500 million facility become undrawable because their conditions would not be met. Net cash roughly $540 million, or about $6.15 a share. This burns down from there at a loss rate that was $39.3 million in the first quarter of 2026.
- Residual asset value: lorundrostat would not be worthless. Two positive registrational trials remain, the mechanism has already been approved by the same agency in the form of AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, and the company now owns the intellectual property. A manufacturing or labelling deficiency is re-fileable within roughly six to twelve months; a clinical or safety deficiency is not. Blend those and carry the asset at roughly $0.6 billion, or about $6.80 a share.
- Pipeline beyond lorundrostat: effectively nil. The obstructive sleep apnoea indication failed its primary endpoint on 10 March 2026 and the chronic kidney disease work is a subgroup of the same drug.

Sum: roughly $540 million of net cash plus about $600 million of residual asset value equals about $1.14 billion, or roughly $13 a share. That figure is corroborated by the market: the shares traded at a 52-week low of $12.59 a year ago, before the pivotal data arrived. It is an estimate of where a demoralised market would clear the stock, not a contractual backstop, and it would be lower still if the rejection cited a safety problem or if the company were forced to raise equity into the wreckage.
MLYS.sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across the two branches of the 22 December 2026 decision. Approval branch, weighted at 90%: about $38 a share, built from roughly $2.9 billion of risk-adjusted value for lorundrostat in uncontrolled high blood pressure (peak sales near $1.8 billion at about three times peak, discounted at 12%), plus about $0.3 billion of ex-United States and partnering optionality, plus about $0.54 billion of net cash, less about $0.2 billion for the remaining Tanabe commercial milestones, across roughly 88.2 million shares with a haircut for launch-period dilution. Rejection branch, weighted at 10%: about $13 a share, being roughly $6.15 of net cash (gross cash near $640 million less the $100 million senior secured loan that ranks ahead of shareholders) plus roughly $6.80 of residual value for a re-fileable asset whose mechanism the agency has already approved. Weighted: 0.90 x $38 + 0.10 x $13 = about $35.50. Sanity check against the street: the consensus target near $49 (range $30 to $56) is a twelve-month launch valuation that assumes commercial share Mineralys has not yet demonstrated; our $35 base case deliberately sits between the market's $26.71 and that consensus, discounting the second-mover position behind AstraZeneca's Baxfendy.
MLYS.risk_reward: About +42% to the $38 approval-resolved target against about -51% to the $13 failure floor — roughly 0.8 to 1 on price alone, which is unattractive in isolation. The odds are what carry it: at a roughly 90% probability of approval the expected value is about $35.50, or +33% from $26.71. This is a favourable-expectancy trade with an unfavourable payoff shape, and the floor is an estimate rather than a contractual backstop, so position size must assume roughly half the capital is genuinely at risk.
MLYS.catalyst_summary: A hard, dated United States regulatory decision on the blood-pressure pill lorundrostat is scheduled for 22 December 2026 — 148 days out — with roughly a nine-in-ten chance of approval worth about $38 a share against a rejection worth about $13, from $26.71 today.
MLYS.dated_milestone: United States Food and Drug Administration target action date for the lorundrostat new drug application: 22 December 2026 (148 days from 27 July 2026). Verified from the company's filing-acceptance announcement in March 2026 and reconfirmed in its first-quarter 2026 results release dated 6 May 2026. The date has not moved and no advisory committee meeting has been announced or scheduled. Secondary dated event: second-quarter 2026 results on 11 August 2026.
MLYS.forcing_function:
The 22 December 2026 decision date is the forcing function, and it is genuinely binding: the agency must issue either an approval or a complete response letter on or about that day, and the clock is set by statute rather than by management's discretion. The stock cannot remain in its current limbo past that date.

Three things make that date unusually decisive here. First, it resolves in one stroke the only question that has kept the shares depressed since the sleep-apnoea failure in March and the competitor approval in May — whether Mineralys owns a commercial product at all. Second, it unlocks the remaining three tranches of the $500 million Pharmakon senior secured facility, whose drawdown conditions are the difference between a funded launch and a dilutive equity raise. Third, it is the gate on any strategic conversation: having paid Tanabe $200 million in June to extinguish the royalty and take assignment of the patents, Mineralys will be a wholly-owned, approved, single-asset cardiovascular company on 23 December — the cleanest possible acquisition target, at a moment when the entire class has just been validated by AstraZeneca's own approval.

Two earlier waypoints matter for timing. Second-quarter results on 11 August 2026 will show the pro-forma balance sheet after the June transactions and the pace of the commercial build. And any announcement of an advisory committee meeting, or a three-month extension of the review clock, would be an immediate and serious negative — the absence of both today is a quiet positive.
MLYS.consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions, which is why this is a four rather than a five.

The market is too pessimistic on the event. The consensus reading of AstraZeneca's baxdrostat approval on 15 May 2026 was that it is bad news for Mineralys, and the shares fell about 25% in six sessions in early June to reflect it. That reading is half wrong. Competitively, yes, it is bad. Regulatorily, it is the best news Mineralys received all year: the agency has now accepted the mechanism, the blood-pressure endpoint and the safety management for this exact class. The probability that lorundrostat is approved on 22 December went up, not down, and the market marked the stock down anyway. Add that the June share sale at $26.50 was forced supply — sold to fund a royalty buyout, not because the business needed rescuing — and the marginal price today reflects mechanics rather than fundamentals. Roughly 14.4% of the free float is sold short into a decision the odds favour.

The market is also too optimistic on the payoff, and this is the part the street will not say aloud. The consensus target of about $49, with published targets of $42 at Goldman Sachs, $48 at Guggenheim, $54 at LifeSci Capital and $56 at H.C. Wainwright, is a twelve-month launch valuation. It embeds commercial share that will not be observable until well into 2027. TD Cowen's assumption of an even split of a $5 billion-plus market between the two drugs is a forecast, not a finding, and it is being made about a drug arriving seven months late against a company with a global cardiovascular sales force. The unaddressed variable in every one of those models is reimbursement: insurers will very likely require patients to fail cheap generic spironolactone before paying for a branded aldosterone synthase inhibitor, which compresses price and eligible volume for the whole class. Nobody has priced that properly because nobody has data on it yet.

Our position is therefore that the December event is worth about $38 a share, not $49, and that this still leaves a 42% gap to today's $26.71. We are buying an under-priced high-probability event, not an under-priced franchise.
MLYS.valley_of_death:
The risky window between now and the decision is unusually mild, which is one of the better features of this setup.

There is no funding cliff. The company held $646.1 million in cash and investments at 31 March 2026 and then transacted from a position of strength on 3 June 2026: $150 million of stock sold at $26.50, $100 million drawn on a new senior secured loan, $200 million paid out to Tanabe. Pro forma gross cash is roughly $640 million against a first-quarter net loss of $39.3 million. There is no maturity wall — the Pharmakon loan runs to June 2031 — and no covenant test that a pre-revenue company would obviously trip before December. Management's stated runway extends into 2028. The financing was done ahead of the event rather than into it, which removes the single most common way these trades go wrong.

The real hazards in the next three to nine months are informational rather than financial. First, an announcement of an advisory committee meeting or a three-month extension of the review clock. Neither has happened, and the absence of both this late in a standard review is meaningfully reassuring, but either would hit the shares hard and immediately. Second, competitive data points: AstraZeneca's Baxfendy has been available since early June 2026, so by the fourth quarter there will be early prescription trends, formulary decisions and payer policies visible for the class. If those show insurers imposing hard step-therapy through generic spironolactone, or Baxfendy locking up formulary positions before Mineralys can even file for coverage, the launch model degrades before Mineralys sells a single pill. Third, second-quarter results on 11 August 2026 will show general and administrative spending continuing to climb — it already more than tripled to $21.0 million from $6.6 million a year earlier — and a widening loss, which reads badly to anyone not underwriting the launch.

The fourth hazard is the one nobody can hedge: a rejection letter. It is roughly a one-in-ten event, and it happens on a known day. There is no way to be long this name into 22 December and not own that risk. The mitigation is sizing, not cleverness.
MLYS.positioning_washout:
The forced-selling has largely already happened, and that is a significant part of why this is actionable now rather than in the autumn.

Three waves cleared the register in the first half of 2026. The sleep-apnoea failure on 10 March removed the platform narrative and with it the growth-oriented specialists who owned the multi-indication story. AstraZeneca's approval on 15 May removed the first-in-class premium. Then on 3 June the company itself put 5.66 million new shares into the market at $26.50 — about 6.4% dilution — to fund the Tanabe royalty buyout, which is the purest form of mechanical supply: stock sold for a corporate purpose, into a falling tape, with no regard for price. The shares lost about 25% over six sessions and the market value fell by roughly $650 million. From a 52-week high of $47.65 the stock is down about 44%, and it sits below both its 50-day average near $27.03 and its 200-day average near $31.87.

What remains is a shareholder base that has been fully re-priced at $26.50 and a short position of roughly 9.5 million shares, about 14.4% of the freely traded stock, which has grown about 22% over the past year. That is a large, one-sided bet against a binary event whose odds favour the other side. Short positions of that size into a scheduled, statutory decision date have a characteristic behaviour: they must either be covered before the date or carried through it, and the cost of carrying them rises as the date approaches and options premiums inflate. Either path is a source of demand into December.

One caution against reading this as pure fuel. The buyers of the June offering at $26.50 are underwater and unlikely to add. And the reason the short interest exists is not irrational — it is a legitimate bet that a second-to-market drug into a big-pharma-dominated class will disappoint commercially. Those shorts do not need the December decision to go their way; they need 2027 prescription data to go their way. A washout in the shareholder base is not, by itself, a thesis.
MLYS.moderator_conclusion:
This is a buy now, sized as a defined-odds bet rather than a defined-risk one — and the distinction matters enough that it is what holds the conviction at four instead of five.

The setup is genuine. There is a hard, statutory, dated event: the United States Food and Drug Administration must decide on lorundrostat, Mineralys's once-daily blood-pressure pill, on or about 22 December 2026 — 148 days from today. The date has not moved since it was set in March. No advisory committee has been called. The filing rests on two registrational trials within five successful Phase 2/3 studies. And most importantly, on 15 May 2026 the same agency approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, which blocks the identical enzyme for the identical patients — meaning the regulator has already accepted the mechanism, the endpoint and the safety profile of this class. A second entrant into a freshly validated class, with a clean review and no committee, is about a nine-in-ten proposition.

Management has staked real money on the same view. In June it paid Tanabe $200 million cash to extinguish the royalty on a drug that is not yet approved and to take assignment of the patents, funded with $150 million of stock at $26.50 and $100 million of a new $500 million senior secured facility. Nobody does that at a depressed price if they expect a rejection letter. It also leaves Mineralys, on 23 December, as a wholly-owned, approved, single-asset cardiovascular company — the cleanest acquisition target imaginable in a class a major pharmaceutical company has just proven out.

And the price has been washed out for reasons that are only half about the fundamentals. The shares are $26.71, down about 44% from a 52-week high of $47.65, below both the 50-day and 200-day averages, with about 14.4% of the free float sold short. Some of that decline is legitimate — the sleep-apnoea study failed its primary endpoint in March, which killed the platform story. Some of it is mechanical — a forced 6.4% equity issue in June into a falling tape. Against a street consensus target near $49, with refreshed post-selloff targets from $42 to $56, the gap is real.

Now the honest part. Two of the three legs a top-conviction event trade requires are here; the third is not.

First, the payoff is negatively skewed. Because the competitor was approved in May, the approval is expected — and expected events do not pay much. A clean approval is worth perhaps a 30% to 40% move, to roughly $38, not to the $49 consensus, which is a twelve-month launch valuation requiring commercial proof that will not exist until deep into 2027. A rejection letter roughly halves the stock. So the shape is +42% against -51%, about 0.8 to 1. It is the odds that make this work — 0.90 x $38 plus 0.10 x $13 gives a base-case value near $35.50, or +33% from here — not the ratio.

Second, and this is the binding constraint, the downside floor is soft. There is no deal price, no contractual payout, no cash backstop near the market. Gross cash of roughly $640 million looks like protection until you note the Pharmakon loan is senior secured — the lender ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets, including that cash — and that the remaining three tranches carry conditions a rejected company would fail. Net cash is about $6.15 a share, just 23% of the price. The realistic $13 support level is our estimate of where a re-fileable asset in an already-approved class would clear, corroborated only by where the stock traded a year ago before the pivotal data. That is a judgement, not a floor, and it is why the margin-of-safety score is a two while the event score is a four.

The timing call: enter now rather than waiting. The reason is asymmetric information flow between here and December. The two things that would break the thesis — an advisory committee being called or the review clock being extended — get less likely with every week that passes this late in a standard review, while the reward for owning the position does not improve by waiting. Second-quarter results on 11 August will show a widening loss and a heavier commercial build, which may offer a slightly better entry, but that is a coin-flip against the risk of the shorts starting to cover into the autumn.

Size it accordingly: a full-conviction thesis at half-conviction size. Underwrite as though roughly half the capital is genuinely at risk on a single day in December, because it is. The correct trim triggers are an advisory committee announcement, a review-clock extension, or early fourth-quarter evidence that insurers are enforcing hard step-therapy through generic spironolactone across the class. The correct hold-through is a clean approval with a broad label — at which point the second question, whether a second-mover can take share from AstraZeneca, becomes the whole thesis and deserves to be re-underwritten from scratch.
MLYS.interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier — Mineralys Therapeutics, Inc. (MLYS)

**Event-driven special situation. Prepared 27 July 2026. Live price $26.71; market value about $2.35 billion on roughly 88.2 million shares.**

This is not a business-quality case. Mineralys has no product on the market and no revenue. The entire question is whether a single, dated regulatory event — the United States Food and Drug Administration's decision on its blood-pressure pill, due 22 December 2026 — resolves favourably, what the shares are worth if it does, and what actually stops the fall if it does not.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Mineralys told investors two years ago was a platform story. Lorundrostat, its once-daily pill, blocks aldosterone synthase — the enzyme that makes aldosterone, a hormone that raises blood pressure and, over time, damages the heart and kidneys. Management framed this as a mechanism that could be pointed at several diseases at once: hard-to-treat high blood pressure first, then chronic kidney disease, then obstructive sleep apnoea (the condition where breathing repeatedly stops during sleep).

That story has narrowed sharply, and the narrowing has been forced rather than chosen.

- **The core indication delivered.** Two registrational trials — the Phase 3 Launch-HTN study and the Phase 2 Advance-HTN study — both showed clinically meaningful reductions in systolic blood pressure on top of existing therapy. The company has now completed five successful Phase 2/3 trials in total. The regulatory filing rests on this body of work.
- **The second leg broke.** On 10 March 2026, alongside the announcement that the FDA had accepted the filing, Mineralys disclosed that its Phase 2 Explore-OSA sleep-apnoea study missed its primary goal: evening-dosed lorundrostat did not produce a clinically meaningful improvement versus placebo on the apnoea-hypopnoea index (the standard count of breathing interruptions per hour). Blood pressure still fell handsomely in that population — 11.1 mmHg from baseline, 6.2 mmHg placebo-adjusted — but the sleep-apnoea indication itself is, for now, gone.
- **The kidney leg survived as a label argument, not a new market.** At the European hypertension meeting on 30 May 2026, a post-hoc analysis of Launch-HTN showed significant blood-pressure reduction and reduced urine albumin (a marker of kidney damage) in patients who also had chronic kidney disease. That is useful commercial ammunition for the label and for prescribers. It is not a separate approval.
- **A competitor got there first.** On 15 May 2026 the FDA approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, marketed as Baxfendy, as the first aldosterone synthase inhibitor for adults with uncontrolled high blood pressure, available from early June 2026. Mineralys is now, definitively, second to market in its own class, roughly seven months behind, against a competitor with a global sales force.

The net effect: what was sold as a multi-indication platform is now a single-drug, single-indication commercial launch into a market where a large rival is already detailing physicians.

## 2. CLAIMS versus THE NUMBERS (forensic)

| Management's claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Five positive clinical trials support the filing" | Filing accepted by the FDA in March 2026 with a standard review clock and a 22 December 2026 decision date. No advisory committee meeting has been announced — the agency has not signalled it needs outside help on the risk-benefit question. | Holds. The regulatory package is genuinely strong. |
| "Cash funds us into 2028" | $646.1 million in cash and investments at 31 March 2026, down only $10.5 million from $656.6 million at year-end 2025, because $6.0 million of interest income and a lighter research bill offset the loss. | Holds, and the balance was strengthened further in June. |
| "The royalty repurchase strengthens the balance sheet" | Partly true and partly spin. On 3 June 2026 the company paid Tanabe $200 million upfront to extinguish the royalty on lorundrostat and secure assignment of the related patents, funded by $150 million of new stock at $26.50 a share and $100 million drawn on a new senior secured loan. | Mixed. It removes a permanent revenue tax and buys the underlying intellectual property — a real, lasting gain. But it converted a contingent obligation into cash out the door plus first-ranking debt, and it diluted holders by about 6.4% at a depressed price. |
| Cost discipline | Research spending fell to $24.4 million in the first quarter of 2026 from $37.9 million a year earlier, while general and administrative spending more than tripled to $21.0 million from $6.6 million. Quarterly net loss $39.3 million. | Consistent with a company shifting from trials to launch preparation. The commercial build is real money being spent before a single prescription exists. |

The financing structure deserves close reading, because it is what defines the downside. The Pharmakon facility is a **senior secured** term loan of up to $500 million across four tranches, $100 million funded at closing, maturing June 2031, priced at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (with a 3.25% floor) plus a 5.50% margin — call it high-single-digit to low-double-digit interest. Senior secured means the lender's claim ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets, including its cash. Any calculation of "the shares are backstopped by the cash pile" must subtract that debt first, and must assume the remaining three tranches carry drawdown conditions the company may not meet in a bad scenario.

There are also up to $265 million of commercial milestone payments still owed to Tanabe over time — $100 million newly agreed plus $165 million pre-existing. Those only trigger on commercial success, so they are a tax on the good outcome, not a risk in the bad one, but they must be netted out of any launch valuation.

## 3. TONE AND CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rising on regulation, defensive on commerce. Management's language around the filing is precise and unhedged — a firm date, a defined package, no talk of information requests or review extensions. Management's language around the competitive setup has become noticeably more conditional: the pitch has shifted from "first in a new class" to arguments about label breadth, the kidney-disease subgroup, and market access.

The most informative signal is not verbal. In June, with the shares near a low, the board chose to spend $200 million of hard cash and take on secured debt to buy out a royalty on a drug that is not yet approved. Companies that doubt an approval do not do that. It is the single most credible statement of internal confidence in the file.

Against that, one governance detail cuts the other way: a roughly $350,000 insider sale in June 2026, reported ahead of the December decision. Small in absolute terms and likely routine, but worth noting when the whole thesis is a binary event.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

High on timelines, unproven on commerce. Mineralys has hit its stated regulatory milestones: trials read out, filing submitted, filing accepted, decision date assigned and unchanged since March. Cash guidance has held. The company has funded itself well ahead of the event rather than into it — a discipline many small biotechs fail.

What has never been tested is commercial delivery. Nobody at Mineralys has sold this drug to a payer or a cardiologist. Every revenue figure in every analyst model is a forecast with no observed data behind it.

Reliability: **High** on process, **Untested** on launch.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur and none has a satisfying answer yet.

1. **Differentiation versus baxdrostat.** Sell-side opinion is genuinely split. TD Cowen's Tara Bancroft sizes the aldosterone-synthase market at more than $5 billion, expects an even split between the two drugs, and argues Mineralys wins on label and pricing. Bearish commentary argues lorundrostat is undifferentiated and structurally disadvantaged in the kidney-disease and SGLT2-combination opportunity where AstraZeneca has more to work with. Management's answer leans on the kidney subgroup data, which is post-hoc.
2. **Payer step-therapy.** Both drugs must be prescribed on top of existing therapy, and insurers will very likely force patients through cheap generic spironolactone — a decades-old drug that also blocks aldosterone's effects — before paying for either. Management has not addressed this directly in public materials.
3. **Who pays for the launch.** A branded cardiovascular launch against AstraZeneca is expensive. The undrawn $400 million of the Pharmakon facility and future equity are the visible answers; neither is free.

## 6. RED FLAGS AND GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning**
- The sleep-apnoea failure was disclosed on the same day as the good news about the filing acceptance (10 March 2026). Burying a miss under a beat is a disclosure choice, not an accident.
- Senior secured debt now sits ahead of shareholders on the cash. That materially weakens the "cash is the floor" argument.
- Short interest is elevated at roughly 14.4% of the freely traded shares and has risen about 22% over the past year. Somebody is positioned for the bad outcome.
- The shares are down about 44% from the 52-week high of $47.65 and trade below both the 50-day (about $27.03) and 200-day (about $31.87) averages. The tape is not confirming the bull case.

**Positive**
- The decision date has not moved and no advisory committee has been called — the two classic tells of a troubled review are both absent.
- A rival drug with the same mechanism was approved by the same agency nine weeks ago. The FDA has already blessed the mechanism, the endpoint and the safety management. That is meaningful de-risking of the approval itself, even as it worsens the commercial picture.
- The royalty buyout means Mineralys keeps 100% of future economics and will own the underlying patents outright — precisely the housekeeping a board does when it wants maximum value from a launch or from a sale of the company.
- Roughly $640 million of gross cash against about $100 million of drawn debt, with funding secured well before the event.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The vocabulary has shifted from "platform" and "comorbidities" to "label" and "access." That is the language of a company preparing to fight for share, not one expecting to define a category.

Second, the sequencing of the June transactions is telling. Buying the royalty *before* approval, at a depressed share price, costs more in dilution than waiting would have. Doing it anyway implies either high internal confidence in the December decision, or a desire to have a clean, wholly-owned asset available for a strategic conversation — or both. Either reading is constructive.

Third, the company's own guidance language stopped referencing sleep apnoea as a value driver after March. Growth drivers that quietly disappear from the script rarely come back.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE — the event is on schedule and fully funded; the commercial story around it has narrowed.**

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing this: **the approval and the payoff have come apart.** Because a competitor with the identical mechanism was approved in May, the probability that lorundrostat is approved on 22 December has gone *up* — and the value of that approval has gone *down*. The market understands this. That is why the shares fell roughly 25% in six sessions in early June and now sit at $26.71 against a street consensus target near $49.

The practical consequence is that this is not a classic wide-spread event trade where a doubtful approval is being mispriced. It is a negatively-skewed binary: roughly a nine-in-ten chance of an outcome that is largely expected and worth perhaps a 30% to 40% re-rate, against roughly a one-in-ten chance of a rejection letter that would likely halve the shares. The expected value is clearly positive, but it is carried by the odds, not by the shape of the payoff.

And the floor is soft. Netting the drawn senior secured loan against roughly $640 million of cash leaves about $6.15 a share of net cash — only 23% of the current price, and it sits behind the lender. The realistic support in a rejection scenario is not cash but the residual worth of a re-fileable drug with two positive registrational trials in an already-approved class: call it $13, which is roughly where the shares traded a year ago at $12.59 before the pivotal data. That is an estimate, not a contractual backstop, and the director should size the position as though half the capital is genuinely at risk.

**Economic moat: none that can yet be evidenced.** There are no revenues, no margins and no returns to measure. What exists is patent exclusivity on a molecule the company will shortly own outright — real protection, but protection of an unproven commercial franchise, and one entering a market where a large competitor is already selling and where cheap generic alternatives anchor what insurers will pay. The structural pressure worth naming is reimbursement: payers will push patients through generic spironolactone first, which compresses both price and volume for the whole class. That is a manageable headwind on the size of the prize, not a terminal threat to the asset's existence.

skeptic.kill_fact: The catalyst survives the kill-check but the entry-timing argument does not. The bull's stated reason to buy now rather than wait is that the two thesis-breakers -- an FDA advisory committee being called, or a three-month extension of the review clock -- 'get less likely with every week that passes this late in a standard review.' That is wrong on the clock. The NDA was accepted 9 March 2026 for a 22 December 2026 action date; as of 27 July 2026 roughly five of about nine and a half review months are still to run. Advisory committee meetings are noticed in the Federal Register typically 30 to 60 days ahead, which puts the announcement window in October and November, entirely in the future. Three-month extensions triggered by a major amendment are likewise issued late in the review. Both risks the bull books as 'quiet positives' sit almost wholly ahead of the position, not behind it. The absence of either today carries close to no information, so the argument against simply waiting for the 11 August results and the autumn payer datapoints collapses. Everything else holds: the 22 December 2026 target action date is confirmed from the company's own filing-acceptance release and reconfirmed in its first-quarter results; the financing structure, the senior secured ranking and the Tanabe milestone tail are confirmed to the dollar; the spread has not closed, with the shares at $26.71 against the bull's own approval-resolved $38. The soft floor is a genuine weakness but it is disclosed, quantified and sized for by the bull rather than hidden, so it is not a disqualifier.
