OLMA.bull_thesis: Olema is one molecule and one experiment, and the experiment is close. Palazestrant is a once-daily pill for the most common form of advanced breast cancer, the kind that grows in response to oestrogen. It is designed to shut the oestrogen receptor down completely, blocking both of the receptor's switches and degrading the receptor itself, where the pills already on the market reliably block only one. The pivotal study, OPERA-01, enrolled about 510 patients whose disease had already progressed on hormone therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and it tests palazestrant on its own against whatever single hormone drug the treating doctor would otherwise choose. Management guided to top-line results in the fall of 2026 when it reported first-quarter figures on 12 May 2026, and the trial registry lists an estimated primary completion date of 30 June 2026 that has now passed on schedule. Nothing in the record shows that guidance being softened or pushed. The bullish case rests on three things the market is not paying for. First, the trial is built to win broadly. Its results are reported separately in patients whose tumours carry an ESR1 mutation, a genetic change that develops under hormone therapy in roughly four of ten patients, and separately in patients who do not carry it. Olema could have registered a mutation-only study and secured a likely approval in a small niche; it deliberately took on the harder population, which is where the whole prize sits. Second, the comparator is weak. These are patients on their second or third line of treatment, measured against a single hormone drug, which historically buys them only a couple of months before the disease grows again. Third, the balance sheet removes the usual way biotech investors lose money before a readout. Olema held $505.4 million of cash and marketable securities against $3.96 million of total debt at 31 March 2026, with no term loan, no convertible note, no covenant and no going-concern language. It does not need to raise money before the answer arrives, and the only shares it has issued this year are routine new-hire option grants. There is a second asset that costs nothing at today's price. OP-3136, aimed at an enzyme called KAT6, showed no dose-limiting toxicities up to 45 mg daily in its first human study reported on 21 May 2026, with tumour shrinkage observed, and on 26 May 2026 Bayer agreed to run a joint study combining it with its prostate-cancer drug darolutamide. A large pharmaceutical company put its own medicine next to Olema's. The final piece is behavioural. On 17 July 2026 Olema registered a second Phase 3 study, about 1,000 patients, testing palazestrant with ribociclib as a first treatment. That is an expensive commitment made months before the validating result. Management cannot see the unblinded data, so it is confidence rather than knowledge, but confidence expressed through spending carries more weight than confidence expressed in a press release. For the bull case to pay, one condition must hold: palazestrant must show a clear delay in disease progression in the patients without an ESR1 mutation, not only in those who have it. If it does, Olema owns the first all-comers oral endocrine therapy after CDK4/6 treatment, in a market where every existing option is confined to the mutation-positive minority.
OLMA.bear_thesis: The bear case is short and it is specific: the drug class has been tested twice in exactly this way, and twice it has won only in the mutation-positive minority. Elacestrant, and more recently Lilly's imlunestrant tested as a single agent after a CDK4/6 inhibitor, both produced convincing results in patients carrying an ESR1 mutation and both failed to establish a clear benefit in the wider population. That is the population OPERA-01 must win to justify anything close to today's price. Olema's answer is mechanistic, not empirical: palazestrant blocks both of the receptor's switches, so in theory it should work whether or not the mutation is present. That theory has never survived a Phase 3. Four months ago the class produced a further warning. Roche's persevERA study of giredestrant, a drug working through the same receptor, enrolled 992 patients, reached its primary completion date on 30 January 2026 and did not succeed against letrozole plus palbociclib in first-line patients. The setting differs from OPERA-01 in line of therapy, comparator and the use of a combination rather than monotherapy, so it is not a direct read-across. But it establishes that this mechanism can lose a large, well-funded, well-designed trial. Olema's shares fell hard on it and have drifted from roughly $17 to $12.01 since, now sitting 31% below their own 200-day average of $17.44. The more uncomfortable point is what the likely outcome is worth. If palazestrant wins only in the mutation-positive group, Olema becomes the third or fourth entrant into a niche that elacestrant and imlunestrant already serve and that AstraZeneca's camizestrant is entering, addressing perhaps four in ten of these patients, with no pricing power and a commercial build to fund from scratch. That outcome is worth roughly what the stock costs today. In other words, the single most likely result pays the buyer nothing. Cash is being consumed faster into the event, not slower. Operating cash outflow rose from $29.9 million in the June 2025 quarter to $46.0 million in the March 2026 quarter, and the company has since started a 1,000-patient first-line study that is worthless if OPERA-01 fails and costly to unwind. By the readout, cash should be near $400 million rather than $505 million. Finally, the published expectations are stale and unreliable as a guide. Twelve analysts carry an average price target of $40.70 against a $12.01 share price, with only one published number, LifeSci Capital's $23, anywhere near where the stock trades. Those models were built for a broad success and have not been re-underwritten since March 2026. A gap that wide is not an opportunity signal; it is evidence that the sell-side has stopped marking its work, and it means there is no institutional support level beneath the stock if the data disappoint. What would confirm the bear case: any softening of the fall-2026 language, a result that reports a benefit only in the mutation-positive analysis, or an equity raise before the data.
OLMA.sop_bull: Event-win value of about $30 per share. Derivation: a clean OPERA-01 result covering both the mutation-positive and mutation-negative populations makes palazestrant the first oral endocrine therapy usable in all patients after CDK4/6 treatment, rather than in the roughly 40% minority the approved competition serves. Against an addressable second-and-later-line population of that size and typical branded oncology pricing, peak annual sales of $1.0 to $1.5 billion are supportable. Applying the 2 to 2.5 times peak-sales multiple that de-risked, single-asset oncology companies have fetched in trade sales gives an enterprise value of $2.2 to $2.7 billion for the palazestrant franchise. Add roughly $400 million of cash expected at the readout and a modest $75 million for OP-3136, now validated enough that Bayer agreed on 26 May 2026 to combine it with darolutamide. Total equity value $2.7 to $3.2 billion. Divided across about 90 million shares, allowing for option issuance, that is $30 to $35 per share; taking the conservative end and haircutting for the time and cost of a commercial build gives $30. The board file's $24 target is the more conservative framing of the same outcome and is used as the headline target here. A trade sale is the likely route rather than a self-funded launch, since AstraZeneca, Lilly, Roche and Pfizer all compete in this exact setting.
OLMA.sop_bear: Verified downside floor of about $4.25 per share, materially below the board file's working floor of $6.50, which is not supportable. Derivation: Olema held $505.35 million of cash and marketable securities against $3.96 million of total debt at 31 March 2026, giving net cash of $501.4 million, or $5.74 per share on 87.35 million shares outstanding. That is the position today, not at the event. Operating cash burn was $46.0 million in the March 2026 quarter and is rising as a second, 1,000-patient Phase 3 starts, so two further quarters take cash to roughly $400 million by a September-to-November readout, or about $4.55 per share. A company that has just failed its pivotal trial does not trade at its cash. It trades below it, because the market discounts the burn still to come and the cost of unwinding two Phase 3 programmes. The empirical anchor is Olema's own 52-week low of $4.47, set in 2025 at roughly 0.8 times the then net cash. Applying 0.8 to 0.9 times post-readout net cash gives $3.65 to $4.10, and adding partial credit for OP-3136, which retains real value with clean first-in-human safety to 45 mg and a named Bayer partnership, brings the floor to about $4.25. The floor is unusually well verified for a biotech because there is nothing structurally ahead of the shareholder: no term loan, no convertible, no covenant, no going-concern qualification and no financing requirement before the data. But it is a floor 65% below the current price. Defined risk is not the same as small risk. The intermediate outcome, a win confined to the mutation-positive population, is worth about $13 per share: peak sales of $250 to $400 million as a third or fourth entrant, an enterprise value of $600 to $800 million, plus $400 million of cash.
OLMA.sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across three discrete outcomes, because the honest distribution here has two humps rather than a smooth range. Broad win, meaning a clear delay in disease progression in both the mutation-positive and the mutation-negative populations: 25% probability, $30 per share. This is the outcome the trial was deliberately designed to chase and the only one that justifies the sell-side's models. Narrow win, meaning a clear result in mutation-positive patients only: 45% probability, $13 per share. This is the single most likely outcome and it is worth roughly today's price, because it makes Olema the third or fourth entrant into a niche two rivals already serve. It is also the outcome both prior trials in this class produced. Clean failure, meaning neither analysis succeeds: 30% probability, $4.25 per share, backed by roughly $400 million of unencumbered cash at the readout plus partial credit for OP-3136. Weighted: 0.25 times $30, plus 0.45 times $13, plus 0.30 times $4.25, equals $14.63, rounded down to $14.50 for the option issuance running through the share count. Cross-check on the enterprise value: at $12.01 per share the market capitalisation is $1.05 billion and enterprise value is $548 million, so just under half the share price is cash in the bank. The market is therefore paying $548 million for a pivotal-stage asset that is worth roughly $2.4 billion if it wins broadly and $700 million if it wins narrowly. That is a coherent price for the odds above, not an obvious mispricing.
OLMA.risk_reward: Upside to the $24 event-win target is plus 100% from $12.01. Downside to the verified $4.25 floor is minus 65%. That is about 1.5 to 1 on the two tails. Measured against the probability-weighted fair value of $14.50, the edge from today's price is about plus 21%. The asymmetry is real but narrower than the headline gap to the $24 target suggests, and the reason is important: the most likely single outcome, a win confined to mutation-positive patients, is worth roughly the current price. An investor is effectively paying par for the middle case in order to hold a 25% ticket on a double, against a 30% chance of losing about two-thirds. That is a legitimate defined-risk binary, not a bargain, and it must be sized accordingly.
OLMA.catalyst_summary: Top-line results from the 510-patient pivotal OPERA-01 study of palazestrant, guided to the fall of 2026 on 12 May 2026 and never softened, with the trial's registered maturity date of 30 June 2026 already passed: about 100% upside to a $24 event-win value against roughly 65% downside to a $4.25 floor backed by around $400 million of unencumbered cash and no debt.

Verified on 28 July 2026 from two independent sources: the company's first-quarter release of 12 May 2026, which states it expects top-line data from the pivotal Phase 3 OPERA-01 trial of palazestrant monotherapy in fall 2026; and the trial registry record NCT06016738, which lists an estimated primary completion date of 30 June 2026, now passed, with study completion estimated 30 September 2027. The event has not fired, has not been withdrawn, and shows no history of slipping. One caveat carried honestly: this is a company-guided season, not a fixed regulatory decision date, and the underlying trial reports when enough disease-progression events have accumulated, so a few weeks of drift is possible. The registry record itself is stale, still showing a recruiting status verified in August 2025 and last updated 13 March 2026.
OLMA.forcing_function: One announcement settles this: the OPERA-01 top-line release, expected between roughly September and November 2026. It is the only event that can move Olema's value materially, because everything the market pays above the $5.74 per share of net cash is the palazestrant programme and nothing else in the pipeline resolves before 2027 at the earliest. The release will report two separate answers, and the second one is what matters. A result in patients carrying an ESR1 mutation is largely expected and mostly priced. A result in patients without that mutation is the outcome no drug in this class has achieved, and it is what separates a $30 share from a $13 one. Two secondary triggers sit alongside it. The second-quarter report, due in August 2026, will either restate the fall window or reveal a softening, and it will show the cash position going into the event. And enrolment progress in the newly registered 1,000-patient first-line study, updated 17 July 2026, is a live read on management's own confidence.
OLMA.consensus_delta: The disagreement here runs against both camps, in opposite directions. The sell-side has stopped marking its work. Twelve analysts carry an average price target of $40.70, a median of $40 and a high of $62, with nine strong-buy ratings, against a share price of $12.01 on 27 July 2026. Only one published number, LifeSci Capital's $23, is anywhere near the tape. A target more than three times the market price is not a forecast; it is a set of models built for a broad success that have not been rebuilt since Roche's persevERA study of the same-class giredestrant failed in the first quarter of 2026. Those models implicitly assign a high probability to palazestrant winning in the mutation-negative population, which no drug in this class has achieved in a Phase 3, and they largely ignore that the most probable outcome, a mutation-only win, puts Olema fourth into a niche market. Our probability-weighted value of $14.50 is about a third of the street's average, and we regard the street as wrong. But the market itself has also over-corrected in a specific, measurable way. At $12.01, enterprise value is $548 million. That is what the market is paying for a pivotal-stage oncology asset reading out within four months in one of the largest cancer indications there is, plus a Bayer-partnered second molecule, plus the free option that a mutation-only win still creates a real, saleable product. Nearly half the share price is cash. The market has moved from pricing the broad win as likely to pricing it as close to an afterthought, and 17.29% of the shares outstanding are sold short. Our view sits between the two: more sceptical than the sell-side on the science, more constructive than the tape on the value of the downside branch.
OLMA.valley_of_death: The next three to six months carry the whole risk of this position, and the reassuring part is that the usual biotech killer is absent. There is no financing cliff. With $505.35 million of cash and marketable securities at 31 March 2026 against $3.96 million of total debt, no term loan, no convertible note, no covenant and no going-concern language, Olema does not need to raise money before the data. That removes the single most common way investors lose money in the window before a readout: a rescue equity raise into weakness. The only shares issued this year have been routine new-hire option grants, 176,150 in June 2026 at $12.71 and 215,800 in July 2026 at $12.08. What can still go wrong before the event is threefold. First, cash consumption is accelerating: operating outflow rose from $29.9 million in the June 2025 quarter to $46.0 million in the March 2026 quarter, and a 1,000-patient first-line study registered on 17 July 2026 adds to it. Cash should be near $400 million at the readout rather than $505 million, which lowers the floor by about $1.20 per share between now and then. Every week of delay costs the holder roughly four cents of downside protection. Second, timing drift. The trial reports when enough disease-progression events have accrued, and fall is a season, not a date. The August 2026 second-quarter report is the checkpoint; any move from fall to year-end would be read badly and would extend the exposure window. Third, and most likely to bite, sentiment contagion. This is a crowded mechanism with several large-company programmes running. Any adverse result from a competitor's oestrogen-receptor programme, or negative commentary at an autumn oncology conference, would hit Olema regardless of its own trial, exactly as persevERA did in March 2026. The stock is 31% below its 200-day average and has already fallen from roughly $17; the March move demonstrated that this name trades on other companies' news.
OLMA.positioning_washout: The shareholder base has already turned over violently, and that is the constructive part of the setup. The 52-week range runs from $4.47 to $36.26 against $12.01 today, a spread that only occurs when a register is bought and sold wholesale twice. The optimists who arrived in late 2025 on favourable sector news, and again before Roche's persevERA result, have largely gone; the stock now sits 31% below its own 200-day average of $17.44. The more interesting number is the short interest: 15.10 million shares, or 17.29% of the 87.35 million shares outstanding. That is a large, committed bet against the trial, and it has two consequences. Ahead of the event it caps rallies, because every rise is met with fresh borrowing by traders who believe the mutation-negative analysis fails. After the event it becomes the mechanism of the move: a broad win forces roughly two weeks of average trading volume to be bought back into an open-ended gap higher, which is precisely why event-driven outcomes in heavily shorted biotech overshoot fair value on the upside. There is no yield-focused or index-driven holder to force out here, and no dividend to cut. The washout has already happened through price, not through mechanical selling, and the register that remains is a mix of specialist healthcare funds and a substantial short base. That is the positioning an event buyer wants: nobody left to panic, and a crowd on the other side that has to cover if the result lands.
OLMA.moderator_conclusion: Buy it now, in small size, and hold it as a binary rather than an investment. This is what the event-driven funnel exists to find, and it clears the structural test cleanly. The catalyst is live, unfired and dated to a window four months out, guided on 12 May 2026 and never softened, with the trial's own registered maturity date of 30 June 2026 already passed on schedule. The price of $12.01 sits at half the $24 event-win value. And the downside is backstopped by something verified rather than argued: $505.35 million of cash and marketable securities against $3.96 million of debt, no covenant, no convertible, no going-concern language, and no need to raise a dollar before the answer arrives. Positioning is already washed out, with the stock 31% below its 200-day average and 17.29% of the shares sold short. What holds this to a four rather than a five is the shape of the distribution, and it is worth being blunt about it. OPERA-01 reports two answers, not one. A result in patients carrying an ESR1 mutation is the likely part and is largely priced; the class has delivered it twice. A result in patients without that mutation is the part that pays, and no oral drug in this class has ever delivered it in a Phase 3, including Lilly's imlunestrant in essentially this exact setting. The honest odds are roughly a quarter on the broad win worth $30, a little under half on the narrow win worth about $13, and three in ten on failure at $4.25. That weights to $14.50, about 21% above the current price. The single most likely outcome pays the buyer nothing. That is still a trade worth making, because the tails are 1.5 to 1 in the buyer's favour, the floor is cash rather than a story, and a broad win in a stock with this short interest would not stop at $24. But it is a trade to be sized so that losing 65% is survivable, because that branch carries a genuine three-in-ten weight rather than being a tail risk. Two corrections to the board file for the record. The working downside floor of $6.50 per share is not supportable: net cash is $5.74 today and roughly $4.55 at the readout, and a company that has just failed its pivotal trial trades below cash, not above it. The realistic floor is $4.25. And the sell-side average target of $40.70 should carry no weight in sizing; those models predate the March 2026 evidence and only one of twelve analysts has published a number within reach of the tape. The exit discipline is simple, because the position has an expiry date built into it. This is held to the announcement and resolved on it. Reassess immediately if the August 2026 second-quarter report softens the fall language, if an equity raise appears, or if a competitor's readout moves the whole class.
OLMA.interrogator_dossier:
# Olema Oncology (OLMA) — Forensic Dossier on an Event, Not a Franchise

*Prepared 28 July 2026. All prices and balance-sheet figures verified against public sources
on 27–28 July 2026. This is an event-driven special situation: the question is not whether
Olema is a good business — it has no revenue and no business yet — but whether one specific
experiment is real, dated, and binding, and what actually backstops the share price if it fails.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Olema has spent five years narrowing rather than broadening. What began as a discovery platform
is now, in practical terms, one molecule and one experiment.

The molecule is palazestrant (internal code OP-1250), a once-daily pill for the most common form
of advanced breast cancer — tumours that grow in response to oestrogen (the medical shorthand is
"ER-positive, HER2-negative"). Roughly seven in ten breast cancers are of this type. Palazestrant
is designed to shut the oestrogen receptor down completely: it blocks both of the receptor's two
switches and also degrades the receptor itself. The competing pills on the market block only one
switch reliably.

The experiment is OPERA-01, registry number NCT06016738. I read the trial record directly on
28 July 2026. It is a Phase 3, open-label, randomised study of about 510 patients whose disease
has already progressed on hormone therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor (the standard first-line
combination, drugs such as palbociclib or ribociclib). Palazestrant on its own is measured against
whatever single hormone drug the treating doctor would otherwise choose — fulvestrant, anastrozole,
letrozole or exemestane. The endpoint is progression-free survival, meaning how long patients live
before the cancer grows again, judged by an independent review panel that does not know which drug
each patient received.

The single most important design detail, and the one the market discusses least: OPERA-01 reads out
in **two separate populations** — patients whose tumours carry an ESR1 mutation (a specific genetic
change that develops under hormone therapy and appears in roughly 40% of these patients), and,
separately, patients whose tumours do **not** carry it. Olema is not hedging its bet into a
mutation-only label. It is explicitly testing the harder claim.

The narrative has also quietly acquired a second leg. In May 2026 the company reported first
human data on OP-3136, a different molecule aimed at an enzyme called KAT6, with no dose-limiting
toxicities up to 45 mg daily and some tumour shrinkage observed. On 26 May 2026 Bayer agreed to
run a joint Phase 1b/2 study combining OP-3136 with its prostate-cancer drug darolutamide in about
36 patients, starting in the second half of 2026. That is a small collaboration, but a real
pharmaceutical company put its name and its drug next to Olema's.

And there is a third development that cuts both ways. On 17 July 2026 the registry was updated for
NCT07085767 — a **new, second Phase 3 trial**, roughly 1,000 patients, testing palazestrant combined
with ribociclib as a *first* treatment, with completion estimated December 2028. Olema is spending
money on a 1,000-patient study before the 510-patient study that validates the drug has reported.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

There are no revenues to test a growth claim against. The claims that matter here are about
solvency, timing, and credibility — and those are testable.

| Management's claim | What the numbers actually show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Top-line data from the pivotal Phase 3 OPERA-01 trial in fall 2026" (stated with Q1 results, 12 May 2026) | The trial registry lists an estimated primary completion date of 30 June 2026 — already passed. Data cleaning and independent-panel adjudication typically take two to four months. A September-to-November announcement is arithmetically consistent, not aspirational. | **Corroborated** |
| The company is fully funded through the readout | $505.35M in cash and marketable securities at 31 March 2026 against $3.96M of total debt. Cash burn from operations was $46.0M in the March 2026 quarter (prior four quarters: $38.3M, $34.5M, $29.9M, $44.0M). Two more quarters at a rising ~$50M leaves roughly $400M at the readout. | **Corroborated, comfortably** |
| No dilution required before the event | No equity offering appears in the 2026 news record. The only share issuances disclosed are routine new-hire option grants — 176,150 shares at $12.71 on 2 June 2026 and 215,800 shares at $12.08 on 2 July 2026. A company quietly hiring is not a company preparing a rescue financing. | **Corroborated** |
| The drug works regardless of ESR1 mutation status | This is the load-bearing claim and it is **not yet supported by any Phase 3 evidence anywhere in the drug class.** It rests on mechanism and on mid-stage data. It is exactly what OPERA-01 is designed to answer. | **Unproven — this is the bet** |

The balance sheet deserves emphasis because it is the only thing standing between an investor and
zero. Enterprise value — market capitalisation minus net cash — is about **$548M** against a
$1.05B market capitalisation at $12.01 per share on 27 July 2026. Put plainly: **just under half
of what you pay for this share is cash sitting in the bank**, and there is essentially no debt
against it. Net cash works out to $5.74 per share today and roughly $4.55 per share by the time
the data arrive.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Stable, and stable in a way that is itself evidence.** The tell is not what management says but
what it has not done. Guidance for OPERA-01 data has pointed at the second half of 2026 and then
specifically at the fall, and I can find no instance of that guidance being walked back, softened
to "around year-end", or converted to "when the required number of events accrue" — the standard
euphemism a biotech reaches for when a trial is running behind. On 12 May 2026 the language was
still direct: top-line data in fall 2026.

The other tone signal is behavioural. Launching a second, 1,000-patient Phase 3 in the first-line
setting in July 2026 — months before the validating readout — is not defensive language. It is a
capital commitment that only makes sense if management believes the first trial will succeed.
Management does not see unblinded results, so this is confidence, not knowledge. But confidence
backed by spending is worth more than confidence expressed in a press release.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High, on the narrow question of timing.** The relevant track record is not earnings beats — there
are no earnings — but whether stated dates have held. They have. The fall-2026 window has been
reiterated rather than revised, the trial's registered maturity date has been reached on schedule,
and the balance sheet removes the most common reason a small biotech quietly delays a readout,
which is that it needs to raise money into a stronger tape first.

One genuine housekeeping gap: the OPERA-01 registry record still shows a status of "Recruiting"
with a verification date of August 2025, and was last updated 13 March 2026. For a trial the company
says will report this autumn, that record is stale. Registry lag is common and I do not read it as
concealment, but it is the sort of untidiness that leaves an investor relying on the company's word
rather than an independent timestamp.

**Reliability: High on timing. Unknown on outcome — and the outcome is what is being priced.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The sell-side is not pressuring management at all, and that is the problem. Twelve analysts cover
the stock. Nine rate it strong buy, two buy, one hold. The average price target is **$40.70**, with
a median of $40, a low of $23 (LifeSci Capital) and a high of $62. The shares closed at **$12.01**
on 27 July 2026.

A consensus target more than three times the market price is not a forecast. It is a set of models
that were built for a broad success and have not been re-underwritten since March 2026, when Roche's
persevERA trial of the same-class drug giredestrant reported. That trial — registry number
NCT04546009, 992 patients, primary completion 30 January 2026, record last updated 19 May 2026 —
tested giredestrant plus palbociclib against letrozole plus palbociclib in first-line patients and
did not succeed. Olema's shares fell sharply and have since drifted from roughly $17 to $12, with
the 200-day average now at $17.44. The targets did not move with the price. Only one of twelve
analysts has published a number anywhere near where the stock trades.

The question no one is pressing management on publicly is the one that decides the trade: what
happens to the wild-type population — the roughly 60% of patients without an ESR1 mutation — given
that no oral drug in this class has yet won there.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **The class has a consistent, unhelpful pattern.** Elacestrant and, more recently, Lilly's
imlunestrant both won convincingly in ESR1-mutant patients and both failed to establish a clear
benefit in the wider population — imlunestrant in essentially OPERA-01's own setting, as a single
agent after a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Two attempts, two mutation-only outcomes. Olema is attempting
precisely the thing the class has not yet done.

🔴 **A same-mechanism Phase 3 failed four months ago.** persevERA is not a perfect read-across —
different line of therapy, different comparator, a combination rather than monotherapy — but it
demonstrates that this receptor-blocking mechanism can lose a large, well-funded Phase 3.

🔴 **The board file's downside floor of $6.50 per share is not supportable.** Net cash is $5.74 per
share *today* and will be roughly $4.55 by the readout. A floor above current net cash implies the
market would pay a premium to cash for a company that had just failed its pivotal trial. It would not.

🔴 **Burn is accelerating into the event.** Operating cash outflow rose from $29.9M in the June 2025
quarter to $46.0M in the March 2026 quarter, and a 1,000-patient first-line study has since started.
That trial has no value if OPERA-01 fails, and unwinding it would cost money.

🟢 **No financing risk before the catalyst.** $505M of unencumbered cash, $3.96M of debt, no term
loan, no convertible, no covenant, no going-concern language. The single most common way a biotech
investor loses money before the data — a dilutive rescue raise at a distressed price — is off the
table here.

🟢 **The positioning is already washed out.** Short interest stands at **15.10 million shares, or
17.29% of shares outstanding.** The 52-week range runs from $4.47 to $36.26 against $12.01 today.
The optimistic shareholder base largely left after March 2026; what remains is heavily shorted and
trading 31% below its own 200-day average. Bad news is at least partly in the price. Good news is
not.

🟢 **Genuine residual value if the main drug fails.** OP-3136 has clean initial safety data
(no dose-limiting toxicities to 45 mg), observed responses, and a named partner in Bayer as of
26 May 2026. That is not a rounding error against a busted-biotech valuation.

🟢 **Management has spent its own capital on the outcome.** The July 2026 first-line study is a
costly expression of belief made before the answer is known.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most informative detail in the entire file is the trial's dual-population design. Olema could
have registered OPERA-01 to read out in mutation-positive patients alone, matched the approved
competition, and secured a high-probability approval in a modest niche. It did not. It registered
a separate primary analysis in mutation-negative patients — the population where the class has
failed. That is a deliberate decision to make the trial harder in exchange for a far larger prize,
and it is why the outcome distribution here is genuinely two-humped rather than a smooth range.

The second signal is what routine hiring implies. Granting new-employee options in both June and
July 2026, at $12.71 and $12.08, tells you a company still building a team on the assumption it
will have something to sell.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE.** Nothing about the setup has deteriorated operationally. What changed in
March 2026 was the market's estimate of the odds, not Olema's execution.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is not a range of outcomes, it is
three discrete ones, and the middle one is worth roughly today's price. A broad win covering both
mutation groups is worth somewhere near $30 per share. A narrow win in mutation-positive patients
only makes Olema the third or fourth entrant into a niche two rivals already serve, worth perhaps
$13. A clean failure leaves cash and an early-stage second molecule, worth about $4.25. The
probability-weighted middle sits a little above the current price, but the *most likely single
outcome* pays roughly nothing from here. Size this as a defined-risk binary — the position must be
small enough that a 65% loss to the cash floor is an acceptable outcome, because that is a live
branch, not a tail.

**Moat:** none, and the question is not really applicable. Olema has no franchise, no customers and
no revenue. What patent protection and mechanism differentiation exist are potential assets that
only become a moat if the trial succeeds. **Secular threat: manageable** — advanced breast cancer
is a growing, well-reimbursed market with no structural force eroding it; the risk here is
competitive and scientific, not secular. The cheapness on conventional metrics is by design and
carries no information.

PRX.AS.bull_thesis: The bull case is that the event resolved well and the market has not paid for what is left. Prosus, the Amsterdam-listed technology holding company, was ordered by Europe's competition regulator to shrink its 26.5% stake in Delivery Hero, the German food-delivery group, as the price of being allowed to buy Just Eat Takeaway.com. Management executed that mandated sale about as well as a forced sale can be executed: 4.5% to Uber at 20 euros a share on 17 April 2026, then 5% to Aspex Management of Hong Kong at 22 euros on 11 May 2026, and finally, on 16 July 2026, a binding, non-withdrawable promise to tender the residual 16.8% into Uber's cash takeover offer at 41.50 euros a share - roughly double what Prosus accepted three months earlier and about 2.8 times Delivery Hero's 52-week low of 14.80 euros. The forced seller is finished, and it sold at premiums rather than into a fire sale. What is left is the real security, and it is cheap on the company's own numbers. Prosus publishes its asset value daily; as of 24 July 2026 it stands at 147.2 billion US dollars, or 61.30 euros per share, against a 37.85-euro price - a 38% discount. Roughly 47.40 euros per share of that is a single liquid holding, about 22.8% of Tencent, the Chinese internet group, so a buyer at 37.85 euros pays 0.80 times the value of the Tencent stake alone and collects the 32.8 billion dollars of unlisted businesses and 7.3 billion dollars of other listed holdings for nothing. Meanwhile the company retires its own stock relentlessly - about 42 billion dollars returned since June 2022, roughly 30% of the free float, with a further 5 billion dollars committed on 29 June 2026 - which lifts value per share by arithmetic every day the discount stays wide (management puts the cumulative gain at 18%). The operating businesses have stopped being a drag: the year to 31 March 2026 delivered about 12% revenue growth, ecosystem adjusted operating earnings up roughly 44%, free cash flow above 1.5 billion dollars, and profitability across all three regional ecosystems for the first time. If Tencent merely steadies and the discount narrows toward 25%, the shares are worth about 46 euros; on a Tencent recovery toward its 200-day average with a 30% discount, closer to 50. Morgan Stanley, upgrading the stock on 25 March 2026, set a 51-euro target on the argument that the discount had reached the top of its range.
PRX.AS.bear_thesis: The bear case has two parts, and the first is fatal to the reason this name sits in an event-driven book at all. The forced selling was in Delivery Hero shares, not in Prosus shares, so there was never a supply overhang on this security to clear - and the residual position is far too small to move the price in any case. Delivery Hero has roughly 304 million shares; the 16.8% Prosus still owns is about 51 million shares, worth about 2.1 billion euros at the 41.50-euro offer. Spread across roughly 2.11 billion Prosus shares, the entire remaining holding is worth about 1.00 euro per Prosus share - about 2.6% of the price and 1.6% of asset value. The part not yet earned, the gap between Delivery Hero's 37.90 euros today and the 41.50 offer, is worth about 0.09 euro per Prosus share, and it does not arrive until the second half of 2027, subject to merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances and to Germany's financial regulator first approving the offer document. A quarter of one percent of the share price, more than a year out, with regulatory conditions attached, is not a special situation. Second, and more seriously, the thing that actually moves this security has no floor under it. About three-quarters of the value is one Chinese equity. Tencent trades at HK$443 against a 52-week high of HK$683, down about 35%, below both its 50-day (about HK$449) and 200-day (about HK$539) averages, pressured by worries about gaming revenue and money rotating out of Chinese internet names into artificial-intelligence trades. Prosus has followed: 37.85 euros against a 52-week high of 63.94, with a 52-week low of 36.17 set within the past week. The floor our board recorded, 37.365, has already been traded through - a level the security has already broken is not a floor, it is a recent price. There is no tender, no cash consideration, no deal price obliging anyone to pay a number here; the support is a mark-to-market on a volatile foreign equity. If Tencent falls another 13-15%, roughly 7 euros a share of value disappears and Prosus can trade to the low 30s without the discount widening at all. The holding-company discount itself is structural and has never durably closed, and the street cannot even agree it is wide: Morgan Stanley upgraded four months ago because the discount was at the top of its range, while Goldman Sachs initiated at neutral on 4 June 2026 with a 41-euro target calling the discount 30% against a 40% historical average - narrow, not wide. Goldman's specific concern also bites: weaker cash flow from the operating businesses could force Prosus to keep selling Tencent shares to fund the buyback, shrinking future value per share. There is also a small negative option outstanding: the European Commission's compliance deadline is 11 October 2026 while the Uber deal does not close until the second half of 2027, and it is not yet formally established that Brussels accepts a 2027 settlement as satisfying a 2026 obligation.

PRX.AS.catalyst_summary: The regulator-mandated Delivery Hero sell-down is finished and was never large enough to matter: Prosus cut 26.5% to 16.8% at premiums (20 euros to Uber on 17 April, 22 euros to Aspex on 11 May 2026) and on 16 July 2026 gave a binding promise to tender the rest into Uber's 41.50-euro cash offer, leaving about 0.09 euro per Prosus share of unearned spread that does not settle until the second half of 2027 - against a security whose price is set, three-quarters of it, by Tencent.
PRX.AS.dated_milestone: Two dates remain, neither of which forces a re-rating in this security. 11 October 2026: the European Commission's extended deadline for Prosus to have complied with its divestment commitment (the two-month extension was confirmed on 2 June 2026, after Naspers asked Brussels on 25 May 2026 to end the forced sale altogether). Prosus's stated position, from its 16 July 2026 announcement, is that the sale to Uber is a fair price and an effective way to comply; whether the Commission formally accepts a settlement that completes in 2027 against a 2026 deadline is the one genuinely open item, and its downside is a small residual placement, not a re-rating. Second half of 2027: expected completion of Uber's voluntary cash takeover offer for Delivery Hero at 41.50 euros a share, announced 16 July 2026, conditional on a minimum acceptance of 50% plus one share (Prosus's binding undertaking takes Uber to about 53% of the economics, so this is effectively pre-satisfied) and on merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances, with Germany's financial regulator required to approve the offer document before publication.
PRX.AS.forcing_function: There is no longer one, and that is the finding. The event that was supposed to force the re-rating has resolved, and the resolution is worth about 0.09 euro per share on a 37.85-euro stock, arriving in the second half of 2027. What remains that could plausibly force a re-rating is not an event but a process: the 5 billion dollar annual buyback committed on 29 June 2026, which retires stock at a 38% discount and has already taken about 30% of the free float out since June 2022, and any move to simplify the ownership structure between Prosus and its parent Naspers. Neither has a date. The nearest thing to a hard date is 11 October 2026, and the honest reading is that it is a compliance checkpoint on 1.6% of asset value, not a trigger. Absent an event, the driver is Tencent's own tape, and Tencent's next scheduled results are the only calendar item that reliably moves this security.
PRX.AS.consensus_delta: There is no disagreement with the market worth owning here, and pretending otherwise is where this position would go wrong. The street's view is straightforward and, as far as we can verify, correct: Prosus is a discounted way to own Tencent, the discount is wide because Chinese internet sentiment is poor, and the buyback is the main thing management controls. Morgan Stanley upgraded to overweight on 25 March 2026 with a 51-euro target, explicitly because the discount had widened to the top of its post-2022 range. That call is four months old and about 5% underwater, which is itself the useful information: the discount being wide was already the consensus reason to buy, and it has widened further. Goldman Sachs then initiated at neutral on 4 June 2026 with a 41-euro target, describing the discount as 30% against a 40% historical average - the opposite framing, from a different asset-value methodology - and warning that weaker operating cash flow could force more Tencent selling to fund the buyback. When two houses cannot agree whether the discount is wide or narrow, 'the discount is at its extreme' is not an edge, it is a methodology choice. Where our board did disagree with the market was in treating the forced Delivery Hero sale as a live supply story on this security, and that disagreement does not survive verification. The selling was in another company's shares; the position was under 2% of value; it has been sold at premiums; and the residual is contracted. If any gap remains between our view and the market's, it runs the other way - the market may still be crediting Prosus with Delivery Hero optionality that has already been converted into a fixed 41.50-euro claim settling in the second half of 2027. The one asymmetry we would defend is arithmetic rather than analytical: at 37.85 euros a buyer pays 0.80 times the marked value of the Tencent stake alone and receives about 14 euros a share of other portfolio, less debt, at no cost. That is a fact about the price, not a variant view.
PRX.AS.valley_of_death: The next three to nine months carry real downside with no offsetting event. The dominant risk is simply Tencent: it trades at HK$443 against a 52-week high of HK$683, below both its 50-day (about HK$449) and 200-day (about HK$539) averages, pressured by concerns about gaming revenue and a rotation of money out of Chinese internet names into artificial-intelligence trades. Prosus is roughly 74% Tencent by value, so a further 15% decline there removes about 7 euros a share and would put the stock in the low 30s on an unchanged discount. Second, the discount can widen independently of the assets, and each point costs roughly 0.6 euro a share. Third, currency: the portfolio is denominated in dollars and Hong Kong dollars while the listing is in euros, so a firmer euro mechanically lowers value per share. Fourth, the 11 October 2026 compliance deadline: if Brussels declines to treat the binding promise to Uber as compliance, Prosus must place a residual Delivery Hero block into the market in the fourth quarter - immaterial to value at about 1.00 euro a share, but an unhelpful headline in a tape already looking for reasons to sell. There is no cash-burn or maturity problem: net debt is 6.8 billion dollars against a 153.9 billion dollar portfolio, roughly 4%, free cash flow was above 1.5 billion dollars in the year to March 2026, and 2027 maturities were refinanced with new bonds raised in July 2026. The near-term risk is entirely price, not solvency.
PRX.AS.positioning_washout: The mechanical selling in this situation was never in Prosus - it was in Delivery Hero, and it is over. Prosus placed 4.5% with Uber at 20 euros and 5% with Aspex at 22 euros, both at or above the prevailing market, and has now contracted the remaining 16.8% to Uber at 41.50 euros; there is no further Prosus supply coming to the Delivery Hero tape, and Delivery Hero has re-rated from a 52-week low of 14.80 euros to 37.90 accordingly. Whatever wash-out premium existed accrued to Delivery Hero's shareholders, not to ours. On Prosus's own register the flow runs the other way and is supportive rather than distressed: the company is the dominant buyer of its own stock, having retired roughly 42 billion dollars since June 2022 - about 30% of the free float - with another 5 billion dollars committed on 29 June 2026. The genuine forced-selling risk today is exogenous: passive and emerging-market funds cutting Chinese internet exposure, which hits Tencent and Prosus together and is precisely the pressure that produced the 36.17-euro low this month. That is a headwind on the position, not a set-up to buy into.
PRX.AS.moderator_conclusion: Pass for now - not because the company is bad, but because this is not the security the board thought it was buying. The event we underwrote has already happened, and it happened well. Prosus was ordered by Europe's competition regulator to shrink a 26.5% stake in Delivery Hero as the condition of buying Just Eat Takeaway.com, and it did so at premiums: 20 euros to Uber on 17 April 2026, 22 euros to Aspex on 11 May, and then on 16 July a binding promise to tender the residual 16.8% into Uber's 41.50-euro cash offer. The forced seller is finished. The re-rating that flowed from it went to Delivery Hero's own shareholders, whose stock went from under 15 euros to 37.90. What reaches us is about 0.09 euro per Prosus share of unearned spread, settling in the second half of 2027 subject to regulatory clearance - roughly a quarter of one percent of the share price. You cannot build a defined-risk position on that. Worse for the trade as written, the downside floor our board recorded at 37.365 has already broken: the shares touched 36.17 within the past week and traded as low as 37.27 today. A level the security has already traded through is a recent price, not a floor, and there is nothing contractual beneath it - no tender, no deal price, no net cash. What actually sets the price is Tencent, about three-quarters of value, down roughly 35% from its 52-week high on gaming-revenue worries and a rotation into artificial-intelligence trades. That is an uncapped exposure wearing a special-situation label, and it does not belong in this book. The separate question is whether the security is cheap, and the honest answer is yes. Prosus's own disclosure on 24 July 2026 puts asset value at 147.2 billion dollars, or 61.30 euros a share, against a 37.85-euro price - a 38% discount. The Tencent stake alone is marked at about 47.40 euros a share, so a buyer pays 0.80 times one liquid holding and gets 32.8 billion dollars of unlisted businesses and the rest for nothing, while the company retires 5 billion dollars a year of its own stock at that discount. The operating side has genuinely turned: about 12% revenue growth in the year to March 2026, ecosystem earnings up roughly 44%, free cash flow above 1.5 billion dollars, every ecosystem profitable. That is a real value case, and it is why the value score is a 3 rather than a 1 - there is substantial asset backing, but it marks to market on a volatile Chinese equity every day, so the margin of safety is genuine without being defined. It is held to a 3 rather than a 4 for two reasons: the street cannot agree the discount is even wide (Goldman Sachs, 4 June 2026, calls it 30% against a 40% historical average), and the buyback that does the compounding may itself have to be funded by selling the asset that provides the backing. Our judgement: this name should be handed to the value book and underwritten as a discounted holding company carrying China risk, sized for that. In the event-driven book, where the entry condition is a live, dated catalyst with a floor beneath it, it is a pass. If it is to be revisited here, the level to wait for is a Tencent stabilisation - a reclaim of its 50-day average near HK$449 - with Prosus holding above 36 euros, or a concrete move to simplify the Prosus-Naspers ownership structure, which would be the first genuine forcing event this security has had.
PRX.AS.interrogator_dossier:
# PRX.AS — Prosus N.V. — Forensic Interrogation of the Event

*Event-driven special situation. Board label: forced seller / forced-divestment flow. Every fact below was checked against public sources on 27 July 2026.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — what the event was, and where it actually stands

The trade our board wrote down was a supply story. Prosus, the Amsterdam-listed technology holding company, was ordered by Europe's competition regulator to shrink a large stake in Delivery Hero, the German food-delivery group. The European Commission made that sell-down a condition of letting Prosus buy Just Eat Takeaway.com, and Prosus committed to cut its 26.5% Delivery Hero holding substantially. The standard way to trade a forced seller is to wait until the seller is finished, then buy the security once the pressure on the price is gone.

The first problem is definitional, and it is fatal. The forced selling was in Delivery Hero shares, not in Prosus shares. There was never an overhang on this security to clear.

The second problem is that the seller has finished — and finished well. The verified sequence:

| Date | Event | Price / terms | Residual stake |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 2025 | Commission clears the Just Eat Takeaway purchase, conditional on a substantial sell-down | — | 26.5% |
| 17 Apr 2026 | 13,582,342 shares (about 4.5%) sold to Uber | €20.00 per share | 21.8% |
| 11 May 2026 | 15,188,284 shares (about 5.0%) sold to Aspex Management of Hong Kong | €22.00 per share | 16.8% |
| 25 May 2026 | Naspers, Prosus's majority owner, asks Brussels for relief | — | 16.8% |
| 2 Jun 2026 | Commission extends the compliance deadline by two months, to 11 October 2026 | — | 16.8% |
| 16 Jul 2026 | Uber launches a voluntary cash takeover offer for all of Delivery Hero; Prosus gives an irrevocable undertaking (a binding, non-withdrawable promise) to tender its entire residual holding | €41.50 per share in cash; about $14.8bn equity value; closing targeted for the second half of 2027 | 16.8%, contractually spoken for |

That is the whole arc. Two placements at premiums, then the balance handed to a strategic buyer at €41.50 — roughly double the €20 accepted three months earlier, and about 2.8 times Delivery Hero's 52-week low of €14.80. The re-rating this produced went overwhelmingly to Delivery Hero's own shareholders: their stock has moved from under €15 to €37.90, against a 200-day average of €24.61.

**The event has fired.** It did not slip and it did not stall. It resolved, and it resolved competently.

## 2. THE LOAD-BEARING TEST — is the event real, dated, binding, and does it move *this* security?

Real: yes. Dated: two dates remain. Binding: yes — and that is exactly the problem, because a binding contract at a known price is a spread, and this spread is tiny.

The two remaining dates:

- **11 October 2026** — the extended deadline by which Prosus must have complied with its divestment commitment. Prosus's stated position, from the 16 July announcement, is that Uber's offer "represents a fair price and effective way to comply with its commitments to the European Commission." Whether Brussels formally accepts a contract that settles in 2027 as satisfying a 2026 obligation is the one genuinely open item; trade-press reporting suggests the Commission is minded to treat Uber's own stake-building as justification for the delay. Either way, the downside of a negative answer is that Prosus places a small block of Delivery Hero shares with someone else — an administrative outcome, not a re-rating.
- **Second half of 2027** — expected completion of Uber's offer, subject to a minimum acceptance of 50% plus one share (Prosus's undertaking takes Uber to roughly 53% of the economics, so that condition is effectively pre-satisfied) and to merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances, with Germany's financial regulator required to approve the offer document before publication.

Now the size test, which is where the thesis dies. Delivery Hero has roughly 304 million shares; Prosus's 16.8% is about 51 million shares, worth about €2.1 billion at the €41.50 offer. Prosus has roughly 2.11 billion shares outstanding. So the **entire remaining Delivery Hero position is worth about €1.00 per Prosus share** — about 2.6% of a €37.85 share price, and 1.6% of stated asset value. The part not yet earned, the gap between Delivery Hero's €37.90 today and the €41.50 offer, is about **€0.09 per Prosus share**, and it does not settle until the second half of 2027, with regulatory conditions attached.

Roughly a quarter of one percent of the share price, more than a year out. You cannot build a defined-risk position in an €81 billion holding company on that.

## 3. WHAT ACTUALLY SETS THE PRICE

Prosus publishes its own asset value. As of **24 July 2026** it stands at $147.2 billion (€129.5 billion), or **€61.3 per share**:

| Component | Value ($bn) | Per Prosus share (€) |
|---|---|---|
| Tencent, the Chinese internet group (about 22.8% of it) | 113.8 | ~47.4 |
| Other listed holdings (this is where the Delivery Hero residual sits) | 7.3 | ~3.0 |
| Unlisted portfolio — Europe, Latin America, India, other | 32.8 | ~13.7 |
| Less net debt | (6.8) | ~(2.8) |
| **Net asset value** | **147.2** | **€61.3** |

At today's €37.85 the shares trade at roughly a **38% discount** to that figure. Put another way: the Tencent stake alone is marked at about €47.40 per Prosus share, so a buyer at €37.85 pays **0.80 times one liquid holding** and collects the $32.8 billion unlisted portfolio and the other listed assets for nothing.

Which means, to about three-quarters of its value, this security is a discounted way to own Tencent — and Tencent is why the stock is where it is. Tencent trades at HK$443 against a 52-week high of HK$683, down about 35%, below both its 50-day average (HK$449) and its 200-day (HK$539). Prosus has tracked it: €37.85 against a 52-week high of €63.94, with a 52-week low of €36.17 set within the past week, a 50-day average of €39.04 and a 200-day of €46.31. The trend is down and has not turned.

## 4. THE FLOOR — the single most important verification, and it fails

Our board recorded a downside floor of €37.365 and a recovery risk-reward of 2.76 against a live price of €39.72. Both inputs are stale and the floor has already given way: the shares traded as low as €36.17 in the past week, and today's session opened at €37.28 and low-ticked €37.27. **A level the security has already traded through is not a floor. It is a recent price.**

Is there any real floor? There is asset backing, which is a different and weaker thing:

- **What supports the price.** The Tencent stake is liquid, marked daily, and worth about €47.40 per Prosus share against a €37.85 price. Prosus is also the dominant buyer of its own stock — roughly $42 billion returned since June 2022, about 30% of the free float retired, with a further $5 billion committed on 29 June 2026. Management puts the cumulative gain in value per share at 18%. Buying back stock at a 38% discount lifts value per share by arithmetic every day the discount persists.
- **Why that is not a floor.** The support marks to market on a volatile foreign equity. If Tencent falls another 15%, roughly €7 per share of Prosus value simply disappears and the stock can trade into the low €30s with the discount unchanged. There is no cash tender, no deal price, no net-cash backstop — net debt is $6.8 billion, small at about 4% of the portfolio, but still a liability rather than a cushion. A special-situation floor is a number somebody is obliged to pay you. There is none here.

The defensible adverse case is therefore not €37.37. It is Tencent retesting the high HK$300s with the discount stuck near 38%, which puts Prosus at roughly **€32**, with the €36.17 low as the first waypoint.

## 5. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning**

- The labelled catalyst is spent, and was never sized to matter — under 2% of asset value even before it resolved.
- The recorded floor broke this month. What sits beneath is Chinese-equity exposure, which is uncapped and unhedged in this book.
- One asset drives roughly three-quarters of the value, and its own tape is deteriorating on a fundamental worry (gaming revenue) plus money rotating out of Chinese internet names into artificial-intelligence trades.
- The holding-company discount is structural and has never durably closed. Morgan Stanley upgraded to overweight on 25 March 2026 with a €51 target, explicitly because the discount had widened to the top end of its range since the open-ended buyback began in 2022. Four months later the shares are about 5% lower and the discount is wider. Buying a wide discount is not the same as being paid for it.
- The street is genuinely split on whether the discount is even wide. Goldman Sachs initiated at neutral on 4 June 2026 with a €41 target, describing the discount as 30% against a 40% historical average — that is, narrow rather than wide. The gap between the two houses is methodology (analyst-target asset values versus traded marks), which means "the discount is at its extreme" is a contested claim, not a fact.
- Goldman's specific worry is worth carrying: weaker cash flow from the operating businesses could force Prosus to keep selling Tencent shares to fund the buyback, which shrinks future value per share.
- The residual regulatory question — whether Brussels accepts a 2027 settlement against an 11 October 2026 deadline — is a small negative option, not a positive one.

**Encouraging**

- Management executed a mandated sale about as well as one can be executed: premiums on both placements, then a strategic exit at €41.50. That is evidence about how they will handle the next forced decision.
- The operating businesses have stopped being a drag. The year to 31 March 2026 delivered about 12% revenue growth, ecosystem adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation up roughly 44%, free cash flow above $1.5 billion, and profitability across all three regional ecosystems for the first time.
- The balance sheet is conservative: $6.8 billion of net debt against a $153.9 billion portfolio, roughly 4% loan-to-value, with 2027 maturities already refinanced.
- The buyback is large, real, and self-reinforcing while the discount is wide.

## 6. HIDDEN SIGNALS

Two things are worth noticing in how this played out. First, Prosus asked Brussels on 25 May 2026 to be released from the forced sale altogether, and settled for a two-month extension instead. That is a management team that knew it was selling into a weak print and tried to avoid it — creditable, and also a reminder that the April €20 placement was a genuinely poor price relative to what arrived eight weeks later. Second, the €41.50 outcome was produced by a third party's strategic appetite, not by anything Prosus engineered. The lesson for underwriting the next mandated sale is that the good result here was substantially luck, and should not be extrapolated into a management skill premium.

## 7. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: stable. The operating businesses are improving and the capital return is disciplined, but neither changes what the security is — a discounted claim on Tencent with a portfolio attached.

The single thing the director must weigh before sizing: **this name does not belong in an event-driven book.** The event that got it here has resolved, it was never large enough to move this price, and what remains is a Chinese-internet exposure wearing a special-situation label. The value case is separately genuine — a 38% discount on the company's own numbers, liquid asset backing at 0.80 times the Tencent stake alone, and a large buyer of its own stock — but it has to be underwritten as a discounted holding company carrying China risk, sized for that, and not as a defined-risk trade with a floor, because there is no floor.

Moat is not a meaningful concept for a holding company: the operating quality sits inside Tencent and belongs to Tencent, not to Prosus. The structural risk to terminal value is Chinese regulatory and geopolitical, which is real, long-known, and manageable rather than newly deteriorating.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STABLE | MOAT: NONE | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

SRRK.bull_thesis:
The catalyst resolves favourably: the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approves apitegromab for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) on or before the 30 September 2026 action date, and Scholar Rock re-rates toward the low-to-mid $60s. The case rests on four verified pillars.

First, the hard part is already done. The Phase 3 SAPPHIRE trial hit its primary endpoint in October 2024 - the stock closed at $7.42 on 4 October 2024 and $34.28 on 7 October 2024 on 42.7 million shares, which tells you the clinical question was the whole company and it was answered. The FDA's September 2025 refusal to approve (a Complete Response Letter) cited observations from a routine general site inspection of Catalent Indiana, the third-party contractor that fills the vials. Scholar Rock's disclosure states those observations were 'not specific to apitegromab' and that the letter 'did not cite any other approvability concerns'. This is the most fixable category of regulatory refusal that exists: nothing was wrong with the medicine.

Second, the fix is structural rather than promissory. Scholar Rock did not sit and wait for Catalent to be cured. It resubmitted on 31 March 2026 with a second U.S.-based fill-finish facility written into the application itself - a site the company describes as 'producing numerous commercial products and in good standing with both the FDA and EMA'. The FDA accepted that resubmission with a 30 September 2026 action date. Changes to the filing were 'limited in scope and primarily composed of a standard safety update', and no advisory committee has been convened, which is the usual signature of a narrow technical review.

Third, and this is where we think the market is currently wrong, the American decision is not gated on Catalent. Scholar Rock's 20 July 2026 release said Europe is waiting because the European filing named only Catalent Indiana - and in the same breath reaffirmed that the second site is already inside the U.S. application with the September date intact. The stock nonetheless fell from $52.86 on 17 July to $47.67 on 24 July, about 10%, and is down 16% from $56.71 on 10 July. Investors sold an American catalyst on European news. That is the entry.

Fourth, the company is funded through the event and positioned for the launch. Cash, equivalents and marketable securities stood at $479.9 million on 31 March 2026, up from $367.6 million at year-end 2025, on $111.8 million of at-the-market equity sales plus a $200 million term loan maturing in 2032. A further $150 million delayed-draw commitment unlocks on approval. General and administrative spending has climbed from $19.0 million in the fourth quarter of 2024 to $50.2 million in the first quarter of 2026 - that is a real commercial organisation being built, not a promise.

On top of the base case sits optionality the market is paying almost nothing for. The Phase 2 EMBRAZE trial showed statistically significant lean-mass preservation when apitegromab was added to tirzepatide-driven weight loss (+4.2 lbs of lean mass, 54.9% preservation, p=0.001) - the central unsolved problem of the obesity-drug era. SRK-439, a purpose-built subcutaneous version, reports Phase 1 data in the second half of 2026, and a Phase 2 trial in facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy began mid-2026.

Positioning helps too: roughly 14.9 million shares are sold short, about 14% of the tradeable float at roughly nine days to cover. An approval forces that cover into a stock with no natural sellers.

Conditions that must hold: the FDA must be satisfied with the second fill-finish site, including any pre-approval inspection of it; no new, non-manufacturing question can surface in the final weeks of review; and the agency must act by 30 September rather than extend the clock.
SRRK.bear_thesis:
The catalyst fails and the stock retraces to roughly $28 - a 41% loss from $47.67 - with a genuine tail below that. The bear case is not that the medicine does not work. It is that this is a $5.7 billion company whose entire value rests on a regulatory decision it does not control, with $2.29 per share of net cash underneath it and nothing else.

Start with the loose thread. The FDA re-inspected Catalent Indiana in April 2026, and Scholar Rock's own guidance was that a classification normally follows within 90 days. As of the 20 July 2026 release, more than 90 days later, there was still no classification. Catalent had been placed in the FDA's most adverse inspection category, 'official action indicated'. The plain reading is that the agency was not satisfied at re-inspection, or is not finished. Either way, an unresolved manufacturing dispute is sitting in the middle of this filing ten weeks before the decision.

The more serious unknown is the second site. Scholar Rock has never named it, and has never disclosed whether the FDA requires a pre-approval inspection of it or whether such an inspection has occurred. If that inspection is outstanding, the September date can slip for reasons entirely separate from Catalent, and outside investors have no way to check. The company's single most load-bearing claim - that the site is in good standing with both regulators - is taken purely on trust.

There is also a tell in the sequencing. In January 2026 the plan was to add the second facility later in the year through a supplemental filing. By March it had been folded into the main resubmission. That was the right call, but it implies management had already stopped believing Catalent would be cured in time. The primary path today is the contingency plan.

The financing structure makes failure compound. The $150 million delayed-draw term loan is available only 'from the date of FDA approval' - it is a facility that vanishes in exactly the scenario where it is needed. Cash of $479.9 million against roughly $105 to $110 million of quarterly burn is four to five quarters. Management guides to 'into 2027', which is true and materially incomplete: it funds the decision, not a launch. A second refusal therefore forces an equity raise into a collapsed price. Dilution is already running - the weighted share count has gone from about 99.8 million in the fourth quarter of 2024 to roughly 119.8 million today.

Finally, valuation offers no protection. The stock is up 76% from its $27.07 refusal-day low and six-fold from the pre-data $7.42. At $47.67 the enterprise is worth about $5.44 billion against analyst peak-sales estimates for apitegromab in SMA that cluster around $1.4 to $1.5 billion - roughly 3.6 times peak sales for a product that has not been approved. A great deal of good news is in the price. The 14% short position that helps on the way up accelerates the move on the way down.

What would confirm the bear case: the 6 August 2026 second-quarter call disclosing an outstanding pre-approval inspection of the second site, a further extension of the action date, confirmation that Catalent Indiana was not reclassified alongside a European refiling, or any FDA information request touching matters other than manufacturing.

Method one, the tape. This experiment has already been run. Approval on or before 30 September 2026 - 78% likelihood, $63 per share. Hard second refusal - 7% likelihood, $28 per share, as built in the adverse sum-of-the-parts above.

SRRK.risk_reward:
Upside to the event-resolved target of $62 to $63 is +$15 per share, or +31% from the $47.67 last close. Downside to the verified floor of $28 is -$19.67 per share, or -41%. The raw payoff ratio is therefore 0.77 to 1 - inverted, meaning you risk more dollars than you stand to make on a single resolution.

What makes the trade work is the odds, not the payoff. Probability-weighted, the expected gain is 0.78 x $15.33 = $11.96 and the expected loss is 0.15 x $9.67 plus 0.07 x $19.67 = $2.83, for a net expected value of +$9.13 per share, or +19% over 65 days. That is an outstanding annualised expected return, but it is earned by being right roughly four times in five rather than by a large payoff when right.

This distinction matters for sizing. A classic defined-risk special situation lets you risk one to make three with a contractual floor. This does the reverse: it risks 1.3 to make 1, with a floor that is an estimate rather than a guarantee. Size it as a position that can lose 40% in a single session, because it can.
